A public, bilingual (English + Urdu) digital textbook for the B.Ed (4-Year) programme. Use the sidebar to browse Semester → Course → Unit, switch language with the اردو / English toggle in the top bar, and search the whole book. Content is authored Semesters 1–4 first; all 8 semesters are scaffolded, and un-authored units are marked coming soon.

This guide explains how to use the B.Ed Mega Textbook platform as a student - from finding your way around the site, to joining a class, submitting work, reading your grades, and using your personal dashboard. Navigate the platform Join a class Submit work Read your grades Use the dashboard If something in this guide doesn't match what you see on screen, the app itself is always the source of truth - this guide describes the intended behaviour, not every detail of the interface.

Your teacher will give you a short join code for their class. To use it: Go to Classes from the app navigation and choose "Join a class." Enter the code exactly as given. If the code is valid, you're enrolled immediately and the class appears in your list - including on your dashboard's Home area. If the code doesn't work, double-check it with your teacher - the same message appears whether a code was mistyped, has expired, or belongs to an archived class, so nothing about why it failed is revealed to a stranger guessing codes. If you were previously removed from a class by your teacher, re-entering the same code won't re-add you - ask your teacher to restore you instead.

The site has two kinds of pages: The textbook - organized by semester, then course, then unit. Use the sidebar or search to find any unit's content, activities, and assessments. Your personal pages - reachable from the navbar once you're signed in: "Dashboard" (your classes, assignments, grades, progress, history, and achievements) and "Guide" (this guide). Use the locale dropdown in the top-right corner to switch between English and Urdu at any time - every page, including your dashboard, renders in either language with correct right-to-left layout in Urdu. If you're signed in as a teacher or admin and open the student dashboard by mistake, you'll see a notice pointing you back to your own tools instead of a broken page.

Your Grades area (part of the dashboard) lists every assignment and quiz you've had marked, across every class, with the mark and the maximum possible for each. Your dashboard Home also previews your 5 most recent results. A few things are true everywhere your grades are shown: No class or cohort average is ever displayed alongside your mark - only your own result. If a teacher corrects a grade after returning it, you always see the corrected value, never the original. Quiz scores are computed automatically the moment you submit an attempt; assignment marks appear once your teacher grades your submission.

Every topic page in a per-topic unit ends with a "Self-assessment checklist" - a short list of "I can..." statements for that topic. Once you're signed in, each item is a live checkbox: tick it once you're confident you can do what it says. Your ticks are saved to your account and follow you across devices - tick an item on your phone, and it shows ticked the next time you open the same topic on a laptop, once you're signed in there too. The Progress area of your dashboard shows a separate completion fraction for these checklists, alongside (not combined with) your usual unit-coverage fraction - ticking every item on a topic never marks the whole unit "studied" for you; that still needs your own separate action. If you tick items while signed out, they're saved to that browser only, with a "sign in to sync across devices" note above the list. The next time you sign in on that same browser, those local ticks are copied into your account automatically, just once - so ticking something else on another device afterwards is never overwritten by an old, already-merged local tick. If a topic's wording changes later, any item whose text no longer matches what you previously ticked shows up unticked again - your other, unchanged ticks on the same topic are left exactly as you left them.

On a topic page, a unit's opening page, its assessment page, its teacher-notes page, or a course-level review page, every reader sees a "Give feedback" button - a tip above it explains the same thing this section does: select a sentence first if your comment is about that exact passage (your quote is shown back to you before you submit); leave nothing selected for a general comment on the page as a whole. After submitting, a "Give more feedback" link lets you leave a second, separate comment on the same page right away - you don't need to reload. This is separate from a teacher's "Suggest improvement" control, which is about the book's content more broadly - use "Give feedback" for a comment tied to something specific on the page you're reading. The curriculum owner reviews everything you submit and may follow up by revising the page; you can see your own feedback items and their status by returning to the same account, but you can't edit a comment once it's sent. You don't need to be signed in to use it - a signed-out visitor gets the same control with an email field in place of an account. Fill it in and submit, then check that inbox: your comment only reaches the curriculum owner once you click the confirmation link that email carries (this confirms the address is real and gives it a moment to catch spam before it enters the queue - it isn't sent anywhere else and isn't shown to any other reader).

Once a teacher publishes an assignment, it appears in your class's assignments list and on your dashboard's Assignments area. Open the assignment and enter text and/or attach a file (up to 10 MB, in an allowed format). You can edit and resubmit your work any time before the due date - a resubmission replaces your previous answer, it doesn't keep old versions. After the due date, your submission locks. Whether a late submission is still accepted depends on that specific assignment - the assignment page and your dashboard's Assignments area both state this clearly. Practice quizzes work differently: you can retake them as many times as you like before the due date, and your best score is the one that counts. Quizzes never accept attempts after their due date. Once your work is graded, the result appears in your Grades area and on your dashboard's Home preview - no separate step needed.
Your dashboard is reachable from the "Dashboard" link in the navbar once you're signed in as a student.

Every dashboard page has a menu down the left with all your areas: Home, Progress, Assignments, Grades, Achievements, Notes, My classes, and History. The area you're on is highlighted. On a phone the menu is a button that opens a panel; press Escape or tap outside it to close.

Enter a join code from your teacher here and you're added to the class straight away, without leaving the dashboard. The same page lists the classes you're currently in. If a code is wrong, already used, or you were removed from that class, the page tells you which.

Your own private notes, visible only to you. Write a general note here, or add a note about a specific unit or topic from the button at the bottom of that page in the textbook; page notes appear here tagged to their course so you can filter by course. You can edit or delete any note.

The first screen you see: your current semester (the highest semester among your active classes), the classes you're enrolled in, anything due soon (items due within 48 hours are listed first), and your 5 most recent grades. If nothing is due, it says so plainly instead of showing a blank area.

Every published assignment and quiz you haven't yet completed, across all your active classes, soonest-due first. Overdue items are clearly marked, and each one states whether a late submission is still accepted or the window has closed - a closed item is never shown as something you can still act on.
Every returned mark, with no class or cohort average shown anywhere. A corrected grade always shows the corrected value.

For each course, how many of its units you've covered - through graded work, a quiz, or your own self-marking - as a simple fraction (e.g. "4 of 8 units"), plus how many of your courses show any progress at all. Courses you have marked any unit studied in are listed here even if you are not in a class for them. Per-topic self-assessment checklists you have completed also show against their course. You can mark any unit "studied" directly from this page, or from that unit's own page in the textbook - either way, a unit only ever counts once toward your coverage, no matter how many times or through how many different ways you complete it.

Once a class's term ends and it's archived, it moves here - a frozen, read-only record of that semester's classes, grades, and coverage exactly as they stood at the time. Nothing here can be edited or resubmitted.

Four milestones are available to every student: your first submission, a 3-day self-study streak, reaching 100% coverage in a course, and completing every assignment in a class on time. Earned badges are marked as such; for ones you haven't earned yet, this page tells you how to reach them. A newly earned badge also appears as a small preview on Home.

This guide explains how to use the B.Ed Mega Textbook platform as a teacher - from managing classes and assignments, to grading, using your teacher dashboard, giving feedback and suggesting improvements to the book, and what becoming a verified teacher unlocks. Manage classes and assignments Grade submissions Use the teacher dashboard Give feedback and suggest improvements Verified-teacher material If something in this guide doesn't match what you see on screen, the app itself is always the source of truth - this guide describes the intended behaviour, not every detail of the interface.
Three controls can appear on book content pages while you're signed in as a teacher - two are teacher-only, and one you share with students, since teachers are readers too.

Available on every book page, including course-overview pages - click it, pick a category (typo, clarity, factual, pedagogy, translation, or other), and write a short note. The page's slug, the nearest section heading, and the page's current language are all captured automatically; you never type these in yourself. Find every suggestion you've filed, and its current status, in "My Suggestions" on your teacher dashboard. An admin moderates every suggestion through submitted → under review → accepted or rejected, and - once any resulting content change ships - published. You'll see the new status and any note the admin left the next time you check "My Suggestions."

Available on a unit's activity, formative, or summative page (not on a course-overview page, since feedback is about one specific activity). Rate it 1–5, note what worked and what didn't, and record how long it actually took. You can reach this same control from a teaching-log entry for that activity too. Re-rating an activity you've already rated updates your one record - it doesn't create a second one. An admin can see the average rating and every recorded issue across all teachers who've rated an activity, to help prioritise which content to revise.

Available on a topic page, a per-topic unit's opening page, its assessment page, its teacher-notes page, or a course-level review page - every reader sees this: students, teachers, and a signed-out visitor alike, not only teachers. Use it for a comment tied to something specific on the page you're reading: leave it on the page as a whole, or select a sentence first (a tip above the button says the same thing) and then click the button to attach your comment to exactly that quoted passage. After submitting, "Give more feedback" lets you leave another, separate comment on the same page without reloading. This is a different control from the two above, and they don't overlap: "Suggest improvement" is a general note about the book's quality on any page (a typo, a factual issue, a pedagogy concern); "Give feedback on this activity" is a teacher-only rating of one specific activity/formative/ summative page. "Give feedback" here is neither - it's a reader's comment on a specific piece of page content, and the curriculum owner triages it separately from both of the others. You can see your own submitted items and their status by returning to the same account, but a comment can't be edited once it's sent. Signed out? The same button still works, with an email field in place of an account - fill it in, submit, then click the confirmation link that address is sent before your comment reaches the curriculum owner's queue. That address is used only for that confirmation and any follow-up the owner chooses to make; it's never shown to any other reader.
Open an assignment's grading queue from its class page to see every actively enrolled student, each shown as not-yet-submitted, submitted, late, or already graded.

Entering a mark and feedback returns the submission to the student in the same action - there is no separate "save draft" step. A mark can't exceed the assignment's own maximum; the system rejects an out-of-range entry and asks for a valid one. You can go back and correct an already-returned grade at any time; the student's next visit shows the corrected value.
If a student's account has since been deleted, their past submissions and grades remain in the gradebook exactly as they were, just displayed without identifying them by name.

If you hold the verified-teacher capability, the official correct-answer reference or marking rubric for a formative or summative unit item is available directly from the grading queue - see Verified-teacher material for what this capability covers and how to get it.
Your classes and assignments live under "Classes" (/app/classes), reachable from the navbar once you're signed in as a teacher.

Create a class by choosing its course from the dropdown (courses are grouped by semester and show their full name; a course with no teaching content yet is not offered), then a name and a term label. Each class gets a join code your students use to enrol themselves - you can reissue a new code at any time (the old one stops working immediately) or revoke it entirely without affecting students already enrolled. From the roster page you can edit a class's name and term. A class can be archived once its term ends, and reactivated later if you're still an eligible teacher; an archived class becomes fully read-only.

Each class has a roster of enrolled students. You can remove a student (their past submissions and grades stay intact, just marked as no longer active) and restore a removed student later - a student cannot rejoin a class they were removed from just by re-entering the join code.

From a class, create an assignment drawn from a unit's activity, formative, or summative item - or a custom assignment with no unit attached. Set a due date, a maximum mark, and whether late submissions are still accepted. You can save an assignment's settings as a template and reuse it later with "from a template" on the create form. After creating an assignment you can edit its title, instructions, due date, maximum mark, and late policy, or delete it - deletion is only allowed while the assignment has no submissions; once a student has submitted, unpublish it instead. Select several assignments with their checkboxes to publish, unpublish, or close them in one action. You can publish or unpublish an assignment at any time, including after students have already submitted work; unpublishing never touches existing submissions or grades. Quizzes are a separate assignment type, scored automatically from a unit's question bank - no manual grading needed for those.

A full gradebook view and a downloadable spreadsheet export are both available from the class page - every student against every assignment, including students who have since been removed, so nothing in the historical record disappears.

Every unit on this platform passes through a set of review gates before it is published. Two of them are judgement calls that a person has to make: G3, the English review, and G5, the Urdu review. The reviewer capability is what lets someone other than the curriculum owner make those calls. Like verified-teacher status, it is granted only by an admin, and it is not something you can switch on for yourself.

One page: Review queue, which lists the units waiting for a G3 or a G5. Open a unit from there and you get what you need to review it - the English text for a G3, and for a G5 the English and the Urdu side by side, so you are comparing rather than reading each in turn. When you are done you choose one of three outcomes: Certify - the unit passes this gate. Request revision - it goes back for rework. Two rounds of this are allowed before the unit is escalated instead. Escalate - the decision is not yours to make. It reaches the curriculum owner, who owns review policy and escalations.

Nothing else. Holding the reviewer capability does not let you: write or edit any unit, grant a capability to anyone, including yourself, change anyone's role, see answer keys or any other restricted teaching material (that is the separate verified-teacher capability), or change a review someone else has already certified. A reviewer judges work. A reviewer does not change work, and does not decide who else may judge it.

You will not be offered a G5 on a unit whose G3 is still open, and the system will refuse a G5 certification that does not name the accepted G3 it was made against. The reason is worth knowing rather than working around: an Urdu review is a comparison against a specific English version. If the English has not itself been accepted, there is nothing settled to compare against, and a G5 made against a moving target tells nobody anything. If the queue will not offer you a G5 you were expecting, its G3 is what is missing.
documents.s: A G5 needs its G3 first

documents.t: This is the part that surprises people. When you certify, nothing on the site changes. Instead you get two downloads: the certification itself, which records what you checked and what you found, and a single line for the unit's tracker. Both are committed to the project's repository through its ordinary review process, the same way the content itself is. That is deliberate. A review is evidence, and evidence that can be changed quietly afterwards is not worth much; putting it in version control means every certification is permanent, attributable and readable long after the fact, including by you. It also means the curriculum owner stays in the loop for the commit - but committing a batch of certifications takes minutes, where reviewing the units they represent takes days. That difference is the entire point of the capability.
documents.s: Certifying produces two files, not a change

documents.t: Two things: You are recorded. Your initials, the courses and stages you are qualified for, and the evidence you were qualified on are written down in the project's reviewer record. Your certifications carry those initials. You are qualified on real units first. You review two or three units the curriculum owner has already reviewed, without seeing their findings, and the two sets are compared. Agreement matters; passing a unit that the owner failed matters more. That comparison is what qualification means here, and it is recorded alongside your entry. If you think you should hold this capability and do not, contact your platform administrator.
Your teacher dashboard is reachable from the "Teacher Dashboard" link in the navbar once you're signed in as a teacher.

Every teacher page has a menu down the left: Overview, Classes, Assignments, Grading, Analytics, Quiz authoring, Teaching log, and Feedback & suggestions. The area you're on is highlighted; on a phone it opens from a button. You never need to type a web address by hand to reach Analytics or a student's record - use the menu, or the links on the Overview.

The first screen you see: an ungraded-submission count for each of your classes shown separately (never combined into one total), the 5 soonest-due assignments across all your classes, and a feed of your students' 10 most recent submissions and quiz attempts. Each class row links straight to its Analytics, Roster, and Grading queue. If nothing is pending, it says so plainly instead of showing a blank area.

Open the command centre for one class to see, in one place, its number of students, the students flagged at risk (with the reason and a link to each one's record), and its next due dates. It links out to the full Analytics, the Grading queue, and the Roster.
These reuse the same Classes area covered in Manage classes and assignments and Grade submissions - the Overview's links take you straight there.

Log a classroom activity in one quick flow - which unit/activity, which class, the date, how long it took, and a short reflection - and see your own log ordered most-recent-first. Logging is independent of assignments; you can log an activity you never assigned formally.

"My Suggestions" lists every improvement suggestion you've filed against the book, with its current status (submitted, under review, accepted, rejected, or published) and any note an admin left. Alongside it, your own Activity Feedback history shows every book activity you've rated.

Open Analytics for one class to see the score distribution per assignment, each student's trend over time, a unit-by-unit class average, and an advisory flag on any student who appears to be struggling - each flag comes with a plain-language reason (either two or more missed deadlines, or a run of three declining scores). This flag is visible only to you; it never appears on a student's own dashboard.
From within a class's Analytics, open one student's record to see their submissions, grades, and unit coverage for that class together, with nothing from any other class mixed in.

If your account is a verified teacher, Quiz authoring lets you write the quiz-item bank and the answer keys for a unit. Choose a course and a unit, then add or edit multiple-choice items (a question, its options, and which option is correct) and the formative and summative marking guidance. Students taking a quiz never see the correct option. If your account is not yet verified, the page explains how to get verified; an unverified teacher and a student cannot author or even read this material.

Every teacher can create classes, assign work, and grade - that's the teacher role itself, and it needs no special approval. A separate capability, verified teacher, unlocks access to restricted material: The official correct-answer reference or marking rubric for a formative or summative unit item, shown directly in the grading queue. The correct-answer data behind practice quizzes (the quiz questions themselves are visible to everyone; only the correct-answer reference is restricted). Verified-teacher status is granted only by an admin - it isn't something you can switch on for yourself, and it doesn't change anything else about your account or your classes. If you believe you should have this capability and don't, contact your platform administrator.

This track holds material assessed by the Sindh Teaching Licence test that the approved 2026 B.Ed (4-Year) scheme does not teach. It is kept apart from the degree programme deliberately. Filing a licence course inside a semester folder would put a false claim in the URL and in the sidebar: that the course is part of the approved scheme. It is not. Everything here is offered because you may be examined on it, not because your degree covers it.

Course Why it is in this track EED-313 Classroom Management Assessed by the licence test; restructured out of the 2026 scheme, so it has no degree course to live in GENG-300 Functional English General Education course in Semester 1 of the B.Ed (4-Year) scheme; assessed by the licence test

Nothing in this track counts toward the B.Ed. Your credit hours, your semester plan and your transcript come from the main textbook, which follows the approved scheme exactly. Use this track to prepare for the licence test, and the main textbook for your programme. Where a topic appears in both, the degree course is the authoritative treatment for your coursework. This track exists to cover what the degree leaves out, not to restate what it already teaches.
documents.s: How this relates to your degree

documents.t: Licence track. This course is not part of the approved 2026 B.Ed scheme. It was EED-313, a Foundation course in the 2025 scheme, which the 2026 revision restructured away with no successor. The Sindh Teaching Licence (Elementary) test still assesses it, at the weight of two sampled constructed-response items, which is why it is authored here rather than inside a degree course.

Four units are specified and not yet authored: Learning theories and classroom management Curriculum and classroom management Routines, schedules, and time management in diverse classrooms Creating shared values and community The unit specifications are in specs/content/eed-313/content-spec.md, and the licence-syllabus mapping is in specs/content/licence-blueprint.md.

This unit asks a question most teacher-training courses leave until the end: before you manage a classroom, what do you believe about how learning happens? Your answer shapes every management choice you make, whether you have thought about it or not. The unit starts there. It sets out the three main accounts of how humans learn, not so you can pick a side, but so you can see what each one makes visible and what each one leaves out. From that base it builds a definition of classroom management centred on learning rather than on quiet, then takes you into a real classroom to practise reading what is actually going on, and closes with the deliberate design of the space your pupils will learn in.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Name the three major learning theories, state what each says learning is, and give one classroom example of each in action. Explain why all three theories still have classroom validity, and what a teacher loses if they rely on only one. Define classroom management as a means of maximising student learning, and distinguish it from discipline. Use a simple observation protocol to record the physical and social features of a described classroom, and separate what you saw from what you inferred. Identify the key features of a well-managed classroom, and analyse a described environment well enough to propose one grounded change. Propose a small, purposeful change to a classroom's physical or social environment and justify it by reference to a learning theory.
None beyond intermediate-level study skills. The unit assumes you have sat in classrooms as a pupil but have not yet studied learning theory. Every technical term is defined where it first appears.

Topic 1.1 - How humans learn: three theories - what learning is, and what behaviourism, cognitivism and constructivism each say about it; why a teacher needs all three. Topic 1.2 - What classroom management is, and is not - management as maximising learning rather than producing compliance; how a teacher's philosophy shapes their management beliefs; the discipline/management distinction. Topic 1.3 - Reading a real classroom - classroom observation, collecting and recording data, and the physical and social features that carry management weight. Topic 1.4 - Designing the environment on purpose - resources, displays, seating arrangements, and using the physical and social environment to support learning.

The four topics are designed to be worked through in order. Topic 1.2's definition of classroom management draws on the three theories from Topic 1.1; Topic 1.3's observation protocol assumes that definition; and Topic 1.4's design work applies everything that came before. Each topic is one complete learning cycle and takes roughly one sitting. The six hours of classroom observation the guide asks for in Week 2 are built into Topic 1.3 as a structured observation protocol you can carry out in a practicum school, a peer's micro-teach, or a recorded lesson if a live classroom is not available to you. The question bank at the end of the unit covers all four topics together. Its answers and mark schemes are in a clearly marked section at the foot of that page; try each item before you read them.

textbook.com.pk Mr Karim teaches Class 3 Urdu in a government primary school in Ghotki. On Monday he introduces a new letter. He says the sound, the class repeats it, he praises the rows that say it clearly, and the rows that falter try again. On Wednesday he introduces the same letter, but this time he asks the class what words they already know that begin with its sound, writes their suggestions on the board, and groups them by pattern. On Friday he gives each pair a set of picture cards and asks them to sort the pictures into "starts with the letter" and "does not start with the letter", then explain their grouping to another pair. Three lessons, three different ideas about what learning is. This topic names those ideas.

Before we name the theories, notice something about Mr Karim's week. He did not contradict himself. Each lesson described a real part of how learning happens: sometimes a pupil needs to practise a response until it sticks, sometimes they need to connect new material to what they already know, and sometimes they need to build the idea for themselves. The three theories below describe those three parts. They compete only if you insist that learning is one single thing.

You arrived in this classroom with years of experience of being taught. That experience has given you beliefs about how learning works, and most of them are half-true. Common ones: "children learn by doing", "practice makes perfect", "a quiet class is a learning class". None of these is wrong. None is the whole story. The reason to surface your beliefs now is that a teacher who has not examined them teaches on autopilot: they manage the classroom for the kind of learning they assume is happening, and miss the rest. Each theory below gives you a lens. The skill is knowing which lens a moment needs.

Behaviourism says that learning is a change in observable behaviour produced by the interaction between a stimulus and a response, shaped by what follows the response. What happens inside the mind is set aside as unobservable; what matters is what the learner does, and whether that doing is reinforced or not. In the classroom this looks like: clear modelling of a target response, repetition, immediate feedback, and reinforcement that makes the wanted response more likely to recur. Mr Karim's Monday lesson is a clean example: he models the sound, the class repeats it, he praises the correct response, and the rows that falter try again until they get it right. The teacher's job, on this account, is to arrange the environment so the right responses are practised and reinforced and the wrong ones are not. Evertson and Emmer (2009) describe this as the backbone of classroom routines and procedures, where consistent practice of expected behaviour builds the automatic responses that keep a classroom running. Behaviourism is strongest where the learning target is a repeatable skill or a clear procedure: letter formation, multiplication tables, lab safety steps, the routine for entering a classroom. It is weakest where the target is understanding, interpretation, or the ability to apply an idea in a new setting.
documents.s: Behaviourism: learning as a change in visible behaviour

documents.t: Cognitivism says that learning is not a change in behaviour but a change in the way information is organised inside the mind. The learner receives information, processes it against what is already stored, and reorganises those internal structures. Behaviour may or may not change as a result; the learning itself is the reorganisation. In the classroom this looks like: activating what pupils already know before introducing something new, organising material so its structure is visible, managing the limited space of working memory, and giving learners strategies for storing and retrieving what they learn. Mr Karim's Wednesday lesson does this: he activates prior knowledge ("what words begin with this sound?"), makes the letter-sound pattern visible on the board, and groups examples so the structure can be seen. The teacher's job, on this account, is to present material in a way the mind can actually process: not too much at once, clearly structured, and connected to existing understanding. Ertmer and Newby (1993) describe the shift from behaviourism to cognitivism as a shift in focus from what the teacher does to the learner to what the learner does with what is presented. Cognitivism is strongest where the learning target is understanding a concept, seeing a relationship, or applying a known procedure to a familiar type of problem. It is weakest where the target requires the learner to build a genuinely new idea that does not yet connect to anything in their experience.
documents.s: Cognitivism: learning as the building and reorganising of mental structures

documents.t: Constructivism says that learning is the active construction of meaning by the learner. Knowledge is not transferred intact from teacher to pupil; each learner builds their own understanding by acting on material, testing it against experience, and revising it when it does not hold. Other people, including the teacher, are a resource in that process, not its source. In the classroom this looks like: a task that requires the learner to do the intellectual work, opportunities to talk through emerging understanding, comparison of one learner's construction with another's, and revision in light of evidence. Mr Karim's Friday lesson does this: the pairs sort picture cards, build a grouping rule, and explain it to another pair, who may have grouped differently. The teacher's job, on this account, is to design the task and the social conditions in which construction happens, then listen carefully enough to hear what the learner is actually building, which is not always what you intended. Ertmer and Newby (1993) stress that on this account the learner's prior knowledge and the social context of the activity are not add-ons; they are the mechanism by which learning occurs. Constructivism is strongest where the learning target is deep understanding, the ability to transfer an idea to an unfamiliar context, or the capacity to work with others on an open task. It is weakest where time is short, the target is a fixed procedure, or the learner does not yet have the prior knowledge the construction requires.
documents.s: Constructivism: learning as the building of personal meaning

documents.t: The single most important idea in this topic is that the three theories describe different parts of the same process, not competing claims about the whole of it. Ertmer and Newby (1993) map them along a continuum: behaviourism best explains the acquisition of foundational responses and procedures, cognitivism best explains the organisation and storage of information, and constructivism best explains the transfer and application of understanding to new situations. A teacher who relies on behaviourism alone produces pupils who can perform a procedure but cannot explain when to use it. A teacher who relies on constructivism alone asks pupils to "discover" things that are more efficiently told. A fluent teacher moves between the three as the learning target demands: drills a routine until it is automatic (behaviourism), makes the structure of a new topic visible (cognitivism), and then sets a task that requires pupils to use that structure in a context the teacher did not fully specify (constructivism). Common misconception. "Behaviourism was disproved and constructivism replaced it." It was not, and it did not. What happened is that researchers kept finding kinds of learning the earlier account could not explain well, and added a new lens. The earlier lens still works for what it was built for. A well-managed classroom uses all three. textbook.com.pk The figure above takes Mr Karim's letter-sound lesson and reads it through all three lenses at once. The management move each lens implies is different, and a skilled teacher draws on all three across a single week.
documents.s: Why all three have classroom validity

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Take the following short lesson description: The teacher introduces the concept of "halves" to Class 2. She has a chart, a set of paper shapes, and a basket of real fruit. Now plan this lesson three ways, one from each theoretical stance. For each version, decide: what the teacher does first, what the pupils do, and what success looks like. Allow 25 minutes. Then, as a group, identify one thing that all three versions have in common and one thing that genuinely differs.

In one sentence each, state what behaviourism, cognitivism and constructivism say learning is. (Remember) A friend says, "Constructivism is just the newest theory, so it is the best one." Using the idea of a continuum, explain what is wrong with that claim. (Understand) A teacher drills multiplication tables every morning for ten minutes. Name which theory this serves best, and explain why it is a defensible use of that theory. (Apply) Look at Mr Karim's Friday lesson. Identify one moment that is best read through a constructivist lens, and explain what the teacher would have to do differently to teach the same content from a behaviourist stance. (Analyze) Give one example from your own schooling of a task that asked you to build understanding yourself rather than repeat a modelled response. Name the theory it served. (Apply)

Behaviourism treats learning as a change in visible behaviour shaped by reinforcement; it is the right lens for building automatic routines and practised skills. Cognitivism treats learning as the reorganisation of mental structures; it is the right lens for making new information processable and connectable. Constructivism treats learning as the active construction of personal meaning; it is the right lens for deep understanding and transfer. The three describe different parts of one process, and a well-managed classroom draws on all three as the learning target demands.

I can state what each of the three theories says learning is, without mixing them up. I can explain why the three theories complement rather than replace each other. I can recognise which theory a described classroom moment is drawing on. I can reject the claim that constructivism has simply made the other two obsolete. I can give a classroom example where each theory is the most useful lens.

Over one full lesson, keep a tally of every management move the teacher makes. For each one, mark it B (it shapes a visible response), C (it makes the structure of the material visible or connects to prior knowledge), or K (it asks pupils to build understanding themselves). At the end, note which letter dominates and write two sentences on whether that dominance fitted the lesson's learning target. Do not mark anything the teacher does that is not a management move. And do not discuss your tally with the teacher unless they ask.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 350 to 400 words on the following. Describe a single topic you might teach in a lower-primary class. Explain how you would teach it once from a behaviourist stance and once from a constructivist stance. Then argue which of two would be more appropriate for a class you know, giving one concrete reason drawn from the pupils or the setting. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Grasp of the two theories (Understand) States accurately what each theory says learning is and what the teacher does in each version Quality of the two lesson versions (Apply) Both versions are concrete and genuinely reflect the theory claimed, not just labelled Fit to context (Analyze) Argues for one version using a specific feature of the described pupils or setting, not a generic preference Register and clarity Writes for a peer, defines any technical term used, stays within the word count

Ertmer, P. A., & Newby, T. J. (1993). Behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism: Comparing critical features from an instructional design perspective. Performance Improvement Quarterly, 6(4), 50-72. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1937-8327.1993.tb00605.x - maps the three theories onto a continuum and is the canonical comparison for Topic 1.1. Evertson, C. M., & Emmer, E. T. (2009). Classroom management for elementary teachers (8th ed.). Pearson. Chapter 1 sets out the learning-theory foundations of classroom management.

textbook.com.pk Two Class 5 teachers in the same school in Multan manage their classrooms very differently. Mrs Ahsan spends the first week of term establishing routines: how to enter, where to put homework, what to do when you have a question. She practises them until they are automatic. By October, the class runs itself for long stretches while she works with a small group. Mrs Bashir spends the first week on rules and consequences, and spends October responding to the breaches. Both care about their pupils. Only one of them is managing the classroom in the sense this course uses the term.

The guide defines the best-managed classroom as one "in which each learner is effectively engaged in constructing knowledge" (ClassroomMgmt_Sept13.txt:128-136). That definition is the spine of this whole course, and it is narrower and more demanding than most people assume.

Classroom management, as this course uses the phrase, is the set of teacher actions whose purpose is to create the conditions in which student learning can happen and to keep those conditions in place. Notice what that definition puts at the centre: not order, not quiet, not compliance, but learning. Order and quiet are sometimes useful means to that end; they are not the end itself. Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) found that the strongest single predictor of pupil learning was not the severity of the rules but the quality of the teacher's management of time, space, transitions and engagement. In other words, the teacher who manages the classroom well is the teacher who has arranged things so that more pupils are actually doing more of the intellectual work for more of the time. This is a demanding standard. A silent class in which every pupil is copying from the board is orderly but not necessarily well managed, because copying is not the same as learning. A class in which pupils are arguing about a problem in small groups is noisy but may be very well managed, because the noise is the sound of the intellectual work happening.

The guide asks a question most training programmes skip: how does your personal philosophy about teaching and learning affect your beliefs about classroom management? (ClassroomMgmt_Sept13.txt:170-172). The answer is that it determines what you treat as the problem. If you believe learning is the transfer of knowledge from teacher to pupil, then the management problem is keeping attention on the teacher, and a pupil looking away is the thing to correct. If you believe learning is the pupil's active construction, then the management problem is keeping the task demanding enough that construction can happen, and a pupil sitting quietly is not necessarily a pupil learning. Neither philosophy is wrong, but each produces a different classroom. The guide's point is not that you must pick one. It is that you must know which one is driving your management at any given moment, because a teacher who has not chosen a philosophy manages by habit, and habit is shaped by how they were taught, not by what their current pupils need. Wong and Wong (1998) put this practically: a teacher with a consistent, conscious management plan spends the first weeks of term teaching the plan, and the rest of the year teaching the curriculum. A teacher without one spends the whole year re-establishing control.
documents.s: How a personal philosophy of teaching shapes management beliefs

documents.t: A well-managed classroom has a handful of observable features, and they are about learning, not about silence: Routines are in place and practised. Pupils know what to do when they enter, when they need help, when they finish early, and the teacher does not have to give the instruction more than once. Evertson and Emmer (2009) treat this as the single most productive management investment a teacher makes in the first weeks. The intellectual demand is high and the disruption is low. Pupils are doing work that requires thought, and the transitions between activities are smooth enough that little time is lost. The teacher is watching. Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) use the term "withitness" for a teacher's accurate awareness of what is happening across the whole room and their willingness to act on it early. The environment supports the learning. The physical and social arrangements, which Topic 1.4 examines, are set up to make the intended learning easier, not harder. Common misconception. "A well-managed classroom is one where nothing unexpected happens." The opposite is closer to the truth. A well-managed classroom is one in which the teacher has built enough routine and enough trust that unexpected things can be handled without the learning falling apart. Surprises are a feature of classrooms; a teacher's management is measured by how they respond, not by whether they prevent every one. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: What happens in a well-managed classroom

documents.t: Discipline and classroom management are not the same thing, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes a new teacher makes. The figure above maps the difference. Classroom management is proactive. It is the teacher's work before and during learning to create the conditions in which learning can happen: the routines, the seating, the pacing, the clarity of the task. It acts on the environment and on the structure of the lesson. Classroom discipline is reactive. It is the teacher's response after a pupil has breached a norm: the reminder, the consequence, the conversation. It acts on the individual pupil's behaviour. The purpose differs too. The purpose of management is to maximise learning time. The purpose of discipline is to restore a norm that has been broken. Success in management looks like a class that runs itself for long stretches. Success in discipline looks like a pupil who understands what went wrong and is trusted to do better. This matters because a teacher who relies almost entirely on discipline is a teacher who spends their day reacting. A teacher who invests in management spends the first weeks building routines and the rest of the year teaching. The guide is explicit: "In its narrowest sense, classroom management is defined in terms of disciplining and controlling students. However, this course places the goal of student learning at the heart of classroom management" (ClassroomMgmt_Sept13.txt:128-136). Common misconception. "Discipline and management are the same thing." They are not. Discipline is a small and necessary part of management, but a classroom can be tightly disciplined and poorly managed if the pupils are quiet but not learning.
documents.s: How classroom discipline and classroom management differ

documents.t: Work in pairs. Below are eight short descriptions of a teacher's action. For each one, decide whether it is primarily an act of management (proactive, acts on the learning environment) or of discipline (reactive, acts on a pupil's breach), and be ready to defend the placement. The teacher practises the "hands up" routine until every pupil can do it without being asked. The teacher moves a pupil to a seat near the front after talking during group work. The teacher arranges the desks in clusters before a discussion lesson. The teacher stays behind to talk to a pupil who refused to hand in homework. The teacher writes the lesson's learning target on the board before starting. The teacher revokes break time after shouting in the corridor. The teacher prepares a "finished early" task for pupils who work quickly. The teacher sends a note home after a pupil is repeatedly late. Allow 15 minutes. Then compare with another pair and find one placement you disagree on. Spend your last five minutes on that disagreement.

In your own words, state the difference between classroom management and classroom discipline, and give one example of each. (Understand) A teacher says, "My class is silent and on task, so my management is excellent." Explain what that claim assumes about the purpose of management, and what it leaves out. (Analyze) Name the four observable features of a well-managed classroom described in this topic. (Remember) A new teacher spends most of every lesson responding to misbehaviour. Using the management/discipline distinction, explain what that teacher is likely not investing in. (Apply) Explain how a teacher who believes "learning is the teacher transferring knowledge" and a teacher who believe "learning is the pupil constructing meaning" would manage the same transition between activities differently. (Analyze)

Classroom management is the proactive work of creating and maintaining the conditions in which student learning happens. It is not the same as discipline, which is the reactive response to a breach of norms. A teacher's personal philosophy of teaching shapes what they treat as the management problem. A well-managed classroom is marked by practised routines, high intellectual demand, teacher withitness, and an environment that supports the learning, not by silence or by the absence of surprises.

I can define classroom management as maximising student learning and distinguish it from discipline. I can explain how a teacher's philosophy of teaching shapes their management choices. I can name the observable features of a well-managed classroom. I can classify a described teacher action as management or as discipline and justify the placement. I can reject the claim that a silent classroom is necessarily a well-managed one.

Over two full lessons taught by the same teacher, keep a tally of every management or discipline move you observe. Mark each one M or D. At the end, calculate the ratio and write half a page on what that ratio suggests about where the teacher invests their management effort, and whether the balance fitted the lessons you watched. Do not name the teacher or the school in your write-up.

textbook.com.pk You have been asked to observe a Class 4 lesson in a government school in Hyderabad. You have a notebook, a chair at the back, and forty minutes. The teacher has not told you what to look for. If you try to write down everything, you will capture nothing useful. If you write down only your impressions, you will capture your own assumptions, not the classroom. This topic gives you a simple protocol for seeing what is actually there.

The guide asks you to spend six hours observing a classroom, in and out of class (ClassroomMgmt_Sept13.txt:174-175). That observation is only as good as the discipline you bring to it. Without a protocol, an observer sees what they expect. With one, they see what is there.

Classroom observation, in this course, is the structured act of watching a classroom with a specific focus, recording what you see in a consistent format, and keeping a hard line between what you saw and what you inferred from it. The focus comes first. You cannot observe "the whole classroom" any more than you can photograph a city by pointing the camera in every direction at once. Before you sit down, decide what you are looking for. This topic gives you four lenses, and a sound observation uses at least two in a single visit: The physical environment. Where the furniture is, where the teacher usually stands, what is on the walls, where the resources are, how the pupils are grouped, and what the traffic paths look like when the class moves. The social environment. Who talks to whom, how the teacher addresses the class, what happens when a pupil disagrees, whether every pupil is visibly part of the room's life. Routines in action. How the lesson starts and ends, what pupils do when they need help, how transitions between activities are handled, and whether the teacher has to give the same instruction twice. Teacher withitness. Where the teacher's eyes are, whether they notice off-task behaviour early, and what they do when they do. Evertson and Poole (IRIS Center) stress that the first question in any observation is not "was this a good lesson?" but "what was actually happening here?" Judgement comes later, and only after the evidence has been recorded.
documents.s: Classroom observation: what to look for

documents.t: A usable observation record has two columns, and the discipline is to keep them separate: What I saw (observation) What I think it means (inference) The teacher stood at the front for the first 12 minutes. The teacher was in control of the pace. Three pupils in the back row talked throughout group work. Those pupils were not engaged by the task. The teacher moved to the back row and stood there. The teacher used proximity to redirect them. The left column is evidence anyone could verify. The right column is your interpretation, and it may be wrong. The three pupils in the back row may have been finishing the task together; you cannot know until you ask. Keeping the two columns apart stops you from confusing what you saw with what you hope it means. Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) describe this as the difference between data and conclusion, and treat the discipline of recording both as a core professional skill. An observer who skips the left column and writes only conclusions is an observer who will not learn from the visit.

The physical environment is the set of material features a teacher can arrange: furniture, displays, resources, lighting, and the use of wall and floor space. The figure at the start of this topic maps them on a floor plan. Each of these carries management weight. Sightlines determine whether the teacher can see every pupil and every pupil can see the board. Traffic paths determine how smoothly the class moves between activities, and a badly placed bookshelf can turn a two-minute transition into a five-minute disruption. Display walls signal what the room values: a wall of pupils' work says something different from a wall of commercial posters, and a bare wall says something different again. Resource corners determine whether pupils can get what they need without asking the teacher, which is the difference between a room that runs itself and one that depends on the teacher for every material. In a low-resource Pakistani government school, many of these features cannot be changed: the furniture is fixed, the walls are cracked, there is no budget for new displays. The management question is not "how do I get the ideal room?" but "given this room, what can I change this week?" Topic 1.4 takes that question up in detail.
documents.s: Features of classroom management: the physical environment

documents.t: The social environment is the set of relationships and norms that govern how people in the room treat each other: between teacher and pupils, among pupils, and between the class and any outsider who enters. The features that carry management weight are harder to see than the physical ones, but they are more powerful: Participation patterns. Who gets called on, who never speaks, and whether the teacher knows the difference. A room in which the same six hands go up for every question is a room in which the teacher is managing the visible few and losing the invisible many. Norms of help. Whether pupils are permitted and expected to help each other, or whether helping is treated as cheating. Evertson and Poole (IRIS Center) treat the establishment of clear norms and expectations as the foundation of the social environment. Responses to error. Whether a wrong answer is treated as a useful event or as a humiliation. A room in which it is safe to be wrong is a room in which learning can happen, because learning requires the risk of being wrong in front of someone. Belonging. Whether every pupil has a visible place in the room's life: a name the teacher uses, a task that matters, a peer group that expects them.
documents.s: Features of classroom management: the social environment

documents.t: Classroom challenges are the recurring frictions that make management harder than the clean routines in a textbook suggest. The guide names the ones a teacher in the Pakistani system meets often: Multigrade and overcrowded rooms. A teacher managing two grades in one room, or sixty pupils in a room built for thirty, is managing a different problem from the one a well-resourced single-grade textbook assumes. Resource scarcity. When there is one textbook between three pupils, the management of the textbook, not just the teaching of the content, becomes the teacher's problem. Diverse preparation. Pupils entering the same class with very different prior knowledge require the teacher to manage several levels of engagement at once. Unpredictability. The event no plan anticipates: a pupil who arrives distressed, a surprise inspection, a power cut in the middle of a carefully prepared activity. The point of naming these is not to discourage you. It is to make the case that management is not a set of tricks that work everywhere. It is the capacity to read a specific classroom and respond to what is actually happening in it, which is exactly what this topic's observation protocol is designed to build. textbook.com.pk The figure above is the observation cycle this topic has been building. It is also the cycle you will use in the practicum task below, and the cycle that turns a passive visit into a professional act.

Work in groups of three. Read the following description of a Class 5 room, then complete the two-column record the topic describes. Aim for at least four rows of evidence in the left column and a genuine inference in the right column for each. The room holds 44 pupils at benches meant for 30. The teacher, Miss Naveed, stands at the front near a worn blackboard for most of the lesson. There is one textbook for every four pupils; she reads from hers while they follow. The back two benches are in shadow because the one working tube light is at the front. The walls are bare except for a faded map of Pakistan. When a pupil at the back asks a question, Miss Naveed does not hear it. When two pupils in the middle begin to talk, she pauses, looks at them, and continues. No pupil speaks unless asked. Allow 20 minutes. Then compare your record with another group and find one row where your left columns agree but your right columns differ. That disagreement is the most useful thing in the room, so spend your last five minutes on it.

Name the four observation lenses this topic gives, and explain why an observer should use at least two in a single visit. (Remember) A classmate writes in her observation notebook: "The teacher clearly does not care about the back benches." Explain why that sentence belongs in the right column, not the left, and rewrite it as a defensible inference. (Analyze) List three features of the physical environment that carry management weight, and for each, state one thing a teacher in a low-resource government school could change this week. (Understand) The description in the Activity says no pupil speaks unless asked. Give two different inferences that observation could support, and state which further evidence would help you choose between them. (Analyze) Explain what "withitness" means, and describe one concrete behaviour from the Activity description that shows its absence. (Apply)

A classroom observation is only as good as its protocol. Decide what to look for before you sit down, record what you actually saw in a left column and what you think it means in a right column, and keep the two apart. The physical environment (sightlines, traffic paths, displays, resources) and the social environment (participation patterns, norms of help, responses to error, belonging) are the two landscapes a managed classroom shapes. The recurring challenges, from overcrowding to unpredictability, are the reason management is the capacity to read a specific room and respond to what is actually happening in it.

I can explain why an observation protocol matters and name the four lenses. I can keep observation and inference apart in a two-column record. I can identify the physical and social features of a described classroom that carry management weight. I can complete the five-step observation cycle on a described room. I can name at least three recurring classroom challenges a Pakistani government-school teacher is likely to face.

textbook.com.pk Mr Hassan teaches Class 6 in a rural school in Sanghar. His room has fixed benches in rows, a cracked blackboard, one locked cupboard, and no budget. He has been teaching in the same layout for two years and has begun to feel that the room is working against him. He cannot move the benches, but he can do more than he thinks. This topic is about what a teacher can change on purpose, even in a room that looks unchangeable.

Topic 1.3 taught you to read a classroom. This topic asks you to design one, or at least to design the small part of it that is within your power. The guide names four design acts for Week 4 (ClassroomMgmt_Sept13.txt:182-189): identify resources, use displays and visuals, arrange seating for different kinds of learning, and employ the physical and social facilities. This topic takes them in order, then adds the question that holds them together: what kind of classroom do I want?

Before you change a single thing, you need an answer to the guide's question: what kind of classroom environment do I want? (ClassroomMgmt_Sept13.txt:181). That question is not about furniture. It is about the learning you are trying to make possible. If your answer is "I want a room in which pupils can practise procedures until they are automatic", then the environment you design will look one way: clear sightlines to the board, a routine for retrieving and returning materials, a seating arrangement that makes repetition easy. If your answer is "I want a room in which pupils argue about ideas and build understanding together", the environment will look different: clusters, a norm of listening to disagreement, displays that make pupil thinking visible. The point is that the design follows the learning goal, not the other way around. A teacher who rearranges the desks because clusters look modern, without a learning reason, has changed the furniture but not the learning. Start with the goal, then choose the environment that serves it.
documents.s: Deciding what kind of classroom environment you want

documents.t: Learning resources are anything in the room a pupil can use to support learning: textbooks, exercise books, the blackboard, posters, real objects, the floor, the wall, and other pupils. The design question is not "what do I wish I had?" but "what is already here that I am not using?" In a low-resource government school, the answer is often more than the teacher assumes. The walls can hold pupil-made displays. The floor can be a sorting space. The pupils themselves are a resource: a pupil who has understood an explanation can explain it to a peer, and both learn from the act. Wong and Wong (1998) treat the teacher's first design task as a resource audit: list everything in the room that could support learning, then decide what is going unused. The management weight of resources is about access. A resource no pupil can reach is not a resource; it is furniture. If there is one set of science materials in a locked cupboard and the key is with the headteacher, the design problem is not the cupboard but the routine for getting the materials to the pupils when they are needed.

A display is not decoration. A well-chosen display is a teaching tool that keeps teaching after you have moved on. The design question is what the display is for. Three kinds of display carry management weight: Learning-target displays. The day's or week's learning target, written where every pupil can see it, answers the question "what are we trying to learn?" without the teacher having to repeat it. Pupil-work displays. A wall of pupils' current work signals that the room belongs to them, that their thinking is visible and valued, and that the standard is "the best we can do this week", not "perfect". Reference displays. A number line, a vocabulary wall, a map, a chart of the routine for asking help. These are tools pupils can use without asking the teacher, which is the difference between a room that depends on the teacher and one that runs itself. In a room with cracked walls and no budget, displays can be made from newspaper, from scrap paper, from the backs of old examination sheets. The constraint is not money; it is the teacher's willingness to make the work visible.
documents.s: Using displays and visuals to enhance the learning environment

documents.t: The figure at the start of this topic shows three common arrangements, and the point of the figure is that none of them is universally right. Each serves a kind of learning and costs something. Rows serve whole-class instruction well: every pupil can see the board, the teacher can see every pupil, and the arrangement signals that the teacher is the focus. The cost is that group work is awkward and the pupils nearest the teacher get more attention than the pupils at the back. Clusters (groups of four to six) serve collaboration well: pupils can talk, share materials, and build understanding together. The cost is that the teacher cannot see every pupil at once, noise rises, and without a clear routine the cluster becomes a chat. Horseshoe (a open rectangle or semicircle) serves discussion and debate well: every pupil can see every other pupil, the teacher is part of the circle rather than outside it, and the arrangement signals that the thinking is shared. The cost is that it needs more space and is awkward for individual written work. Mr Hassan's benches are fixed in rows, and he cannot change that. But he can, on discussion days, ask pupils to turn to face the side or the back, creating temporary clusters within a row layout. The design principle is: match the arrangement to the learning, and when you cannot change the furniture, change how the pupils orient within it. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: Arranging seating for different kinds of learning experiences

documents.t: The physical and the social are not separate design acts. The room's physical arrangement shapes how people treat each other, and the social norms determine whether the physical arrangement works. A cluster layout without a norm of listening to disagreement is just noisy. A display of pupil work without a norm of respectful feedback is just a wall. Building the social environment on purpose means establishing, practising and maintaining the norms the learning requires: A norm that a wrong answer is useful, not shameful, if you want pupils to take the risk of thinking in front of others. A norm that pupils help each other, if you want the cluster arrangement to produce learning rather than copying. A norm that every voice matters, if you want the back benches to participate as fully as the front. Evertson and Emmer (2009) are clear that these norms do not establish themselves. The teacher states them, models them, practises them in the first weeks, and responds consistently when them are breached. That is management work, and it is the work that makes the physical design actually function.
documents.s: Employing physical facilities and building the social environment

documents.t: Work in pairs. Take the description of Mr Hassan's room from the start of this topic (fixed benches, cracked blackboard, one locked cupboard, no budget). Decide on one learning goal he might have for a single lesson: either "practise procedures" or "build understanding together". For your chosen goal, complete the audit table from the figure: what to look for, why it matters, what he can change this week, and a first step. Then present your audit to another pair that chose the other goal, and explain why your environment differs from theirs. Allow 25 minutes.
documents.s: Activity: The room you have, the room you want

documents.t: Name the four design acts the guide lists for Week 4. (Remember) A teacher puts up a colourful commercial poster of a film star. Using this topic's account of what a display is for, explain whether that counts as a learning display. (Understand) A teacher always uses clusters "because group work is good". Explain what that reasoning leaves out, and name the learning goal that would make clusters the right choice. (Analyze) For the same fixed-bench room as the Activity, propose one change to the social environment that would make a discussion lesson more workable, and explain why the change is social rather than physical. (Apply) A friend says, "I cannot design my classroom because the benches are fixed and I have no budget." Using two ideas from this topic, explain what she can still change this week. (Apply)

Designing the environment on purpose starts with a learning goal, not with furniture. The four design acts are: identify the resources already in the room, make displays that keep teaching, match the seating arrangement to the learning it needs to serve, and build the social norms that make the physical design actually work. In a low-resource government school, the constraint is real but narrower than it first appears: the teacher can change how the room is used, how the walls are read, how pupils orient, and how they treat each other, even when the benches do not move.

I can explain why the learning goal must come before the physical design. I can conduct a simple resource audit of a described classroom. I can match a seating arrangement to the learning experience it serves and name what it costs. I can distinguish a learning display from a decoration. I can name at least three social norms a teacher would need to establish on purpose.

Carry out a resource audit of one classroom you have access to. List every resource currently in the room, mark which ones pupils can actually reach and use during a lesson, and identify one resource that is going unused. Then propose one display the teacher could create this week from materials already available, and write half a page on what it would teach and how it would need to be introduced. Chapter 1 frames environmental design as a proactive management strategy.

Learning is explained by three major theories, and a fluent teacher moves between them as the learning target demands. Behaviourism treats learning as a change in visible behaviour shaped by reinforcement; it is the right lens for building automatic routines and practised skills. Cognitivism treats learning as the reorganisation of mental structures; it is the right lens for making new information processable and connectable. Constructivism treats learning as the active construction of personal meaning; it is the right lens for deep understanding and transfer. Classroom management, as this course uses the phrase, is the proactive work of creating and maintaining the conditions in which student learning happens. It is not the same as discipline, which is the reactive response to a breach of norms. A teacher's personal philosophy of teaching shapes what they treat as the management problem, and a well-managed classroom is marked by practised routines, high intellectual demand, teacher withitness, and an environment that supports the learning. Reading a classroom requires a protocol: decide what to look for, record what you actually saw in a left column and what you think it means in a right column, and keep the two apart. The physical environment (sightlines, traffic paths, displays, resources) and the social environment (participation patterns, norms of help, responses to error, belonging) are the two landscapes a managed classroom shapes. Designing the environment on purpose starts with a learning goal, not with furniture. The four design acts are: identify the resources already in the room, make displays that keep teaching, match the seating arrangement to the learning it needs to serve, and build the social norms that make the physical design actually work.

Behaviourism says that learning is best described as: (Remember) a) the reorganisation of mental structures b) the active construction of personal meaning c) a change in observable behaviour shaped by reinforcement d) the transfer of understanding to a new context A teacher activates pupils' prior knowledge before introducing a new topic. This move is best read through which theoretical lens? (Understand) a) Behaviourism b) Cognitivism c) Constructivism d) None of the three Which feature most distinguishes a well-managed classroom from a merely orderly one? (Understand) a) The pupils are silent for most of the lesson b) The pupils are engaged in intellectually demanding work for most of the lesson c) The teacher gives instructions only once d) No pupil ever breaches a rule In a two-column observation record, the sentence "the teacher used proximity to redirect the talking pupils" belongs in: (Apply) a) the left column, because it records what was seen b) the right column, because it is an inference about what the action meant c) either column, because it is both an observation and an inference d) neither column, because it is a judgement A teacher arranges desks in clusters for a discussion lesson, then is frustrated that the class is noisy. The most likely design failure is: (Apply) a) choosing clusters for a task that needs rows b) not establishing a norm of listening to disagreement before the discussion c) using constructivism when behaviourism was needed d) placing the display wall on the wrong side of the room Wong and Wong (1998) argue that a teacher with a consistent management plan spends the first weeks of term: (Remember) a) establishing consequences for every rule b) teaching the plan, then teaching the curriculum c) letting pupils discover the routines themselves d) focusing on relationship-building before any routines Which pair correctly matches a learning theory with the kind of learning target it serves best? (Understand) a) Behaviourism - interpreting a poem b) Cognitivism - building a new scientific concept from scratch c) Constructivism - practising letter formation until it is automatic d) Behaviourism - drilling a routine until it is automatic A teacher in a low-resource government school cannot move the benches. According to Topic 1.4, what can she still change this week? (Apply) a) Nothing, because the physical environment is fixed b) Only the social environment, because the physical one is fixed c) How the room is used, how the walls are read, how pupils orient, and how they treat each other d) Only the displays, because seating is fixed "Withitness" refers to a teacher's: (Remember) a) ability to teach three theories in one week b) accurate awareness of what is happening across the whole room and willingness to act early c) skill at designing displays from scrap materials d) habit of separating observation from inference A trainee observes a lesson and writes only conclusions in her notebook, with no record of the evidence they are based on. Which observation skill has she not yet developed? (Apply) a) Choosing a focus b) Separating observation from inference c) Using the four lenses d) Completing the five-step cycle

Design a management plan for that room that does all three of the following: draws on at least two of the three learning theories, includes at least one change to the physical and one to the social environment, and explains how your plan shifts the teacher's balance from reactive discipline toward proactive management. Justify each choice. (Create)

c - behaviourism defines learning as a change in observable behaviour shaped by reinforcement; (a) is cognitivism, (b) is constructivism. b - activating prior knowledge is a cognitivist move, organising new information against existing mental structures. b - a well-managed classroom is defined by the quality of pupil engagement, not by the absence of noise or breaches. b - the sentence interprets the teacher's action; it is an inference, not a verifiable observation. b - clusters serve discussion, but without a norm of listening to disagreement the noise is unmanaged rather than a sign of learning. b - Wong and Wong's management-plan approach invests the first weeks in teaching the plan, then frees the teacher to teach the curriculum. d - behaviourism best explains the drilling of a routine until it is automatic; (a), (b) and (c) each pair a theory with a target it serves poorly. c - Topic 1.4 argues that even a fixed-bench, no-budget room leaves the teacher multiple levers: use, displays, pupil orientation and social norms. b - withitness is Marzano, Marzano and Pickering's term for accurate whole-room awareness and early action. b - recording conclusions without evidence is the failure to separate observation from inference, which is the core discipline of the two-column protocol.
