diagnosis versus procedure - and shows why this case favours one Handling of uncertainty Treats suspicion as proof Notes the evidence is circumstantial Builds a course of action appropriate to circumstantial evidence, including what would confirm it

The unit is built to be taught in order, and the dependency is real rather than presentational: Topic 2.4 applies the models from Topic 2.3, which assume the codes from Topic 2.2. A workable division for Weeks 4 and 5 is Topic 2.1 and Topic 2.2 in the first week, Topic 2.3 early in the second, and Topic 2.4 with the unit assessment at the end. If the block is compressed, compress Topic 2.2 rather than Topic 2.3. The codes can be read; the models need to be worked through with a group. Topic 2.3 is the load-bearing topic of the unit. If only one topic is taught well, it should be that one, because it is what the trainee will still be using in five years.

Four come up almost every cohort. Each is named inside the topic that corrects it, but they are worth anticipating. "Ethics is just being a good person, so it cannot be taught." The strongest counter is not an argument but the Miss Rabia case in Topic 2.1: a conscientious, well-meaning teacher who wronged a pupil, where more decency would not have helped. Let the class reach that conclusion rather than asserting it. "If it is not in the code, it is allowed." Trainees who have worked in tightly-regulated settings hold this firmly. The nested-circles figure in Topic 2.2 is designed for this moment; the gaps between the rings are the point of the diagram. "Knowing what is right is enough." This is what Rest's model exists to defeat. The two teachers in the Topic 2.3 vignette, one who did not notice and one who noticed and did not act, are the fastest route to it. "A dilemma means there must be a right answer I have not found yet." The most persistent of the four. Trainees search for the costless option and become frustrated. Name it early in Topic 2.4: something will be lost, and the professional task is to choose where the loss falls and to limit it.
documents.s: The misconceptions that recur, and how to handle them

documents.t: Three of the four activities ask trainees to discuss real cases. Two cautions. Anonymity is not optional. In the Topic 2.4 dilemma exchange, trainees write accounts of real situations. Establish before they start that no pupil, teacher or school may be identifiable, and be willing to stop an account that drifts into identification. A cohort that has watched you enforce this once will handle the rest of the unit more honestly, not less. Some accounts will involve harm to the trainee. Where a trainee's own schooling included humiliation or worse, the Topic 2.1 activity can reach it unexpectedly. Give an explicit alternative: any trainee may work from a hypothetical rather than a remembered case, with no explanation required, and say so before the activity rather than afterwards. If a trainee discloses something that suggests a current safeguarding concern, that is not a teaching moment. Follow your institution's procedure.

The Topic 2.1 sorting activity produces an argument about item 3, the teacher who does not pray, and about item 8, the teacher who lends money to a family. This is by design; both sit on the boundary between personal morality and professional ethics. The failure mode is that the group settles it by majority and moves on. Intervene if that happens. The value is entirely in the disagreement, and the instruction to spend the last five minutes on the one placement they disagree about exists to force it. Ask the group to state what would have to be true for the other placement to be correct.
documents.s: The activity that most often goes wrong

documents.t: Observation task (Week 4). The Topic 2.1 practicum task, tallying which pupils a teacher calls on, produces the unit's most reliable evidence that routine decisions carry ethical weight. Collect the half-page reflections and read a selection aloud, anonymised, at the start of Week 5. Trainees discount the point when they read it; they accept it when they hear three peers report the same pattern. Decision log (Week 5). The Topic 2.3 log is the transfer task that matters most. Set it on the first day of Week 5 so there is a full week of entries. Do not collect it. Ask instead, in the final session, how many found the same Rest component recurring in their own entries; a show of hands makes the point without requiring anyone to disclose. Code audit (either week). The Topic 2.2 practicum task assumes the school has a written code. Many will not. Prepare for that answer: ask those trainees what fills the gap instead, and the resulting list of unwritten local norms is usually a better discussion than the document would have been.

The bank is on the unit assessment page with model answers and analytic rubrics. Two notes. The RRQ mark schemes are point-by-point and total more than a typical paper would carry; select from them rather than setting all ten. For the ERQs, the rubric caps a response that does not reach "Adequate" on the analysis criterion at 10 out of 20, whatever its other merits. This is deliberate. A fluent, well-organised answer that never analyses anything is the most common strong-looking weak response at this level, and the cap is what stops it scoring like a good one.

Unit 1 asked what a profession is. Unit 2 asked what it obliges you to do. This unit asks the question those two lead to: what actually makes a teacher good at the work? It is a harder question than it sounds, and the honest answer begins with a warning. There is no single agreed definition of an effective teacher, and the definitions in use disagree with each other in ways that matter. A teacher judged effective by one measure can be judged ineffective by another, on the same evidence. This unit gives you the competing accounts rather than a tidy one, because a trainee who leaves with a tidy one will be surprised by the first appraisal they sit. What the unit does offer is a set of components you can observe, and four things that carry effectiveness in practice: the qualities you bring, the relationships you build, the way you communicate, and the roles you take on.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain what teacher effectiveness means, describe at least two competing conceptions of it, and say what each captures and misses. Name the components used to evaluate teacher effectiveness and distinguish within-classroom processes from factors beyond the classroom. Describe the personal and professional qualities associated with effective teaching, including attitude toward the profession and professional image, and explain how a trait can help or harm depending on degree. Build and describe positive relationships with pupils, parents, colleagues and the community, and set out a defensible sequence for handling conflict without losing professionalism. Distinguish verbal and non-verbal communication, name the types of non-verbal channel and their classroom use, and explain what happens when the two channels contradict each other. Explain the evolving roles of the teacher as facilitator, researcher, change agent, moral agent and life-long learner, and give a concrete classroom act that expresses each.

Units 1 and 2. Unit 1 supplies the idea of professionalism and its dimensions. Unit 2 supplies the ethical obligations that constrain what "effective" is permitted to mean, and that constraint runs through this whole unit: a method that raises marks and damages pupils is not effective teaching, it is a different thing wearing its name.

Topic 3.1 - What "an effective teacher" actually means - the competing definitions, why they disagree, and the components used to evaluate effectiveness. Topic 3.2 - The qualities an effective teacher brings - attitude toward the profession, professional image, the named personality traits and how each fails when overdone. Topic 3.3 - Relationships, and what to do when they go wrong - the stakeholder web around a teacher, and a workable sequence for conflict. Topic 3.4 - Saying it so it lands - verbal and non-verbal communication, the types of non-verbal channel, and what learners do when the channels disagree. Topic 3.5 - The roles a teacher now has to play - facilitator, researcher, change agent, moral agent and life-long learner.

Work through the topics in order. Topic 3.1 sets up a distinction the other four keep using: the difference between what is measured and what is meant. Topics 3.2 and 3.4 both ask you to look at yourself, and both are more useful done with someone who has seen you teach. If you are on practicum, save the transfer tasks in those two topics for a week when you have a mentor available. The question bank at the end covers all five topics. Its answers and mark schemes are in a clearly marked section at the foot of that page.

textbook.com.pk Two teachers take Class 9 mathematics in neighbouring rooms of the same government school in Larkana. At the end of the year their board results are almost identical. Mr Junaid's room is silent. He works through the past five years of board papers, question by question. Pupils copy his worked solutions and reproduce them. Anyone who asks a question that is not on the syllabus is told there is no time. His pupils pass. Miss Shazia's room is noisier. She spends the first term on why the methods work, which costs her three weeks she never gets back, and she pushes pupils to attempt problems before she has shown them how. Two of her weakest pupils fail the mock badly and recover by March. Her pupils pass at the same rate as Mr Junaid's. Which of them is the effective teacher? The honest answer is that it depends entirely on what you decided to count before you walked in, and this topic is about taking that decision seriously rather than pretending it has already been made for you.

Teacher effectiveness is usually defined as the effect a teacher has on what their pupils learn. That sentence sounds settled and is not, because everything depends on which effects you count and how you detect them. Goe, Bell and Little (2008) report that there is no generally agreed method for evaluating teacher effectiveness. Grouping what they and others describe, the definitions in use fall into three recognisable families. The grouping below is this book's, offered as a way to hold the field in mind rather than as their taxonomy: Effectiveness as achievement gain. The teacher's effect is the improvement in pupils' measured attainment over a year, ideally compared against what similar pupils elsewhere achieved. It has the great merit of being about learning rather than about the teacher's manner. Its weakness is that it counts only what the test tests. Mr Junaid does extremely well on this definition. Effectiveness as observed practice. The teacher's effect is inferred from what they are seen to do: how they explain, question, respond, manage time. It captures things a test cannot, and it is what most classroom observation instruments measure. Its weakness is that it can reward a performance. A lesson can look excellent and teach nobody anything, and observers are not immune to being impressed. Effectiveness as breadth of learner outcomes. The teacher's effect includes attainment but also what else changed: whether pupils became more willing to attempt hard problems, whether attendance held, whether a pupil who intended to leave stayed. Miss Shazia looks strongest here. Its weakness is that these outcomes are genuinely hard to measure, and what is hard to measure is easy to assert. Taylor and Thion (2023) put a sharper point, though note what they studied: reviewing the research literature on teaching effectiveness, they found many papers using inaccurate or merely implied definitions, so that the definition stated and the thing actually measured came apart. Their subject is research, not school appraisal. The same gap is easy to recognise in a school, where an institution may say it values deep understanding and appraise its teachers on examination results, and the appraisal is what teachers respond to. That extension is a reasonable inference rather than their finding. So what should a trainee conclude? Not that effectiveness is meaningless. The three families agree on more than they disagree about. What follows is narrower and more useful: whenever someone calls a teacher effective, ask what was counted. And when you are evaluated, find out which definition is in force before you plan your year around the wrong one. This dismantles a misconception worth naming: an effective teacher is one whose class gets high marks. That is one definition, not the definition, and it is the one most vulnerable to being achieved in ways nobody wants. A teacher can raise marks by narrowing teaching to the test, which raises the measure and lowers the learning it was supposed to indicate.
documents.s: Redefining effective teaching and the effective teacher

documents.t: textbook.com.pk Rather than one definition, it is more workable to hold a set of components, each of which can be observed and none of which is sufficient alone. The figure above groups them in the way the research literature tends to: what happens inside the room, and what happens outside it. Within-classroom processes Subject and pedagogical knowledge. Knowing the content, and knowing how that particular content is learned and misunderstood. The second is not implied by the first, which is why a brilliant mathematician can teach mathematics badly. Planning and structure. Whether a lesson has a destination, and whether the parts serve it. Explanation and questioning. Whether ideas are made available, and whether questions discover what pupils think or merely check that someone can say the right words. Use of assessment. Whether the teacher finds out what pupils have understood and then does something different because of it. A teacher who tests frequently and teaches identically afterwards is not using assessment. Classroom climate and management. Whether the room is a place where a pupil can risk being wrong. Unit 2's account of trust is this component seen from the ethical side. Beyond the classroom Contribution to colleagues. Whether the teacher's practice improves anyone else's. Relationships with parents and community. Covered in Topic 3.3. Professional learning. Whether the teacher is still changing. Covered in Topic 3.5. Two cautions about using components at all. First, components are evidence, not a score. Adding them up produces a number that feels objective and hides every judgement that went into it. Goe and colleagues are explicit that different components are appropriate for different purposes, and that an instrument built for professional development should not be reused for high-stakes appraisal. Second, the components interact. Strong subject knowledge with a hostile climate produces less learning than moderate subject knowledge with a safe one, because pupils in the second room will admit what they do not understand. Reading the list as independent boxes to tick misses the thing that actually makes a classroom work. Return to Mr Junaid and Miss Shazia with the components in hand and the picture sharpens. Mr Junaid is strong on structure and weak on questioning and assessment use, because nothing he does discovers what pupils think. Miss Shazia is strong on climate, questioning and assessment use, and paid three weeks for it. Neither is simply better. But only one of them could tell you what their pupils misunderstand, and that is the difference that compounds over a career.
documents.s: The components of teacher effectiveness, and what each can and cannot show

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Each group takes one of the three definitions from the figure at the top of this topic: achievement gain, observed practice, or breadth of learner outcomes. From your definition alone, write the appraisal you would give Mr Junaid and the appraisal you would give Miss Shazia. Be specific: state what evidence you would collect and what verdict it supports. Then hear all three groups in turn. Two questions for the class afterwards. Which teacher's appraisal changed most between definitions, and why? And which definition would you want applied to you in your first year of teaching, given what you would be able to demonstrate? Allow 25 minutes.

State three competing definitions of teacher effectiveness and, for each, one thing it captures well. (Remember) Explain why a teacher can be judged effective on one definition and ineffective on another using the same evidence. (Understand) Distinguish within-classroom processes from factors beyond the classroom, giving two examples of each. (Remember) A teacher tests their class every fortnight and teaches the next unit identically regardless of the results. Which component are they failing, and why does frequent testing not rescue it? (Apply) Explain why adding the components into a single score is a worse instrument than holding them separately. (Analyze)

Teacher effectiveness means the effect a teacher has on pupils' learning, but the definitions in use disagree about which effects count. Achievement gain counts what the test tests; observed practice counts what an observer can see and can be satisfied by performance; breadth of learner outcomes counts more of what matters and measures it less reliably. Institutions frequently state one definition and appraise against another. More workable than a definition is a set of components: subject and pedagogical knowledge, planning, explanation and questioning, use of assessment, and classroom climate within the room; contribution to colleagues, relationships beyond it, and continued professional learning outside. The components are evidence rather than a score, they are chosen for a purpose, and they interact, so a strong component can be cancelled by a weak one.

I can state three competing definitions of teacher effectiveness and what each misses. I can explain why the definition an institution states and the measure it uses often differ. I can name the components of teacher effectiveness and sort them into within-classroom and beyond-classroom. I can judge a described teacher against the components rather than by overall impression. I can explain why using assessment means changing what you do next, not testing more often.

Find out how teachers in your practicum school are actually appraised. Ask your mentor what is looked at, who looks at it, and how often. Then compare what you are told against the three definitions in this topic. Write half a page identifying which definition the school's appraisal is closest to, what that definition rewards, and one thing a teacher in that school could do to score well without teaching better. That last part is not cynicism; it is the standard test of whether a measure is robust.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Mr Junaid and Miss Shazia produced the same board results. Judge them both against the components of teacher effectiveness and reach a defensible verdict. Your answer must use at least four named components, cite specific evidence from the vignette rather than impressions, state clearly what evidence you do not have and would need, and reach a verdict rather than concluding that both have strengths. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Use of components (Apply) Names at least four components and applies each to both teachers, not just the convenient ones Evidence discipline Distinguishes what the vignette states from what the writer is inferring Reasoned verdict (Evaluate) Reaches a verdict and defends the criterion it rests on, rather than retreating to "both have strengths" Recognition of limits States what further evidence would change the verdict and why

Goe, L., Bell, C., & Little, O. (2008). Approaches to evaluating teacher effectiveness: A research synthesis. National Comprehensive Center for Teacher Quality. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED521228.pdf Taylor, S., & Thion, S. (2023). How has teaching effectiveness been conceptualized? Questioning the consistency between definition and measure. Frontiers in Education, 8. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2023.1253622

textbook.com.pk Two days before her first practicum lesson, Ayesha is worried about her shoes. She has been told the school is strict about appearance. She has spent an evening on it. She has not yet read the chapter she is teaching beyond the summary, and she has not thought at all about what her Class 6 pupils are likely to already believe about fractions. Her friend Bushra has the opposite problem. Bushra knows the content thoroughly and intends to arrive in whatever she was wearing, because "clothes are surface and teaching is substance". Both of them are about to learn that the question is not which of the two matters, but what each one is actually for.

Attitude toward the profession is the disposition a teacher holds toward the work itself: whether they regard it as a career they chose and intend to be good at, or as employment they fell into and endure. It matters because it is visible and it is contagious. Pupils can tell. A teacher who conveys that the subject is tedious and the job is a burden has taught something durable about both. Hurst and Reding (2009) catalogue the day-to-day markers of professional conduct, and the striking thing about their list is how ordinary it is: punctuality, preparedness, the willingness to be interrupted by a pupil's question, follow-through on what was promised. None of it is dramatic, and all of it communicates whether the person takes the work seriously. In Pakistan this deserves a frank treatment rather than an exhortation. Many trainees enter teaching because it was available, or because family expected it, or because other doors were shut. Pretending otherwise would be dishonest, and a unit that lectures such a trainee about passion will simply lose them. The useful reframing is that attitude is not a feeling you must manufacture but a stance you can choose. You may not have arrived enthusiastic. You can still decide to be someone who prepares, who finds out why a method works, and who treats a pupil's confusion as interesting rather than irritating. Enthusiasm, where it comes, usually follows competence rather than preceding it.
documents.s: A teacher's attitude toward the teaching profession

documents.t: textbook.com.pk Professional image is the impression a teacher's presentation creates before they have taught anything. Dressing and grooming are the part of it visible in the first four seconds. Two errors are common, and Ayesha and Bushra have one each. Treating appearance as the whole of it. It is the outermost and thinnest band in the figure above. It buys attention and a presumption of seriousness, and it buys them only briefly. A well-presented teacher who cannot explain the lesson has spent that credit by the second week. Treating appearance as nothing. This is Bushra's error and it is the more common one among able trainees. Appearance is a signal about respect: for the occasion, for the pupils, and for the institution. In a government school where many pupils own one good set of clothes, a teacher who arrives carelessly dressed is making a statement about how much the occasion is worth, and it is heard. The workable standard is neither expensive nor elaborate. It is clean, modest, appropriate to the setting, and consistent. A misconception worth naming here is that professional image means expensive clothes; it does not, and in most Pakistani government schools an expensively dressed teacher reads as distant rather than professional. Beneath appearance sit the bands that actually carry a career: conduct, reliability and competence. They take longer to establish and cannot be assembled the night before, which is exactly why Ayesha's evening was misallocated.
documents.s: Dressing and grooming as dimensions of professional image

documents.t: The course guide names seven and leaves the list open with an "etc.": empathy, patience, self-control, optimism, humour, resilience and adaptability. Treat these as the seven you are expected to know, not as the complete set of traits that matter; fairness, curiosity and enthusiasm would all have a claim. Each is genuinely associated with effective practice. Each also has a failure mode at excess, which is the part usually left out and which the figure at the top of this topic records. Empathy is the capacity to understand a pupil's situation from inside it. It makes a pupil willing to admit confusion. Overdone, it becomes the teacher who excuses everything, lowers expectations out of sympathy, and thereby tells a pupil they are not expected to manage. Patience is tolerance of the time learning actually takes. It allows a pupil to reach an idea rather than be handed it. Overdone, it becomes passivity: a class drifting for a term because the teacher is waiting for something that is not going to arrive without intervention. Self-control is the regulation of your own reaction, particularly to provocation. Its absence is the single most damaging trait failure in a classroom, because a teacher who loses control in front of thirty children has forfeited the trust Unit 2 described. Overdone, it becomes flatness, a teacher so controlled that pupils cannot read them and stop trying to. Optimism is the working belief that a pupil can improve. It is close to the most important of the seven, because a pupil's belief about themselves tends to track their teacher's. Overdone, it becomes denial: cheerfulness in the face of a pupil who is drowning and needs the problem named. Humour lowers the cost of being wrong. Overdone, it becomes the classroom where the teacher is entertaining and nobody learns. Humour also has a second failure that the other six do not, and it is worth separating rather than folding in. Humour aimed at a pupil is not too much humour; it is humour pointed the wrong way. Since the trait's whole function is to lower the cost of being wrong, a joke at a pupil's expense raises that cost, which makes it the trait inverted rather than unbalanced. Watch for both, and note that the remedies differ: less of it in the first case, a change of target in the second. Resilience is recovering from a bad lesson, a hostile parent or a failed innovation without abandoning the attempt. Overdone, it becomes stubbornness: persisting with a method for four years because giving it up would feel like defeat. Adaptability is changing the plan when the room tells you to. Overdone, it becomes incoherence, a class that never experiences a sequence because every lesson is improvised. Note what these failure modes have in common. With one exception, none is the opposite of the trait. Each is the trait itself, unbalanced by the others, which is why the list has to be held together rather than pursued one at a time. The exception is humour aimed at a pupil, noted above: that one is a change of direction rather than of quantity, and it is the only failure in the seven that a teacher cannot correct by doing less.

How much do these traits actually determine effectiveness? Less than folk wisdom claims, and in a more specific way. The traits do not produce learning directly. They operate on the components from Topic 3.1. Empathy and optimism shape classroom climate. Self-control shapes climate and management. Adaptability shapes use of assessment, because changing what you do next in response to what pupils show you is adaptability in its professional form. Resilience determines whether professional learning continues after the first discouragement. This matters for a misconception that stops trainees improving: personality is fixed, so either you have it or you do not. Two things are wrong with it. The traits as they matter here are behaviours in a role, not the whole of a personality: a naturally impatient person can conduct a lesson patiently, and doing so repeatedly is what the pupils experience. And the failure modes above show that more of a trait is not better, so "having it" was never the goal. Brookfield (2017) supplies the mechanism for change: a teacher who examines their own practice against evidence, including the evidence of how pupils actually experienced a lesson, can alter what they habitually do. The traits are not a lottery result. They are a description of habits that can be built, and the building is the subject of Topic 3.5.
documents.s: The influence of personality traits on teacher effectiveness

documents.t: Work in groups of four. Assign each member two of the seven traits. For each trait, write two short classroom vignettes: one showing the trait working well, and one showing the same trait at excess doing harm. The two vignettes must feature the same teacher and the same trait, not a good teacher and a bad one. Read them to the group without saying which trait you were given, and have the group identify the trait and name what was missing in the excess case that would have balanced it. Allow 30 minutes. The identification is usually easy; the naming of what was missing is the part that teaches.

Name the seven personality traits the course guide lists, and say why the guide's "etc." matters. (Remember) Explain why appearance matters without being the substance of professional image, using the layered model. (Understand) Choose any three traits and describe the failure mode of each at excess. (Apply) Explain how the traits influence effectiveness indirectly, naming at least two components from Topic 3.1 that they operate on. (Analyze) A trainee says they are "just not a patient person" and so will never be good with young classes. Identify the two errors in that reasoning. (Analyze)

Attitude toward the profession is a stance rather than a feeling, it is visible in ordinary conduct, and enthusiasm more often follows competence than precedes it. Professional image is layered: appearance is the thin outer band that buys brief attention, while conduct, reliability and competence carry a career and cannot be assembled overnight. The seven named traits each help, and each has a failure mode at excess that is the trait unbalanced rather than its opposite. Humour carries a second, different failure: aimed at a pupil it is the trait inverted, and it is corrected by changing target rather than by doing less. The traits do not produce learning directly; they operate on the components of effectiveness, chiefly climate, management, assessment use and continued learning. Because they are behaviours in a role rather than fixed dispositions, and because more is not better, "either you have it or you do not" is not a defensible position.

I can describe what attitude toward the profession looks like in ordinary conduct. I can explain what professional image is for, and why neither ignoring it nor over-investing in it is sound. I can name the seven traits and give the excess failure mode of each, and explain why humour has a second failure the others do not. I can explain how a trait affects effectiveness through a named component rather than directly. I can answer the claim that personality is fixed and therefore not worth working on.

Ask your mentor teacher which of the seven traits they think they rely on most, and which one they have had to work at. Then, separately, watch one of their lessons with the seven traits in front of you and record where you see each one. Compare what you observed with what they told you. Write half a page on any gap. The common finding is that experienced teachers underestimate the trait they have automated, because it no longer feels like effort to them.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Take one trait from the seven and write a case study of a teacher whose strength in that trait became a liability. Your case must show the same trait producing good practice earlier and harm later, identify what was missing that would have balanced it, and say what the teacher could reasonably have noticed at the point where it began to go wrong. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Grasp of the trait (Understand) Describes the trait accurately in its working form before showing the excess Continuity of the case The same teacher and trait throughout, rather than a contrast between two people Analysis of the imbalance (Analyze) Names the balancing trait or component that was absent, and explains the mechanism by which its absence produced harm Plausible detection point Identifies a realistic moment and signal the teacher could have noticed, not a benefit of hindsight

Hurst, B., & Reding, G. (2009). Professionalism in teaching. Pearson Education. A catalogue of the ordinary daily markers by which professional attitude is read. Brookfield, S. D. (2017). Becoming a critically reflective teacher (2nd ed.). Jossey-Bass. On examining habitual practice against evidence, including how pupils experienced it.

textbook.com.pk A father arrives at the school gate at the end of the day. His daughter Hina has come home with a failing mark in the term test and the news that her teacher said she "does not try". He is angry. He has been waiting since two o'clock. He begins in the corridor, in front of other parents and several pupils, and the first thing he says is that the school is punishing his daughter because the family cannot pay for tuition. Miss Rehana has thirty seconds to decide what kind of conversation this is going to be. What she does in those thirty seconds will determine whether Hina gets help this term.

The figure above deliberately labels each link with what the relationship is for rather than who is on the other end. Relationships in teaching are not decoration and they are not primarily about being liked. Each one exists because some part of the work is impossible without it. Pupils. The relationship exists so that a pupil will admit confusion, attempt something they might fail at, and tell you when something is wrong. This is Unit 2's trust seen from the effectiveness side. It is built by reliability far more than by warmth: marking returned when promised, a rule applied the same way on a Thursday as on a Monday, a question taken seriously rather than deflected. A misconception to clear early: a good relationship with pupils means being liked. Being liked is pleasant and it is not the goal, and pursuing it directly tends to produce a teacher who avoids the honest feedback a pupil needs. Pupils will forgive a teacher who is demanding. They do not forgive one who is unfair or unpredictable. Parents. The relationship exists so that a parent will act at home, and so that you learn what you cannot see. A parent knows things about a child's week that no classroom observation will reveal. In a Pakistani context this relationship is often asymmetric in ways worth naming: a parent who did not complete school may find the building intimidating and a teacher's vocabulary excluding. The work of making the relationship usable falls on the teacher, because the teacher is the one with institutional power. Colleagues. The relationship exists so that practice improves and so that a pupil is not handled inconsistently by six different teachers. It is also, as Unit 2 noted, where a profession's standing is held collectively. The head and the institution. The relationship exists so that you can get things done that require permission, and so that when you raise something difficult it is heard rather than filed. The wider community. The relationship exists because a school that the community trusts can ask things of it, and one it does not trust cannot. In rural Sindh this frequently determines whether girls stay in school past Class 5. The common thread is that every one of these is a working relationship with a purpose. Judge them by whether they let the work happen, not by whether they are comfortable.
documents.s: Building positive relationships with pupils, parents, colleagues and the community

documents.t: textbook.com.pk Conflict in a school is not a failure of relationships; it is a normal condition of a job where many people have a stake in the same child. What distinguishes a professional is the handling. The sequence in the figure above is a workable default. Four decision points, in order. Is this the right place? Almost never, if the answer involves a corridor and an audience. Moving the conversation is not evasion; it protects the other person's dignity as much as yours, and a parent who has lost face in front of neighbours cannot climb down. Miss Rehana's first move is to invite Hina's father to sit down somewhere else. Not to answer him yet. Can this person hear a reply yet? An angry person is not processing argument. The move is to let them finish, and then to demonstrate you understood by summarising their concern back to them in their own terms before you say anything else. This is not a technique for managing people; it is genuinely finding out what the complaint is, and it is often not what the opening sentence claimed. Do I have the facts? Frequently not. "I do not know, and I will find out and tell you by Thursday" is a stronger professional answer than a confident guess, and unlike a guess it can survive being checked. The obligation it creates is that you must then actually do it. Is this within my authority? Some things are not yours to settle: a fee dispute, an allegation against a colleague, anything touching a pupil's safety. Escalating is not weakness. Escalating without recording why is, because it leaves the next person with no information. Three things to hold throughout, which is where the professionalism in the heading lives: Separate the person from the position. Hina's father is not the problem; the belief that his daughter is being penalised for poverty is. Do not defend a colleague reflexively, and do not sacrifice one either. "I will find out what was said" is available and honest. Never make a pupil the currency. Whatever happens between adults, it cannot land on Hina. Applied to the vignette: Miss Rehana moves the conversation, lets him finish, reflects back that he believes Hina is being treated differently because of what the family can afford, says that she does not know what was said and will find out, and tells him what she does know, which is the actual mark and what specifically Hina cannot yet do in the subject. That last part converts the meeting from a grievance into something the father can act on, which is what Topic 2.2 meant about accurate information a parent can use.

Work in pairs, and take turns. One person plays a stakeholder arriving in conflict; the other is the teacher. Run only the first thirty seconds and then stop. Scenarios: an angry parent in a corridor; a colleague who believes you undermined them in front of a class; a head teacher who has told you to change a mark; a community elder objecting to something you taught. After each thirty seconds, the pair identifies which of the four decision points was actually in play and whether the teacher's opening move served it. Swap roles and run a different scenario. Allow 25 minutes total. Resist the urge to play out the whole conversation: the opening is where most conflicts are decided and it is the part trainees have never practised.

State what each of the five stakeholder relationships covered in this topic is for. (Remember) Explain why reliability builds a stronger relationship with pupils than warmth does. (Understand) Name the four decision points in the de-escalation sequence, in order, and say what each one protects. (Remember) Apply the sequence to Hina's father and state Miss Rehana's first three moves. (Apply) A teacher answers a parent's complaint immediately and confidently, and is later found to have been wrong about a fact. Analyse what that costs beyond the immediate error. (Analyze)

Every stakeholder relationship a teacher holds exists for a purpose that some part of the work depends on: pupils so that confusion is admitted, parents so that action happens at home and so that you learn what you cannot see, colleagues so that practice improves and handling is consistent, the institution so that things can be authorised, and the community so that a school can ask things of it. Judge relationships by whether they let the work happen, not by comfort or by being liked. Conflict is normal in a job where many people have a stake in one child. The professional difference is in the handling: move the conversation somewhere dignified, let the person finish and show you understood, admit when you do not have the facts and commit to a time, and escalate what is not yours to settle while recording why. Throughout, separate the person from the position, decline to either defend or sacrifice a colleague reflexively, and never let the dispute land on the pupil.

I can state what each stakeholder relationship is for rather than describing it as good or bad. I can explain why being liked is a poor goal and reliability a better one. I can work through the four de-escalation decision points in order. I can give an honest answer when I do not have the facts, in a form that creates a commitment. I can identify what is outside my authority and escalate it with the reason recorded.

Ask your mentor teacher to describe a conflict with a parent that ended well, and one that ended badly. Ask specifically what happened in the first few minutes of each. Write half a page comparing the two openings against the four decision points. Most teachers cannot say why one went better, and the comparison usually reveals that the difference was location, audience, or whether the parent was allowed to finish. Do not record identifying details.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Miss Rehana has thirty seconds. Write what she should do, and defend it. Set out her first three moves in order, justify each against a decision point, and then address the strongest objection: that moving the conversation and declining to answer immediately will read to an already-suspicious parent as the school closing ranks. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Use of the sequence (Apply) Moves are in a defensible order and each is tied to a decision point Realism Accounts for the corridor, the audience and the waiting since two o'clock, not an idealised meeting Answering the objection (Analyze) Takes seriously that de-escalation can look like evasion to a suspicious parent, and shows what specifically prevents that reading Protection of the pupil Shows how Hina is kept out of the dispute and ends with something actionable for her

Hurst, B., & Reding, G. (2009). Professionalism in teaching. Pearson Education. Goe, L., Bell, C., & Little, O. (2008). Approaches to evaluating teacher effectiveness: A research synthesis. National Comprehensive Center for Teacher Quality. Cited here for relationships beyond the classroom as a component of effectiveness (sub-topic U3-07). It does not address conflict handling, which this topic's de-escalation sequence sets out as a reasoned default rather than a sourced finding. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED521228.pdf

textbook.com.pk Mr Tariq says, to a Class 7 that has just produced a very poor set of homework: "It is fine. We will go over it again. Nobody is in trouble." While he says it he is standing behind his desk with his arms folded, he has not looked up from the pile of exercise books, and his voice has dropped at the end of each sentence. He then calls the register in a flat tone and moves on. He has told them, in words, that they are safe. Almost none of them believe it, and for the rest of the lesson very few of them ask anything.

Verbal communication is the words themselves: what is said, how it is structured and whether it can be followed by the person hearing it. In a classroom it does four distinct jobs, and teachers are usually much better at the first than the other three. Explaining. Making an idea available. The common failures are vocabulary the class does not hold, and a sequence that makes sense to someone who already understands. A worked example before the rule usually beats the rule before the example, because the example gives the rule something to be about. Instructing. Telling a class what to do. Instructions fail for mundane reasons: too many steps at once, given while pupils are already moving, or given in a form that cannot be checked. "Open your books, turn to page forty, answer the first three questions in your notebooks, and you have eight minutes" is four instructions and a time limit delivered in one breath. Half the room will have retained two of them. Questioning. This is where verbal skill most separates teachers. A question either discovers what pupils think or confirms that somebody can say the right words. "Does everyone understand?" does neither; it samples confidence, not comprehension, and it systematically over-samples the pupils who are already fine. Asking a pupil to explain the step to a neighbour, or to say which of two wrong answers is closer and why, discovers something. Responding. What a teacher says immediately after a pupil speaks. This is the single most consequential sentence in the exchange, because it teaches the rest of the class what happens to people who answer. A wrong answer met with "no, who else?" closes the room. The same wrong answer met with "what made you think that?" keeps it open and usually surfaces the misconception the whole class is holding. Furlich (2016) found verbal immediacy behaviours, which include using pupils' names, inviting questions, and referring to shared classroom experience, associated with learner motivation. These are small verbal habits rather than a style, and they are learnable.

textbook.com.pk Non-verbal communication is everything carried outside the words. Research on teacher non-verbal immediacy works with a fairly consistent set of channels, used across the immediacy studies this topic draws on, including eye contact, gesture, relaxed and directed body position, smiling, vocal expressiveness, movement and proximity. Keelson and colleagues (2024) measure a subset of these directly, reporting significant associations between facial expression and gesture and students' perceptions of teaching quality. The figure above places them in a room. Proximity. Where you stand. Distance reads as detachment; moving among desks reads as availability and, incidentally, makes off-task behaviour visible without a word being said. Body orientation. Which way you face. Facing the board while explaining sends the explanation to the board. Facing a pupil who is speaking tells the class that answering is worth the teacher's attention. Gaze and eye contact. Who you look at, and how the looking is distributed. Most untrained teachers over-attend to one side of a room and to the front three rows, and the pupils in the neglected zone reliably disengage. This is measurable in a single lesson and easy to fix once seen. Facial expression, including smiling. The channel pupils read fastest, and the one a teacher is least aware of moment to moment, which is why it so often reports a state the teacher did not intend to announce. Gesture. Used well, gesture carries structure that words cannot: the shape of a graph, the sequence of three steps held on three fingers. Used absently, it is noise. Vocal variety. Pace, pitch, volume and pause. This is the most under-used channel by trainees, who tend to a flat delivery under nerves. A pause before a key sentence does more work than repeating it. A misconception about the whole list: non-verbal communication is body language you can fake. Some of it can be performed for a few minutes, which is why an observed lesson is an unreliable sample. Across a term it cannot, because the channels run continuously and you cannot attend to all of them while also teaching. What actually changes them is changing the underlying thing: a teacher who genuinely finds a pupil's wrong answer interesting does not have to remember to look up. Abekah Keelson and colleagues (2024) found that learners' ratings of teaching quality were associated with a lecturer's facial expressions and gestures. That is the professional significance: the channel is not decoration, it is part of what is being judged. Read the evidence with its scope attached. That study surveyed 614 university students in Ghana by self-report questionnaire. Furlich (2016) studied instructor immediacy and student motivation at a small liberal arts university, and found the verbal immediacy relationship with motivation significant while the non-verbal one was not. The published abstract gives neither a sample size nor a country, so treat both as unstated rather than small and American. Neither study was conducted in a school, in Pakistan, or with children. They are the best evidence available here and they are evidence about university lecturing. Treat the channels as worth attending to, and treat any precise claim about how much they matter to a Class 7 pupil as unestablished. A misconception to discard, and a caution about its replacement. You may meet the claim that a fixed large percentage of communication, commonly 93%, is non-verbal. It comes from Mehrabian's 1967 experiments on how people judge a speaker's attitude from single words and tone, and it does not support any general claim about classroom talk. Do not repeat it. Now the caution, because it applies to this book as much as to anyone. The claim usually offered in its place, that the non-verbal channel wins when the two channels disagree, comes from the same small experiments. Discarding the number while keeping the conclusion drawn from it would be the same citation failure wearing better clothes. So treat it as what it is: a practitioner's heuristic, widely held, consistent with what experienced teachers report, and not established for classroom instruction by the evidence cited in this topic. It is worth acting on, because the cost of acting on it is low and the cost of ignoring it is a class that does not believe you. It is not worth asserting as a research finding, and you should not write it in an assignment as though it were one.
documents.s: Non-verbal communication: its types and their classroom use

documents.t: That last point is the whole of the Mr Tariq vignette. His words said safe; his folded arms, absent gaze and falling intonation said displeased. They did not believe the words. Whether that is a general law or a strong regularity is exactly what the previous section said is unestablished, but you do not need the general law to teach well here: this class, on this day, read the posture. This has three practical consequences. Reassurance is not a verbal act. If you intend to tell a class they are safe to be wrong, the posture, the gaze and the pause have to carry it, or the sentence is worse than useless because it also teaches that what the teacher says is unreliable. Praise inherits the same problem. Praise delivered without looking up is heard as dismissal. Your state leaks. A teacher who is tired, worried about something at home, or frustrated by the previous class will transmit it whatever the words. The professional response is not to pretend, which fails, but to name it briefly and truthfully where appropriate: a class told "I am short of sleep today, so tell me if I go too fast" is given a way to read the signals correctly instead of concluding they are the cause.

Work in groups of three, with one observer per round. Take a single instruction, for example: "Work in pairs and produce three examples of an improper fraction, in five minutes." Deliver it four times, changing only the non-verbal channel each time: once from behind a desk with no eye contact; once moving into the room with distributed gaze; once flat in vocal tone; once with a deliberate pause before the time limit. The observer records, each time, what they would actually do as a pupil, and how confident they are about what was expected. Rotate so everyone delivers and observes. Allow 25 minutes. The finding that lands hardest is usually that the words were identical every time.

Name the four jobs verbal communication does in a classroom. (Remember) Explain why "does everyone understand?" is a poor comprehension check and give a better alternative. (Understand) List five non-verbal channels and state the classroom use of each. (Remember) Mr Tariq's class did not believe him. Explain what happened, using the idea of contradicting channels. (Apply) A trainee cites the claim that 93% of communication is non-verbal. Explain what is wrong with the claim, and explain why simply replacing it with "the non-verbal channel wins when they disagree" does not fix the underlying problem. (Analyze)

Verbal communication does four jobs in a classroom: explaining, instructing, questioning and responding. Teachers are typically strongest at explaining and weakest at questioning, where the difference between discovering what pupils think and confirming that someone can say the right words is the difference between a useful lesson and a comfortable one. The sentence immediately after a pupil speaks teaches the whole class whether answering is safe. Non-verbal communication runs on identifiable channels: proximity, body orientation, gaze, facial expression, gesture and vocal variety. Learners read these as evidence about teaching quality, not merely about mood. The commonly quoted percentage claim about non-verbal communication is not supportable and should not be repeated; the defensible and more useful point is that non-verbal channels are read fast and continuously. The further claim that learners follow the non-verbal channel when the two contradict is a practitioner's heuristic worth acting on, not a finding the evidence in this topic establishes, and it descends from the same experiments the 93% claim does. The evidence cited here comes from university students, not from schoolchildren, and Furlich's non-verbal result was not significant.

I can name the four jobs of verbal communication and identify which I am weakest at. I can replace a confidence-sampling question with one that discovers what pupils think. I can name the non-verbal channels and say what each is for in a classroom. I can say what is heuristic and what is established about channels contradicting each other. I can explain why the 93% claim is not usable, and why its usual replacement inherits the same weakness.

Ask a peer or your mentor to observe one of your lessons recording only two things: where you stood, minute by minute, and which pupils you made eye contact with. Map the results onto a seating plan afterwards. Nearly every trainee finds a neglected zone, usually one side of the room or the back corner furthest from the door. Note who sits there and how they behaved during the lesson. Teach the same class again with the single goal of reaching that zone, and have the observer repeat the record.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Rewrite Mr Tariq's moment so that the class believes him, and explain why your version works. Give the words you would use and describe the non-verbal delivery precisely: position, orientation, gaze, pace, pause. Then explain what each element is doing, and address the objection that the class's poor homework does in fact warrant displeasure and that a warmer delivery would misrepresent the situation. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Verbal content (Apply) The words are specific and usable, not a paraphrase of "be encouraging" Non-verbal specification Names position, orientation, gaze, pace and pause concretely enough to be enacted Analysis of the objection (Analyze) Engages with the real tension between honesty about poor work and keeping the room open, rather than choosing warmth and ignoring it Mechanism Explains why each element works, and marks which part of the reasoning is established evidence and which is practitioner heuristic

Furlich, S. A. (2016). Understanding instructor nonverbal immediacy, verbal immediacy, and student motivation at a small liberal arts university. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 16(3), 11-22. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v16i3.19284 Note the setting: a small liberal arts university, per the paper's own title. The abstract states no sample size and names no country. Furlich found the verbal immediacy relationship significant and the non-verbal one not significant. Abekah Keelson, S., Odei Addo, J., & Dodor, A. (2024). The influence of lecturer non-verbal cues on student perceptions of teaching quality: The role of gender and age. Cogent Education, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/2331186X.2024.2325788 614 university students in Ghana, self-report.

textbook.com.pk Mr Imran has taught Class 8 general science for eleven years. He is good at it in the way Topic 3.1 would recognise: his explanations are clear, his room is orderly, his results are steady. This year he tried something. He had noticed that pupils could state Newton's third law and could not use it, so he replaced two lessons of explanation with a sequence where pairs had to predict what would happen in four situations and then test them. He kept the marks from last year's class on the same topic, and compared. The results were slightly worse. He kept the approach anyway, but changed how the pairs report back, because what the comparison actually showed him was that the pupils who struggled were the ones who had never been asked to commit to a prediction in front of a partner. Everything in this topic is visible in that paragraph.

textbook.com.pk Facilitator. The facilitator arranges the conditions under which pupils do the intellectual work, rather than doing it in front of them. The distinction is not about talking less. A facilitator may talk a great deal; what changes is who is doing the thinking at the moment that matters. This is the role most often misunderstood in training. It does not mean withdrawing, and it does not mean that explanation is obsolete. A class cannot discover a convention, and letting them try wastes their time. What a facilitator judges is which parts of a topic are worth the cost of being worked out and which should simply be told. Mr Imran's two lessons were facilitation; his explanations of the units of force were not, and should not have been. Researcher. The researcher treats their own classroom as a source of evidence about their own practice. Not published research: the ordinary, small version. Notice something, form a question, change one thing, collect something that would show whether it worked, and be willing to find out that it did not. Mr Imran kept last year's marks. That single act is what separates a teacher who tries things from a teacher who learns from trying things. Most changes in teaching are adopted or abandoned on the basis of how the lesson felt, and how a lesson felt is a poor guide, because a lesson that feels smooth is often one in which nobody was made to struggle. This role is the load-bearing one, and it is why it is paired with facilitator here. Facilitation introduces uncertainty into a lesson; the researcher role is what converts that uncertainty into information instead of anxiety.
documents.s: The teacher as facilitator and as researcher

documents.t: Change agent. The change agent improves something beyond their own room: a colleague's practice, a departmental habit, a school routine that is quietly failing pupils. Trainees tend to hear this as a call for grand initiatives, and then, reasonably, conclude it does not apply to someone in their first year with no authority. The realistic version is smaller and available immediately: sharing a method that worked, raising a pattern you have noticed in a department meeting, declining to participate in a practice you judge harmful. Unit 2's account of obligations toward colleagues is this role seen from the ethical side. The change agent role also has a failure mode worth naming: the new teacher who arrives convinced everything is wrong and says so. That is not change agency, it is a way of ensuring nobody listens to you for two years. Change requires standing, and standing is earned by being visibly good at the ordinary work first. Moral agent. The moral agent recognises that teaching forms people, and that this happens whether or not it is intended. Unit 2 established the ground: a teacher is an ethical model because pupils learn conduct by watching an adult with authority. What this role adds is deliberateness. A moral agent notices that the way marks are returned, the way a struggling pupil is spoken to, and who gets the benefit of the doubt are all teaching something about fairness, and chooses what to teach rather than leaving it to habit.
documents.s: The teacher as change agent and as moral agent

documents.t: The life-long learner keeps developing after qualification, including in the years when nobody is requiring it. The argument for it is not exhortation. The content changes, the pupils change, and a method that worked for one cohort in one school does not transfer unexamined. More pointedly, the alternative to continued learning is not stability; it is the slow drift of a practice built for conditions that no longer exist. Brookfield (2017) supplies the discipline: development that consists of collecting courses is weaker than development that involves examining your own habitual practice against evidence, including evidence of how pupils actually experienced it. Suarez and McGrath (2022) add the identity dimension, that a teacher's sense of who they are professionally keeps developing and needs support during change rather than being fixed at qualification. This topic is deliberately last in the unit, because it is what makes the other four survivable. A facilitator will run lessons that fail. A researcher will discover that a favourite method does not work. A change agent will be rebuffed. None of that is sustainable for a person who expects to have arrived.

One caution about the timeline at the top of this topic. It is easy to read a sequence of eras as a story in which each role supersedes the last, and to conclude that a modern teacher does not transmit content. That reading is wrong and does real damage. Pupils still need to be told things by someone who knows them. What has changed is that transmitting content is no longer sufficient, and the four later roles are what has been added on top. A teacher who facilitates but cannot explain has not advanced past transmission; they have skipped it.
documents.s: Why these are additions, not replacements

documents.t: Work in groups of five, one role each. For your role, write one specific act a first-year teacher could perform next Monday that would express it. It must be something a person with no authority and no budget could actually do, and it must be observable: someone watching the classroom should be able to see that it happened. Read the five aloud. Then, as a group, identify which two of the five acts would be hardest to sustain for a whole term, and say what would make them fail. Allow 25 minutes.

Name the five roles and give one concrete classroom act for each. (Remember) Explain the difference between a teacher who tries new things and a teacher in the researcher role. (Understand) Why is facilitation not the same as talking less? Give an example of a topic that should simply be explained. (Apply) Explain why a new teacher who criticises everything is not acting as a change agent, and what they would have to do first. (Analyze) Explain why reading the timeline as a sequence of replacements is a mistake, and what damage that reading does. (Analyze)

Five roles have been added to the teacher's job beyond transmitting content. The facilitator arranges conditions so pupils do the thinking, judging which parts of a topic are worth working out and which should be told. The researcher treats their own classroom as evidence about their own practice, and is what converts a tried change into a learned one. The change agent improves something beyond their own room, which requires standing earned by ordinary competence first. The moral agent recognises that teaching forms people and chooses deliberately what its habits teach. The life-long learner keeps developing afterwards, which is what makes the other four survivable, because each of them guarantees some failure. These roles are additions to transmission, not replacements for it. A teacher who facilitates but cannot explain has skipped a stage rather than advanced beyond it.

I can name the five roles and give a concrete, observable act for each. I can explain what the researcher role adds to simply trying new things. I can judge which parts of a topic warrant facilitation and which warrant explanation. I can describe a realistic change-agent act for someone with no authority. I can explain why the roles are cumulative rather than sequential.

Do one small piece of classroom research. Pick one thing you have noticed about your class, change one thing about how you teach it, and decide in advance what you will collect that would show whether it worked. The decision in advance is the whole exercise. A measure chosen afterwards will confirm whatever you hoped, and choosing it beforehand is what makes the result capable of surprising you. Write half a page on what you found, including whether you were willing to conclude that it did not work.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 450 to 500 words. Take Mr Imran's case from the top of this topic. Identify every role he exercised, and evaluate his decision to keep an approach whose results were slightly worse. Name each role with the specific evidence in the vignette, then argue whether keeping the approach was defensible. Your answer must engage with the obvious objection that results got worse and that a professional should follow the evidence. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Role identification (Apply) Names each role with the exact evidence, rather than asserting the roles are present Grasp of the researcher role Recognises that the comparison, not the innovation, is what makes his practice researched Evaluation of the decision (Evaluate) Engages seriously with "the results got worse", distinguishes the measure from the learning, and reaches a defended verdict rather than praising him for trying Use of evidence Distinguishes what the vignette states from what is inferred

Brookfield, S. D. (2017). Becoming a critically reflective teacher (2nd ed.). Jossey-Bass. Suarez, V., & McGrath, J. (2022). Teacher professional identity: How to develop and support it in times of change (OECD Education Working Paper No. 267). OECD Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1787/b19f5af7-en

Teacher effectiveness means the effect a teacher has on pupils' learning, but the definitions in use disagree about which effects count. Achievement gain counts what the test tests; observed practice can be satisfied by a performance; breadth of learner outcomes counts more of what matters and measures it less reliably. Institutions often state one definition and appraise against another. More workable than a single definition is a set of components, within the classroom and beyond it, held as evidence rather than summed into a score. The qualities a teacher brings work on those components rather than producing learning directly. Attitude toward the profession is a stance rather than a feeling. Professional image is layered, with appearance the thin outer band and competence the core. Each of the seven named traits has a failure mode at excess which is the trait unbalanced rather than its opposite, so more is not better and "you either have it or you do not" does not hold. Humour is the one exception: aimed at a pupil it is the trait inverted rather than overdone, and it is corrected by changing target. Every stakeholder relationship exists for a purpose the work depends on, and is built by reliability rather than by being liked. Conflict is normal; the professional difference lies in moving the conversation, letting the person finish, admitting missing facts with a commitment, and escalating what is not yours while recording why. Communication runs on two channels. Verbal communication explains, instructs, questions and responds, and questioning is where teachers most differ. Non-verbal communication runs on proximity, orientation, gaze, expression, gesture and vocal variety, and learners read it as evidence about teaching quality, on evidence drawn from university students rather than schoolchildren. That the non-verbal channel prevails when the two contradict is a practitioner's heuristic worth acting on rather than a finding this unit's sources establish. Five roles have been added to transmitting content: facilitator, researcher, change agent, moral agent and life-long learner. They are cumulative, not sequential, and the researcher role is what turns a tried change into a learned one.

A teacher raises examination marks by narrowing teaching to past papers. On which definition of effectiveness does this look best, and which does it damage? (Understand) a) Best on observed practice; damages achievement gain b) Best on breadth of outcomes; damages observed practice c) Best on achievement gain; damages breadth of learner outcomes d) It looks equally good on all three Which of the following is a factor beyond classroom processes? (Remember) a) Contribution to colleagues b) Explanation and questioning c) Use of assessment d) Classroom climate A teacher's attitude toward the profession is best evidenced by: (Understand) a) stated enthusiasm for the subject b) ordinary conduct such as preparedness, punctuality and follow-through c) length of service d) qualifications held Empathy at excess most characteristically produces a teacher who: (Apply) a) is cold toward pupils in difficulty b) avoids contact with parents c) enforces rules inconsistently d) excuses everything and lowers what is expected The relationship between a teacher and a pupil's parents primarily exists so that: (Understand) a) the parent will act at home and the teacher learns what they cannot see b) the teacher is liked in the community c) complaints are reduced d) attendance figures improve In the de-escalation sequence, the reason for moving an angry conversation out of a corridor is chiefly that: (Understand) a) it is quieter b) school rules require it c) it protects the other person's dignity, and someone who has lost face cannot climb down d) it delays the conversation "Does everyone understand?" is a weak comprehension check mainly because it: (Apply) a) takes too long b) cannot be asked of a large class c) is too informal d) samples confidence rather than comprehension, and over-samples pupils already secure The claim that learners follow the non-verbal channel when the two contradict is best described as: (Understand) a) an established finding of the studies cited in this unit b) a practitioner's heuristic that descends from the same experiments as the 93% claim c) a claim disproved by Furlich's study d) a rule that applies only to university students A teacher changes one thing about a topic, decides in advance what evidence would show whether it worked, and keeps last year's results to compare. This is chiefly the role of: (Apply) a) researcher b) facilitator c) change agent d) moral agent The five evolving roles are best understood as: (Understand) a) replacements for transmitting content b) stages a teacher passes through in order c) alternatives from which a teacher chooses one d) additions on top of transmitting content

State three competing definitions of teacher effectiveness and, for each, name one thing it captures and one it misses. (Understand) Explain why summing the components of effectiveness into a single score is a worse instrument than holding them separately. (Analyze) Explain the layered model of professional image, and say why investing an evening in appearance before a first lesson is a misallocation. (Understand) Choose three of the seven personality traits. For each, state the working form and the failure mode at excess, and name what would balance it. (Analyze) State what each of the five stakeholder relationships is for, in terms of what part of the work depends on it. (Remember) A teacher answers a parent's complaint immediately and confidently and is later shown to have been wrong on a fact. Explain what this costs beyond the immediate error. (Analyze) Name the four jobs of verbal communication, and explain why the sentence immediately after a pupil answers is the most consequential one. (Understand) List five non-verbal channels and give the classroom use of each. (Remember) Explain the difference between a teacher who tries new methods and a teacher exercising the researcher role. (Understand) Explain why a newly qualified teacher who criticises established practice is not thereby a change agent, and state what would have to come first. (Analyze)

Integrative. Mr Junaid and Miss Shazia produced identical board results by opposite methods. Judge them both against the components of teacher effectiveness, drawing evidence from the qualities, relationships, communication and roles covered across this unit. Reach a defended verdict and state what further evidence would change it. (Evaluate) Take one of the seven personality traits and write a case study of a teacher whose strength in it became a liability. Identify what was missing that would have balanced it, and the point at which the teacher could reasonably have noticed. (Analyze) A parent arrives angry, in a corridor, in front of other parents, convinced their child has been penalised because the family cannot pay for tuition. Set out how you would handle the first five minutes and defend each move, then address the objection that de-escalation reads as the school closing ranks. (Evaluate) Design a short sequence of instruction for a topic of your choice in which the verbal and non-verbal channels are deliberately coordinated. Specify both channels concretely, and explain what each element is doing and how you would know whether it worked. (Create) "The five evolving roles are unrealistic for a teacher in a Pakistani government school with sixty pupils in a class and no resources." Evaluate this claim. Your answer must take the objection seriously, distinguish which roles it genuinely constrains from which it does not, and reach a position. (Evaluate)

c - narrowing to the test raises measured attainment while reducing the breadth of what was learned. a - contribution to colleagues sits outside classroom processes; the other three are within. b - attitude is read from ordinary conduct, which is why it cannot be asserted. d - the excess of empathy is excusing, which communicates lowered expectation. a - the relationship is instrumental in both directions: action at home, and information the classroom cannot supply. c - dignity, and the practical impossibility of retreating in front of an audience. d - it samples confidence, and the pupils who answer are the ones who least need checking. b - worth acting on, and not established by the sources cited here; discarding the number while keeping its conclusion would be the same citation failure. Calling it disproved by Furlich overstates: that null result concerned immediacy and motivation, not channel contradiction. a - the advance decision about evidence and the comparison are what make it research. d - cumulative; a teacher who cannot explain has skipped transmission, not surpassed it.

1. (6 marks) One mark per definition correctly stated (3); one mark per apt captures/misses pair (3). Achievement gain: captures learning, misses what the test omits. Observed practice: captures process, can be satisfied by performance. Breadth: captures more of what matters, measures unreliably. 2. (4 marks) A total conceals the judgements in the weighting (1); components serve different purposes and an instrument built for development is not fit for appraisal (1); components interact, so a sum implies an independence that does not hold (1); a number invites comparison it cannot support (1). 3. (4 marks) Names the layers in order, appearance, conduct, reliability, competence (2); explains that appearance buys brief attention and is quickly spent (1); identifies that the inner layers carry a career and cannot be assembled overnight, which is why the evening was misallocated (1). 4. (9 marks) Three marks per trait: working form (1), failure mode (1), the balancing trait or component (1). The failure mode must normally be the trait unbalanced rather than its opposite. Humour is the exception: a candidate who gives "aimed at a pupil" as humour's failure is correct and should receive full credit, provided they identify it as inversion rather than excess. Do not mark it down for not being an excess. 5. (5 marks) One mark each: pupils, so confusion is admitted; parents, so action happens at home and the teacher learns what they cannot see; colleagues, so practice improves and handling is consistent; the institution, so things can be authorised and concerns heard; the community, so the school can ask things of it. 6. (4 marks) The factual error itself (1); the loss of the parent's trust in anything the teacher says subsequently (1); the precedent that the teacher answers before checking (1); the cost to the pupil, whose issue is now entangled with an adult dispute (1). 7. (5 marks) Explaining, instructing, questioning, responding (2); the response teaches the whole class what happens to people who answer (2); a wrong answer met with curiosity surfaces a misconception the class shares (1). 8. (5 marks) One mark per channel with an apt classroom use, from proximity, body orientation, gaze and eye contact, facial expression, gesture, vocal variety. 9. (4 marks) Trying is adopting or abandoning on how the lesson felt (1); the researcher forms a question and changes one thing (1); decides in advance what evidence would show whether it worked (1); is willing to conclude it did not (1). 10. (4 marks) Change requires standing (1); standing is earned by visible competence in the ordinary work (1); arriving critical ensures the criticism is not heard (1); states what comes first, namely doing the core job well and building credit (1).
documents.s: RRQ model answers and mark schemes

documents.t: Each ERQ is marked out of 20 across four criteria. A response that does not reach "Adequate" on the analysis or evaluation criterion cannot exceed 10 overall, whatever its other merits.
