Are the roles realistic? Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) Engagement with the objection Dismisses it Concedes real constraints Takes the strongest form of the objection Discrimination between roles Treats all five alike Separates constrained from unconstrained Argues per role with the specific constraint named Position reached (Evaluate) No position A position A defended position that survives the objection rather than avoiding it Contextual grounding Generic Refers to Pakistani conditions Uses specific conditions, such as class size or resources, in the argument

Five topics over three weeks divides naturally as 3.1 and 3.2 in Week 6, 3.3 and 3.4 in Week 7, and 3.5 plus the assessment in Week 8. Topic 3.1 must come first and must not be rushed. It establishes that effectiveness has competing definitions, and every later topic leans on that. A cohort that leaves 3.1 with one tidy definition will read the rest of the unit as a list of tips. If the block is compressed, compress 3.5. Its content is the most straightforward and the most recoverable later, whereas 3.4 needs the delivery activity to land at all.

Five, each named inside the topic that corrects it. "An effective teacher is one whose class gets high marks." The Junaid and Shazia vignette is built to defeat this. Do not resolve it for the class; let the three definition groups in the Topic 3.1 activity produce three different appraisals and let the class sit with the result. "Personality is fixed." This one stops trainees working on anything, so it is worth time. The strongest counter is the failure-mode column: if more of a trait can be worse, then "having it" was never the goal, and the question becomes which behaviours you enact in role. "Professional image means expensive clothes." Common in cohorts from lower-income backgrounds and quietly demoralising. The layered diagram exists for this. Be explicit that in most government schools an expensively dressed teacher reads as distant, not professional. "A good relationship with pupils means being liked." Trainees resist this correction because being liked is pleasant. The useful evidence is their own schooling: ask which teacher they trusted most and whether that teacher was the most likeable one. "93% of communication is non-verbal." This will be quoted by somebody. Correct it directly. It comes from Mehrabian's 1967 attitude experiments, and repeating it in an assignment is a citation failure as much as a factual one. Do not let the class settle for the usual replacement either. "The non-verbal channel wins when they disagree" descends from the same experiments, and the topic now marks it explicitly as a practitioner's heuristic rather than a finding. This is the unit's best opportunity to teach citation discipline, because the book applies the rule to itself.

Three practicum tasks in this unit involve observing a serving teacher: the appraisal enquiry in 3.1, the trait observation in 3.2, and the conflict interview in 3.3. Two cautions. These can read as evaluation of the mentor. Frame them before trainees go out: the task is to understand a system or a practice, not to grade a host teacher who is doing them a favour. A trainee who arrives with a checklist and a clipboard will damage a relationship the placement depends on. The 3.1 task can surface uncomfortable findings. Asking how teachers are appraised sometimes produces an answer that the appraisal is nominal, or that results are adjusted. Decide in advance how you will handle that in the debrief. The productive framing is what the measure rewards, which is a systems question, rather than what the school is doing wrong, which will get a trainee into trouble.

The Topic 3.4 delivery activity, in which one instruction is delivered four ways, fails if trainees change the words. They will, almost without noticing, because it is very hard to deliver identical words in a flat tone once you know the point. Intervene by writing the instruction on the board and requiring it verbatim each time. The whole finding depends on the words being constant, and the moment a group varies them the observer attributes the difference to the wording and the point is lost.
documents.s: The activity that most often goes wrong

documents.t: Seating-plan gaze map (Week 7). The Topic 3.4 transfer task is the single most reliably useful thing in this unit. Nearly every trainee discovers a neglected zone. Collect the maps and display a few anonymised; the pattern across a whole cohort is more persuasive than any individual result. Arrange peer observation pairs in advance, because trainees who have to find an observer usually do not. Classroom research (Week 8). The Topic 3.5 task requires deciding the evidence in advance. That is the part to police. Ask each trainee to tell you their measure before they teach the lesson, and record it. In the debrief, ask specifically who found that their change did not work, and treat that answer as the strongest result in the room rather than a disappointment. If nobody reports a negative finding across a whole cohort, the measures were chosen after the fact. Trait self-audit (Week 6). The Topic 3.2 material supports a private self-audit against the seven traits. Keep it private and do not collect it; a self-audit that will be read becomes a self-presentation.

The bank is on the unit assessment page with model answers and analytic rubrics. Two notes. The RRQ mark schemes are point-by-point and total more than a single paper should carry; select from them. And the ERQ rubrics cap a response that does not reach "Adequate" on the analysis or evaluation criterion at 10 out of 20. At this level the most common strong-looking weak answer is a fluent description of all five roles, or all seven traits, that never analyses or judges anything. The cap is what stops it scoring like a good answer. ERQ 1 is the integrative item and is the best single indicator of whether the unit landed, because it cannot be answered from any one topic.

Unit 2 asked how a teacher should act. Unit 3 asked what effective teaching is. This unit asks the question that follows both: can any of that be written down in a form that a whole system can use? That is what a professional standard attempts. It is a documented statement of what a competent member of the profession knows, values and can do, written so that training, hiring, appraisal and public accountability can all point at the same thing. The attempt is worth taking seriously and worth being sceptical about at the same time. A standard makes quality visible and comparable, which is the only way a system larger than one school can improve. A standard also flattens judgement into indicators, and what cannot be written into an indicator tends to stop counting. This unit teaches you to use standards and to see their limits, because you will spend your career being measured by them.
documents.s: The Professional Standards and Competencies for Teachers

documents.t: By the end of this unit you should be able to: Define a professional standard, distinguish it from a code of conduct and from a curriculum, and explain what question each answers. Describe global and national perspectives on teacher standards and explain how standards are used to pursue teacher quality and accountability. Describe the structure of Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers, including how each standard is internally organised and how domains relate to indicators. Use a standard to evaluate your own practice, and assemble defensible evidence against a single indicator. Explain how standards connect to teacher licensing, certification and appraisal, and analyse what changes when one instrument is used for both development and a promotion decision.

Units 1 to 3. Unit 1 supplies professionalism, accreditation and professional bodies. Unit 2 supplies codes of conduct, which standards are most often confused with, and the difference between the two is the first thing this unit establishes. Unit 3 supplies the components of effectiveness, which a standard is an attempt to write down in usable form.

Topic 4.1 - What professional standards are for - the concept, global and national perspectives, and the accountability argument. Topic 4.2 - Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers - the structure of the standards, the domains they cover, and how an indicator evidences a domain. Topic 4.3 - Using a standard on yourself - self-evaluation against an indicator, and what counts as evidence. Topic 4.4 - Licensing, certification and appraisal - where standards meet a career, and what happens when an instrument is used for a purpose it was not designed for.

Work through in order. Topic 4.2 assumes the purposes established in 4.1, and Topic 4.3 cannot be done without 4.2. Topic 4.3 is the one to do slowly. Self-evaluation against a standard is a skill you will use every year of your career, and most teachers never learn it properly, which is why appraisal so often feels like something done to them rather than something they participate in. A note on the primary document. Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers is referenced throughout and is not reproduced here. Obtain a copy and read it alongside Topic 4.2; this unit teaches you how it is built and how to use it, not what every line of it says.

textbook.com.pk A district education office has to decide whether to confirm two teachers at the end of their probation year. About the first, the head reports: "She is good. The parents like her, the class is quiet, and I have no complaints." About the second: "He is difficult. He argues in meetings. His results are fine." On that basis the office confirms the first and hesitates over the second. Nothing here is corrupt. Everyone involved is acting in good faith. But notice what the decision actually rests on: one head teacher's impression, expressed in terms that cannot be checked, compared with nothing. Now imagine the same two cases with a written standard on the table, and a requirement that the head's report cite evidence against named parts of it. The decision might come out the same way. It would at least be a different kind of decision, and one the second teacher could contest.

A professional standard is a documented statement of the knowledge, values and practice expected of a competent member of a profession, written in terms specific enough that someone can judge whether it has been met. Three features do the work. It is written. An unwritten expectation cannot be taught to a trainee, cannot be appealed against, and changes silently depending on who holds it. Writing it down is not bureaucracy; it is what converts an opinion into something that can be argued with. It is shared. The same statement applies across schools and districts, so quality does not depend on the accident of which head teacher you were assigned. It is specific enough to be evidenced. "Be a good teacher" is not a standard. "Plans lessons with clear learning objectives that take account of what pupils already know" is close to one, because you could look for evidence either way. The first thing to fix is the confusion the figure above addresses, because it defeats a lot of trainees: A code of conduct (Unit 2) answers how should I behave? It governs conduct, and the consequence of breaching it is disciplinary. A curriculum answers what should pupils learn? It governs content. A professional standard answers what does competent teaching look like, in a form that can be checked? It governs practice, and the consequence of not meeting it is developmental before it is disciplinary. They overlap. Most standards frameworks include conduct among their expectations, which is why Pakistan's standards contain a code-of-conduct element. But a standard is not primarily a rule about behaviour; it is a description of competent work. A misconception worth naming now: a standard tells you how to teach. It does not, and a standard that did would be a bad one. A standard describes what competent practice achieves and leaves the method to the teacher's judgement. That space is deliberate, and Topic 3.5's facilitator discussion is what fills it.
documents.s: The concept of a professional standard, and what it is for

documents.t: Standards frameworks are not a Pakistani invention or a donor imposition; they are close to universal in school systems that have tried to raise teaching quality at scale over the last thirty years. UNESCO and the International Task Force on Teachers published a global framework of professional teaching standards precisely to give countries a common reference point. What the international picture shows is a family resemblance rather than one model. Frameworks differ on: Scope. Some cover only classroom practice; others include professional conduct, collegial contribution and continuing development. Granularity. Some are a page of principles; others run to hundreds of indicators. Stakes. In some systems a standard governs entry to the profession and nothing else; in others it drives annual appraisal, pay and promotion. The differences matter more than the similarities when you are reading your own system's framework, because they tell you what the framework is for, and therefore how it will be used on you.

Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers were developed by the Ministry of Education in 2009, with support from UNESCO and USAID, and they are the framework this country's teacher education is built to. Topic 4.2 deals with them in detail. The national dimension matters for a reason beyond administration. A standard imported unchanged from a system with small classes, reliable electricity and a well-stocked library will contain indicators that a teacher in interior Sindh cannot meet for reasons that have nothing to do with their competence. A national framework is an attempt to state what competent teaching looks like here, under the conditions that actually obtain. That attempt can succeed or fail, and it is fair to examine a framework on exactly that question. When you read Pakistan's standards in the next topic, one useful test is to ask, of each expectation, whether a committed teacher in an under-resourced government school could demonstrate it.

textbook.com.pk A standard is put to four distinct uses, shown in the figure above, and a great deal of confusion about standards comes from not noticing which use is in play. Guiding initial training. The standard tells a teacher education programme what it is preparing people for. This is why your own degree is designed around it. Guiding continuing development. A serving teacher uses the standard to find the gap between current and competent practice, and to choose what to work on. Topic 4.3 is this use. Informing appraisal. A school or system uses the standard as the reference for judging performance. Topic 4.4 is this use. Public accountability. The profession uses the standard to make a claim to society: this is what we hold ourselves to. Unit 1's account of professionalism depends on being able to make such a claim. The four uses pull against each other, which the figure marks and which is the analytical point of this topic. A standard good for development is generous, developmental in tone, and safe to admit failure against. A standard good for accountability is precise, evidenced and consequential. Serving both fully in one document is correspondingly hard, and Isoré (2009), reviewing teacher evaluation across OECD countries, found this tension to be the central design problem of teacher evaluation systems rather than an incidental flaw in any one of them. She is careful to call the purposes conflicting rather than incompatible: systems that hold both exist, and they do it by deciding the trade-off openly instead of leaving it to chance. This gives you the answer to a common and reasonable complaint: standards are a bureaucratic import with no bearing on a real classroom. Sometimes true, and when it is true, the usual cause is that a framework built for one of the four uses is being applied for another. A development tool used for promotion decisions will be experienced as surveillance, and teachers will respond by managing their evidence instead of improving their practice. That is not cynicism about teachers; it is what any sensible person does when a tool for reflection is repurposed into a tool for judgement.
documents.s: Using standards to ensure teacher quality and accountability

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Below are six situations in which a teaching standard is invoked. For each, identify which of the four uses is in play, and say what the standard would need to look like for that use to work well. A university revises its B.Ed curriculum. A head teacher completes an annual report that feeds into a promotion decision. A teacher chooses which of three training courses to attend. A provincial minister answers a journalist's question about teaching quality. A mentor and a trainee agree what to focus on during a practicum. A district draws up a list of teachers to be transferred. Then identify the two situations in the list where a standard designed for a different use is most likely to be borrowed, and say what goes wrong when it is. Allow 25 minutes.

Define a professional standard and name the three features that make it usable. (Remember) Distinguish a professional standard from a code of conduct and from a curriculum by the question each answers. (Understand) Name the four uses a standard is put to, and state what each use requires of the standard. (Remember) Explain why "be a good teacher" fails as a standard while "plans lessons with clear learning objectives that take account of what pupils already know" comes closer. (Apply) Explain why a standard good for development and one good for accountability pull against each other, and what a system must settle in advance to serve both. (Analyze)

A professional standard is a written, shared, evidence-specific statement of what competent practice in a profession looks like. It differs from a code of conduct, which governs behaviour, and from a curriculum, which governs content: a standard governs practice and answers what competent teaching looks like in a checkable form. It does not prescribe method, and one that did would be a poor standard. Standards frameworks are near-universal internationally and differ in scope, granularity and stakes; those differences tell you what a given framework is for. Pakistan's national framework, developed in 2009 with UNESCO and USAID support, is the reference this country's teacher education is built to, and a fair test of any national framework is whether a committed teacher under local conditions could actually demonstrate it. Standards serve four uses: initial training, continuing development, appraisal, and public accountability. The four pull against each other, and most complaints that standards are irrelevant bureaucracy trace to a framework built for one use being applied for another.

I can define a professional standard and say what makes one usable. I can distinguish a standard from a code of conduct and a curriculum by the question each answers. I can name the four uses and identify which is in play in a described situation. I can explain why a development standard and an accountability standard pull against each other, and what has to be decided in advance for one document to serve both. I can test a framework by asking whether a teacher in local conditions could demonstrate it.

Ask your mentor teacher two questions: whether they have ever read the National Professional Standards, and what happens in their annual appraisal. Write half a page on the relationship between the two answers. The common finding is that the standards exist and the appraisal does not refer to them, or refers to them only formally. If that is what you find, identify which of the four uses is actually operating in that school, and which are absent.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Return to the two probationary teachers at the start of this topic. Argue whether introducing a written standard into that decision would improve it. Your answer must say specifically what the standard would change about the head teacher's report, identify which of the four uses is in play, and engage with the strongest objection: that a standard would let a compliant but mediocre teacher be confirmed while a difficult, effective one is not. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Grasp of the concept (Understand) Uses the three features of a usable standard rather than praising standards in general Identification of use (Apply) Names the use in play and shows why it changes what the standard must contain Engagement with the objection (Analyze) Takes seriously that evidence requirements can favour the compliant, and says what in the standard's design would or would not prevent it Specificity Says concretely what the head's report would have to contain instead

textbook.com.pk Sadia has been teaching Class 5 for two years. Her head tells her that her appraisal this year will be "against the standards", hands her a photocopied form, and moves on. The form has boxes. Some of them say things like "demonstrates knowledge of learners' development" and "creates a supportive learning environment". Sadia reads them and has no idea what she is supposed to write, or what evidence anyone expects, or whether her own honest answer of "some days" is permitted. This is what happens when a teacher meets a standards framework without ever having been taught how one is built. The form is not the problem. Not knowing the architecture behind it is.

The National Professional Standards for Teachers were issued by the Ministry of Education, Government of Pakistan, in 2009, developed with support from UNESCO and USAID. They are the framework against which teacher education programmes in Pakistan are designed, which is why they shape your own degree as well as your later practice. The architecture has three levels, and the figure above shows them nested. The standard. A broad area of professional competence. There are ten. The three internal parts. Each standard is divided the same way, and this is the piece Sadia was never told: Knowledge and understanding - what the teacher knows about that area. Dispositions - the attitudes and values the teacher holds in relation to it. Performance and skills - what the teacher can actually do. This three-part division is the most useful single thing in the framework, because it separates three genuinely different kinds of shortfall. A teacher may know the theory of assessment, believe in its importance, and still be unable to write a decent test item. Those are three different problems with three different remedies, and a framework that only asked "is this teacher good at assessment?" would hide the distinction. Indicators. Beneath the parts sit indicators: specific, observable statements of what meeting that part looks like in practice. Indicators are what an appraiser actually looks for and what a teacher actually collects evidence against.
documents.s: The structure of Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers

documents.t: textbook.com.pk The ten standards cover the following areas: Subject matter knowledge Human growth and development Knowledge of Islamic ethical values and social life skills Instructional planning and strategies Assessment Learning environment Effective communication and proficient use of information and communication technologies Collaboration and partnership Continuous professional development and code of conduct Teaching of English as a second or foreign language Read that list against the previous three units and the design becomes legible. Standard 9 contains Unit 2's code of conduct and Unit 6's continuing development. Standard 6 is Unit 3's classroom climate. Standard 8 is Unit 3's relationships with colleagues and community. The framework is not a separate subject from the rest of this course; it is the course written in the form a system can act on. Three observations about the list itself, which are the kind of thing you should notice about any framework. It is a mixture of kinds. Some entries are knowledge areas (subject matter, human development), some are practices (planning, assessment), one is a values area, and one is subject-specific (English language teaching). That mixture is normal in national frameworks and it means the standards are not parallel: they cannot all be evidenced the same way. It reflects a particular country at a particular time. The inclusion of English language teaching and of information technology tells you what Pakistan's education system judged itself to be short of in 2009. The full text matters and is not here. This topic teaches the architecture. The standards themselves, with their indicators, are in the document, and you should read it. Per the citation policy of this course, the primary document is referenced rather than reproduced.

An indicator is where a framework becomes usable or becomes theatre, so it repays attention. Goe, Bell and Little (2008) reach the same point from the measurement side: there is no single measure that captures every way a teacher contributes, so multiple measures, each designed for a different aspect, have to be used together. A good indicator is observable, specific to the standard, and achievable under real conditions. Consider three attempts at an indicator for the learning-environment standard: "Maintains a positive classroom climate." Not observable. Two appraisers would disagree and neither could be shown wrong. "Displays pupils' work on the classroom walls." Observable and specific, and a poor indicator, because it can be satisfied in an afternoon by a teacher whose climate is hostile. It measures a proxy that is easier to produce than the thing itself. "Pupils volunteer answers, including incorrect ones, without prompting." Observable, genuinely difficult to fake, and closely tied to what the standard is about. The third is harder to assess and worth far more. This is the recurring trade-off in indicator design: the easier an indicator is to check, the more likely it is to measure a proxy. Now trace one practice through the whole architecture, which is the skill this topic exists to build. Sadia notices that when she asks a question, the same four pupils answer. Standard: learning environment. Part: performance and skills, since she knows why it matters and cares about it; what she cannot yet do is change it. Indicator: pupils across the room, not only the front, contribute without prompting. Evidence: a seating map with contributions marked, which is precisely the Topic 3.4 practicum task. That trace is what Sadia needed and did not have. With it, the photocopied form stops being a mystery: each box is a standard, what goes in it is evidence against an indicator, and "some days" becomes a defensible answer if you can say which days and what you are doing about it. A misconception to name: meeting the indicators is the goal. It is not. The indicator is a sign of the thing, not the thing. A teacher who pursues indicators directly, by displaying work they did not value or recording contributions they engineered, has optimised the sign and abandoned what it signified. Unit 3's warning about measures that can be satisfied without teaching better is the same warning in a different place.
documents.s: Indicators, and how a domain is evidenced in practice

documents.t: Work in pairs. Choose any three of the ten standards. For each, write one indicator that meets all three tests: observable, specific to that standard, and achievable in an under-resourced government school. Then write one deliberately bad indicator for the same standard that would be easy to satisfy without the underlying competence. Exchange with another pair. Their task is to find a way to "pass" each of your good indicators without actually meeting the standard. If they succeed, the indicator needs work. Allow 30 minutes. The attempt to game a peer's indicator is the part that teaches, because it is exactly what a system does to an indicator over time.

Name the three internal parts into which each of Pakistan's standards is divided. (Remember) Explain why separating knowledge, dispositions and performance is more useful than a single judgement about a standard. (Understand) List five of the ten areas the standards cover. (Remember) Trace one classroom practice of your own from standard, to part, to indicator, to evidence. (Apply) Explain why an indicator that is easy to check is often a worse indicator, using an example. (Analyze)

Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers, issued in 2009 by the Ministry of Education with UNESCO and USAID support, are the framework this country's teacher education is built to. They are set out in three levels: ten standards, each divided into knowledge and understanding, dispositions, and performance and skills, with indicators beneath that state observably what meeting a part looks like. The three-part division is the framework's most useful feature, because it separates knowing, valuing and being able to do, which are different shortfalls with different remedies. The ten standards mix knowledge areas, practices, a values area and a subject-specific area, so they cannot all be evidenced the same way, and the list reflects what Pakistan judged itself short of in 2009. A good indicator is observable, specific and achievable under real conditions, and there is a standing trade-off: the easier an indicator is to check, the more likely it measures a proxy that can be produced without the competence it stands for.

I can describe the three-level architecture of the standards. I can explain what separating knowledge, dispositions and performance buys. I can name most of the ten areas the standards cover. I can trace a practice from standard to indicator to evidence. I can judge whether an indicator is observable, specific and achievable, and spot one that measures a proxy.

Obtain a copy of the National Professional Standards for Teachers and read one standard in full, including its knowledge, dispositions and performance statements. Then watch one lesson at your practicum school with only that standard in front of you. Record what you observed against its indicators, noting where you could not tell from observation alone and what else you would have needed. Write half a page on what observation can and cannot establish about that standard. Most trainees discover that the dispositions part is nearly impossible to evidence by watching, which is a real limitation of appraisal by observation and prepares Topic 4.3.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

Your answer must set out the three levels, trace her specific problem from standard to evidence, and address why her honest answer of "some days" is or is not an acceptable thing to record. textbook.com.pk Two teachers in the same school are told to complete a self-evaluation against the standards. Nadia works through the whole framework, ticks "satisfactory" in most boxes, "good" in a few, and finishes in forty minutes. Her form is complete, consistent and entirely useless. She has learned nothing, and neither will anyone reading it. Kashif picks one indicator, about pupils contributing without prompting. He records who contributes for three lessons, finds that eleven of his thirty-eight pupils never speak, and writes that down. His form looks worse than Nadia's. It is the only one of the two that will change anything.

Self-evaluation against a standard is a cycle, not a form. The figure above gives the five stations, and the discipline is in doing them one indicator at a time. Choose one indicator. Not a standard, not a domain: one indicator. This is the instruction trainees most often ignore, and ignoring it is what produced Nadia's forty minutes. A framework with ten standards and many indicators cannot be worked on at once, and an evaluation that covers everything examines nothing. Choose by a simple test: which indicator, if you got better at it, would change the most for the pupils in front of you? Not the one you are weakest at in the abstract, and not the one that is easiest to evidence. Collect evidence of current practice. Before judging. This ordering matters more than it looks, because a judgement formed first will select the evidence that confirms it. Kashif counted before he concluded. Judge the gap honestly. Against the indicator's wording, not against your intentions. The useful question is what someone watching would have recorded, not what you were trying to do. Plan one change. Specific, small, and yours to make without permission. Re-collect the same evidence. The same measure, so the comparison means something. This is Unit 3's researcher role applied to yourself, and it is the station that converts self-evaluation from an opinion into a finding. The cycle breaks in two predictable places, marked in the figure. One is choosing too many indicators, which produces Nadia's form. The other is subtler and worse: changing the evidence rather than the practice. A teacher who finds that eleven pupils never speak and responds by calling on them once each on the day of the observation has improved the record and changed nothing.
documents.s: Using a standard to evaluate your own practice

documents.t: textbook.com.pk This is Goe, Bell and Little's (2008) recommendation applied to one teacher: consider the purpose of the evaluation before choosing the measure, because a measure that answers one question well answers another badly. Standards are met by evidence, and the kinds of evidence available are not equivalent. The figure above sets them against each other; the argument is below. Pupil work. The strongest evidence for anything about learning, because it is the output the teaching was for. It shows what pupils can do. It cannot show how they came to be able to do it, which means it under-credits a teacher who inherited a weak class and over-credits one who inherited a strong one. Observation by a colleague. Shows practice directly, including the things a teacher cannot see themselves, such as which side of the room they neglect. It is expensive, it samples one lesson, and the lesson observed is rarely typical, because knowing you are observed changes what you do. Planning documents. Show intention and structure, and are the easiest of all to produce without the underlying competence. A beautiful scheme of work is evidence of an afternoon's writing, not of a term's teaching. Pupil voice. Pupils asked properly are surprisingly accurate about whether they feel able to ask questions, whether marking helps them, and whether the teacher notices them. It is the most under-used evidence in most schools. It requires care: pupils asked in the teacher's presence will say what is safe. The teacher's own record. Counts, tallies, notes kept over time. Weak as proof to somebody else and excellent for the purpose that matters here, which is finding out something you did not know about your own room. The practical rule: triangulate cheaply. Two kinds of evidence that fail in different ways are worth far more than one kind collected thoroughly. Kashif's tally plus five minutes of pupil voice would establish something neither could alone. A second rule follows from the whole topic and is worth stating plainly. Self-evaluation and appraisal must not be the same document. The moment a teacher's honest record of a weakness feeds a promotion decision, honest records stop appearing. Kashif's finding, that eleven pupils never speak, is the most professionally valuable sentence either teacher wrote, and in a system that used it against him he would never have written it. Isoré (2009) records the conflict between developmental and accountability purposes as a design problem rather than a failure of individual integrity. Her evidence that evaluation can distort what teachers do is specific to high-stakes schemes built on standardised test scores, so treat the general claim as a well-founded risk to design against, not as a measured law about every mixed system. Topic 4.4 takes that problem up directly.

Work in pairs. Each person chooses one indicator relevant to a class they teach or have observed. State it aloud, then plan two kinds of evidence from the figure that fail in different ways, and say exactly what you would collect, when, and what result would count as a gap. Your partner's job is to attack the plan on one question only: how could you satisfy this evidence without actually improving? Revise the plan until the attack fails or until you can say why the risk is acceptable. Allow 25 minutes.
documents.s: Activity: One indicator, two kinds of evidence

documents.t: Name the five stations of the self-evaluation cycle in order. (Remember) Explain why evidence should be collected before the judgement is formed. (Understand) Nadia and Kashif produced very different forms. Explain which is more professionally useful and why the better one looks worse. (Apply) For any three kinds of evidence, state what each shows well and what it cannot show. (Remember) Explain why self-evaluation and appraisal should not be the same document, using Kashif's finding as the example. (Analyze)

Self-evaluation against a standard is a five-station cycle: choose one indicator, collect evidence of current practice, judge the gap against the indicator's wording, plan one change you can make without permission, and re-collect the same evidence. It breaks in two places: taking on too many indicators at once, and changing the evidence rather than the practice. Kinds of evidence are not equivalent. Pupil work shows outcomes but not attribution; observation shows practice but samples an atypical lesson; planning documents are the easiest to produce without competence; pupil voice is accurate and under-used but must be collected carefully; a teacher's own record is weak as proof and excellent for discovery. Triangulating two kinds that fail differently beats collecting one thoroughly. Because an honest self-evaluation records weakness, it cannot safely be the same document as an appraisal that carries consequences. Mixing the purposes degrades the developmental one, which is a design problem rather than a failure of individual honesty.

I can run the self-evaluation cycle on one indicator without expanding it to cover everything. I can collect evidence before forming the judgement. I can name what each kind of evidence shows and fails to show. I can design a two-kind triangulation for an indicator I care about. I can explain why honest self-evaluation requires separation from consequential appraisal.

Run one full cycle. Choose a single indicator, collect evidence across three lessons, judge the gap in writing, make one change, and re-collect the same evidence. Three lessons is enough for the first four stations and probably not enough for the fifth to show anything, and that is a genuine finding to report rather than a failure of the exercise. Write half a page including what you would need to see a real change, and be explicit about whether you were tempted at any point to improve the record instead of the practice.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Nadia's form was complete and useless; Kashif's looked worse and was not. Evaluate the two self-evaluations, and design the system that would produce more Kashifs. Your answer must analyse what each teacher's form achieves, identify what in a school's handling of self-evaluation produces Nadia's behaviour, and propose concrete arrangements. Address the obvious objection that a system which never records a weakness against a teacher cannot hold anyone accountable. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Analysis of the two forms (Apply) Explains the professional value of each rather than praising honesty in general Diagnosis of cause (Analyze) Locates Nadia's behaviour in the system's handling, not in her character Design proposal (Create) Proposes concrete arrangements, including what separates development from appraisal, that a real school could adopt Handling of the accountability objection (Evaluate) Answers how accountability survives separation, rather than choosing development and ignoring it

textbook.com.pk A province announces a reform. From next year, the annual self-evaluation that teachers have been completing for professional development will also be used to decide promotions. The stated reasoning is efficient and sounds unanswerable: teachers already complete the form, the form is already aligned to the standards, and the province needs an evidence-based promotion process. Nobody is acting in bad faith. Within one cycle, the forms change. Weaknesses stop appearing. The "areas for development" section fills with things that are safe to admit and irrelevant to improve. Mentors find their teachers no longer bring them real problems. The province now has an evidence-based promotion process and has destroyed the only honest record of teaching quality it had. This topic is about why that was predictable.

Three terms get used interchangeably and are not the same thing. Certification is the confirmation that a person has completed the required preparation and met the entry standard for the profession. It is usually awarded once, on completion of an recognised programme. Your B.Ed, built to the National Professional Standards, is the mechanism by which you will be certified. Licensing is permission to practise, issued by an authority, usually time-limited and renewable. Where licensing exists, it separates "was trained" from "is currently permitted to teach", and renewal can be made conditional on continued professional development. Not every system licenses teachers; many, including much of Pakistan's public sector historically, rely on certification plus employment rather than a distinct licence. Appraisal is the periodic judgement of a serving teacher's practice. It recurs, and it is where most teachers meet the standards most often. The distinction matters practically. Certification asks was this person prepared? Licensing asks is this person currently fit to practise? Appraisal asks how is this person doing, and what next? A system that runs all three through one instrument is asking one document to answer three different questions about three different time horizons. The figure above maps where each lands across a career. Notice how many of the points are entry gates and how few are about the twenty-five years after them, which is the structural weakness of most teacher-quality systems: enormous attention to getting in, very little to what happens afterwards.

textbook.com.pk Isoré (2009), reviewing teacher evaluation across OECD countries, identifies the division that organises the whole field: Formative appraisal exists to improve practice. Its question is what to work on next. For it to work, a teacher must be able to say "I cannot do this yet" without cost. Its natural evidence is Kashif's tally from Topic 4.3, and its natural output is a development plan. Summative appraisal exists to reach a decision: confirm, promote, pay, or in serious cases remove. Its question is whether a threshold has been met. For it to work it must be comparable across teachers, properly evidenced, and appealable. The requirements are not merely different; they pull against each other, which is what the bar across the figure marks: Formative appraisal needs candour; summative appraisal penalises candour. Formative appraisal is best done by someone trusted, ideally a mentor; summative appraisal must be done by someone with authority and distance. Formative appraisal should focus on the weakest area; summative appraisal invites a teacher to present their strongest. Be careful how strongly you state this. Isoré calls the two purposes "often conflicting", and then immediately adds "but not necessarily incompatible". She reports that countries rarely use a pure form of either, that a single framework "can serve both summative and formative purposes", and she devotes an annex section to conciliating the summative and formative purposes in a comprehensive approach. The tension is real and it is the design problem of the field. It is not a proof that one document can never do both. What follows from that is practical rather than defeatist. A system that wants both must decide in advance which purpose each conversation serves, who sees what, and what carries consequence. Where that is left unstated, the summative purpose wins by default, because it is the one with a decision attached. A teacher facing one document serving both will resolve the conflict rationally, by treating it as summative, because that is the version with consequences. Everything formative is then lost. This is not a failure of professional maturity. It is what the incentive structure asks for. A misconception this corrects: appraisal and professional development are the same process. They are related and must be connected, and the two purposes pull against each other inside any single instrument that serves both. The connection is that the summative judgement should identify a need; the development work on that need then happens somewhere the teacher can be honest. A system that wants one instrument to do both has to decide in advance which purpose each conversation carries, because otherwise the summative one wins by default.
documents.s: Appraisal, and the difference between formative and summative purposes

documents.t: The province in the vignette made a specific, common error, and Topic 4.1's four uses name it: a framework and an instrument built for continuing development were repurposed for accountability. Three consequences follow, and they are predictable enough to be worth memorising. The record degrades. Honest weakness disappears first. Within a cycle or two, the data the system relies on describes a teaching force with almost no development needs. Behaviour optimises to the indicator. Where the indicator is a proxy, as Topic 4.2 discussed, the proxy gets produced. Displayed work appears the week before observation. This is the same mechanism as narrowing teaching to the test in Unit 3. Trust between teacher and mentor is spent. A mentor who also reports on you is not someone you bring a problem to, and the mentoring relationship, which is the cheapest and most effective development mechanism a school has, quietly stops working. None of this argues against accountability. A profession that cannot be held to account has no claim on public trust, which Unit 1 established. The argument is narrower and more useful: accountability and development both work better when they are run through separate instruments that are connected deliberately, rather than one instrument asked to do both. What that separation looks like in practice is modest. A summative appraisal with clear evidence, comparability and a right of appeal, held perhaps annually. A separate, confidential developmental cycle of the kind in Topic 4.3, owned by the teacher, not collected. And a defined connection: the summative process may state a development priority, and the teacher's developmental work addresses it, without the developmental record itself becoming evidence.
documents.s: What happens when a standard is used for a purpose it was not designed for

documents.t: Work in groups of four. The province wants an evidence-based promotion process and does not want to lose the honest developmental record. Both aims are legitimate. Design the arrangement. Specify: what instrument is used for promotion and what evidence it draws on; what happens to the developmental self-evaluation; who sees each; and what the defined connection between them is. Then, as a group, identify the weakest point in your own design: where would a determined administrator, or a determined teacher, be able to collapse the separation you built? Allow 30 minutes, and spend the last ten on that question.

Distinguish certification, licensing and appraisal by the question each answers. (Remember) Explain what a system must decide in advance if one document is to serve both formative and summative appraisal, and what happens when it leaves that unstated. (Understand) The province's reform was made in good faith. Explain, in sequence, what went wrong. (Apply) Explain why a mentor who also reports on a teacher is less useful as a mentor, and what that costs a school. (Analyze) Someone argues that separating development from accountability means teachers are never held to account. Identify what is wrong with that inference. (Analyze)

Certification confirms that a person was prepared; licensing, where it exists, confirms they are currently permitted to practise and can be tied to continued development; appraisal is the recurring judgement of a serving teacher. Most systems concentrate effort on entry gates and attend far less to the decades afterwards. Appraisal serves two purposes whose requirements pull against each other. Formative appraisal needs candour, a trusted appraiser and a focus on weakness. Summative appraisal needs comparability, distance and appeal rights, and it rewards presenting strength. A single document serving both will be treated as summative, because that is the version with consequences, and the formative value is lost. Using a development instrument for accountability predictably degrades the record, optimises behaviour toward proxy indicators, and spends the trust that makes mentoring work. The remedy is not to abandon accountability but to run the two through separate, deliberately connected instruments.

I can distinguish certification, licensing and appraisal. I can state the requirements of formative and summative appraisal and show why they conflict. I can predict what happens when a developmental instrument is used for promotion. I can explain why the mentoring relationship is damaged by combined roles. I can describe a separation that preserves accountability rather than avoiding it.

Find out what actually happens in your practicum school's appraisal: who conducts it, what evidence is used, whether the outcome affects anything, and whether the same person mentors the teacher. Write half a page identifying which purpose the process actually serves. Many schools will turn out to run a process that is formally summative and consequentially inert, which is a third case this topic does not cover: an appraisal that decides nothing. Consider what that does to how seriously it is taken, and whether it is better or worse than the province's error.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 450 to 500 words. Evaluate the province's reform and propose what it should have done instead. Your answer must trace the mechanism by which the reform destroys the developmental record, distinguish the formative and summative requirements precisely, and propose a workable alternative that still delivers the evidence-based promotion process the province legitimately wants. Address the objection that maintaining two processes is unaffordable in a system already short of administrative capacity. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Mechanism (Analyze) Traces the degradation step by step rather than asserting that morale falls Command of the distinction States the requirements of each purpose and why they conflict in one document Alternative proposed (Create) Delivers the province's legitimate aim rather than refusing it, and specifies the defined connection between the two processes Cost objection (Evaluate) Engages with administrative capacity honestly, rather than proposing a design that assumes resources the system lacks

A professional standard is a written, shared, evidence-specific statement of what competent practice looks like. It differs from a code of conduct, which governs behaviour, and from a curriculum, which governs content. It does not prescribe method. Standards serve four uses - initial training, continuing development, appraisal and public accountability - and those uses pull against one another, which is the source of most complaints that standards are irrelevant bureaucracy. Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers, issued in 2009 by the Ministry of Education with UNESCO and USAID support, are the framework this country's teacher education is built to. They are set out in three levels: ten standards, each divided into knowledge and understanding, dispositions, and performance and skills, with indicators stating observably what meeting a part looks like. The three-part division separates knowing, valuing and being able to do. Good indicators are observable, specific and achievable, and there is a standing trade-off in which the easiest indicators to check are the most likely to measure a producible proxy. Self-evaluation is a five-station cycle run on one indicator at a time: choose, collect, judge, change, re-collect. It breaks by taking on too much and by improving the record rather than the practice. Kinds of evidence are not equivalent, and triangulating two that fail differently beats collecting one thoroughly. Certification confirms preparation, licensing confirms current permission to practise, and appraisal is the recurring judgement of serving practice. Appraisal serves formative and summative purposes whose requirements pull against each other: candour against comparability, a trusted appraiser against a distant one, weakness against strength. A combined instrument will be treated as summative and the formative value lost. The remedy is separate, deliberately connected processes rather than abandoning accountability.

A professional standard answers which question? (Understand) a) How should I behave? b) What does competent practice look like, in a checkable form? c) What should pupils learn? d) Which teaching method is correct? "Be a good teacher" fails as a standard chiefly because it is not: (Remember) a) written down b) shared across schools c) approved by a ministry d) specific enough to be evidenced A framework built for continuing development is used to decide promotions. This is best described as: (Apply) a) applying a standard for a use it was not designed for b) efficient reuse of an existing instrument c) a breach of the code of conduct d) summative appraisal working as intended Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers were issued in: (Remember) a) 1999 by the Higher Education Commission b) 2015 by NACTE c) 2009 by the Ministry of Education d) 2009 by UNESCO alone Each of Pakistan's standards is internally divided into: (Remember) a) aims, methods and outcomes b) knowledge and understanding, dispositions, and performance and skills c) novice, proficient and expert levels d) primary, elementary and secondary bands Which is the strongest indicator for a learning-environment standard? (Apply) a) Maintains a positive classroom climate b) Displays pupils' work on the classroom walls c) Keeps an up-to-date seating plan d) Pupils volunteer answers, including incorrect ones, without prompting In the self-evaluation cycle, evidence is collected before the judgement is formed because: (Understand) a) it is quicker b) the appraiser requires it in that order c) a judgement formed first selects the evidence that confirms it d) evidence is harder to collect afterwards Which evidence type is easiest to produce without the underlying competence? (Understand) a) Planning documents b) Pupil voice c) Pupil work d) Observation by a colleague Licensing differs from certification chiefly in that licensing asks: (Understand) a) was this person prepared? b) is this person currently fit to practise? c) how is this person doing this year? d) which subject may this person teach? A single appraisal document serving both formative and summative purposes will in practice be treated by teachers as: (Understand) a) formative, because development matters more b) neither, because it will be ignored c) summative, because that is the version with consequences d) both equally

Certification, licensing and periodic appraisal all apply the same standards at different career points. State what question each one asks, and explain why a teacher can hold a valid certificate and still fail a licensing requirement. (Understand) Distinguish a professional standard, a code of conduct and a curriculum by the question each answers and what each governs, and name one way national standards frameworks differ from one another. (Understand) Name the four uses a standard is put to, state what each use requires of the standard, and explain why any two of those requirements pull against each other. (Understand) Explain why a standard designed for development and one designed for accountability pull against each other, and what a system must decide in advance if it wants one document to serve both. (Analyze) Describe the three-level architecture of Pakistan's National Professional Standards, and explain why the ten standards cannot all be evidenced in the same way. (Understand) Explain what separating knowledge, dispositions and performance within a standard buys that a single judgement would not. (Understand) Give three tests of a good indicator, and explain why an indicator that is easy to check is often worse. (Analyze) Name the five stations of the self-evaluation cycle, identify the two places it commonly breaks, and explain for each break why it makes the cycle unable to show whether anything changed. (Understand) For any three evidence types, state what each shows well, what it cannot show, and how easily it can be produced without the competence. (Understand) Explain why a mentor who also writes a teacher's appraisal is less useful as a mentor, and what this costs a school. (Analyze)

A district must decide whether to confirm two probationary teachers, one well-liked with a quiet class and one difficult with adequate results. Argue whether introducing a written standard would improve that decision, addressing the objection that evidence requirements favour the compliant over the effective. (Evaluate) Integrative. A teacher is described as follows: she plans thoroughly, marks late, knows her subject well, rarely changes her approach when pupils struggle, and has a warm but quiet classroom in which four pupils do all the answering. Map this practice to specific standards and to the knowledge, dispositions or performance part in each case, then argue what her appraisal should say and what her development priority should be. (Analyze) Write an indicator for any standard that is observable, specific and achievable in an under-resourced government school. Then explain in detail how a teacher could satisfy it without the underlying competence, and revise the indicator to close that gap. (Create) Nadia's self-evaluation was complete and useless; Kashif's looked worse and was not. Evaluate both, diagnose what in a school's handling produces Nadia's behaviour, and design arrangements that would produce more Kashifs while preserving accountability. (Evaluate) A province decides that the annual developmental self-evaluation will now also determine promotions. Evaluate the reform, trace the mechanism by which it degrades the record, and propose an alternative that still delivers evidence-based promotion. Address the objection that two separate processes are unaffordable. (Evaluate)

b - a standard governs practice. "How should I behave?" is the question a code of conduct answers, and "What should pupils learn?" is the curriculum's. d - it fails the evidence-specificity test; it could be written and shared and still be unusable. a - the four uses make this diagnosis available, and it is the province's error in Topic 4.4. c - Ministry of Education, 2009, with UNESCO and USAID support. b - knowledge and understanding; dispositions; performance and skills. d - observable, specific, and genuinely hard to produce without the competence. Displaying pupils' work on the walls is the proxy trap: it is easy to arrange and shows nothing about whether the climate is safe to be wrong in. c - order protects against confirmation, which is why Kashif counted before concluding. a - planning documents evidence an afternoon's writing, not a term's teaching. b - licensing is about current permission and can be renewable; certification is about preparation. c - rational response to where the consequences sit, not a failure of maturity.

1. (4 marks) Certification asks whether this person was prepared (1); licensing asks whether they are currently fit to practise (1); periodic appraisal asks how they are doing this year (1); explains that certification is a judgement about past preparation and does not expire, while licensing is a judgement about present fitness and can lapse or be withdrawn, so the two can disagree about the same teacher (1). 2. (7 marks) Two marks per instrument: the question it answers and what it governs. Standard: what competent practice looks like, governs practice. Code: how to behave, governs conduct. Curriculum: what pupils learn, governs content. One further mark for naming a real way national frameworks differ, for example in scope, in granularity, or in whether they carry licensing consequences; accept any difference the unit's topic-01 supports. 3. (8 marks) One mark per use named (4); one mark per apt requirement (3); one mark for naming a real tension between two requirements, for example that development needs a standard safe to admit failure against while accountability needs one precise enough to carry a consequence (1). Initial training needs alignment with preparation; development needs generosity and safety; appraisal needs precision and evidence; accountability needs a public claim. 4. (4 marks) Development needs candour and appraisal penalises it (1); development is best with a trusted appraiser, accountability needs distance (1); development targets weakness, accountability invites strength (1); concludes that a system serving both must settle in advance which purpose each conversation carries, because otherwise the summative purpose wins by default (1). Do not award an answer whose conclusion is that one document cannot hold both: topic-04 teaches, from Isore's own wording, that the purposes are conflicting but not incompatible. 5. (5 marks) Ten standards, each a broad area of professional competence (1); each divided into knowledge and understanding, dispositions, and performance and skills (2); indicators beneath the parts, stating observably what meeting a part looks like (1); explains that the ten mix knowledge areas, practices, a values area and a subject-specific area, so they are not parallel and cannot all be evidenced the same way (1). 6. (4 marks) Identifies three distinct shortfalls: not knowing, not valuing, not able (2); explains that each has a different remedy (1); notes that a single judgement hides which applies (1). 7. (5 marks) Observable, specific to the standard, achievable under real conditions (3); easy indicators tend to measure proxies (1); proxies can be produced without the competence (1). 8. (9 marks) Choose one indicator, collect evidence, judge the gap, plan one change, re-collect the same evidence (5); breaks by taking on too many indicators (1); breaks by changing the evidence rather than the practice (1); explains that too many indicators leave each one measured too thinly to attribute a change to anything (1); explains that changing the evidence makes the comparison meaningless, because station five no longer measures what station two did (1). 9. (9 marks) Three marks per evidence type: what it shows, what it cannot show, ease of production without competence. 10. (4 marks) A teacher will not bring a real problem to someone who reports on them (1); the mentoring relationship is the cheapest effective development mechanism a school has (1); its loss is invisible because nothing visibly fails (1); the school retains the appearance of mentoring without the function (1).
