This unit describes conditions that are genuinely difficult and, in several respects, not the trainee's fault. Taught badly it produces either despair or cynicism, and cynicism in a pre-service cohort is expensive: it arrives before they have taught anything, and it is the burnout dimension Topic 5.1 warns about, acquired second-hand. Two things prevent that. Reach Topic 5.4. Do not let the block run out with the difficulties described and the response untaught. If you are short of time, compress Topic 5.2, not 5.4. A unit that stops after three topics is worse than not teaching the unit at all. Do not soften the description to protect morale. Trainees who are told that good technique overcomes sixty-two pupils will discover otherwise in their first term and will then distrust everything else the course told them. The unit's own answer is better: the conditions are real, some of them are not yours to fix, and there is still a short honest list of what is.
documents.s: The thing to get right in this unit

documents.t: Four topics over two weeks: 5.1 and 5.2 in Week 12, 5.3 and 5.4 in Week 13. Topic 5.1 is the longest in the course and carries five sub-topics. Give it two sessions if you can, splitting after burnout and before the multilingual and multi-grade material.

"Burnout is just being very tired." Correct this early and precisely, because the three dimensions do real work later. The most useful moment is the cynicism point: ask the class whether they have met a teacher who advised them not to bother with a weak class, and let them reinterpret that memory. "The home language is the problem." In some cohorts this is a firmly held position with institutional backing, and trainees may have been taught it. Argue it on cognitive load rather than on rights, at least first; the rights argument lands better once the practical one is accepted. "Integrating technology means using it in every lesson." Trainees who have seen technology used as display will recognise the correction quickly. "A teacher's status is fixed and nothing I do affects it." The status and recognition distinction is the repair. Do not let it collapse into "be respected instead of paid properly", which is a different and much worse claim. "The answer to difficult conditions is resilience." The most important of the five, and the one most likely to be reinforced elsewhere in a trainee's experience. Topic 5.4 names it directly.

Two predictable moments. Some trainees will say they chose teaching because nothing else was available. Topic 3.2 said this is common and should not be met with exhortation. In this unit it may surface more sharply, because the conditions are being described honestly for the first time. The useful response is that attitude is a stance rather than a feeling, and that this unit's final topic is about what remains available regardless of how anyone arrived. Some trainees will be angry, and the anger is frequently justified. Do not manage it away. Direct it: Unit 1's professional associations and Topic 5.4's second region, what you can influence, are where collective pressure belongs, and a cohort that leaves knowing the difference between what to endure, what to change and what to organise about has understood the unit.
documents.s: Handling what this unit surfaces about the profession

documents.t: Shadow and itemise (Week 12). The Topic 5.1 task. Reliable and often the most affecting thing in the unit: trainees consistently find that uncounted work exceeds timetabled work. Ask for the ratio rather than the detail in the debrief, and collect the ratios on the board. The distribution makes the point better than any individual account. Brief trainees that this is not an audit of their host teacher. The framing is "what does this job actually consist of", and a trainee who presents it otherwise will damage a placement. Three people, one question (Week 12). The Topic 5.2 task. If parent access is difficult in your setting, two respondents are enough; do not let the task be dropped because the third is unavailable. Judge one technology use (Week 13). The Topic 5.3 task. Many practicum schools will have almost no technology, and "there is none" is a legitimate finding. Redirect those trainees to a photocopied internet resource, which every school has and which raises the accuracy and alignment question. Place it and change it (Week 13). The Topic 5.4 task, and the one to protect if time is short. Require the change to be makeable without permission, and check that requirement when you read the half-pages. The commonest failure is a plan that depends on the head agreeing to something.

The bank is on the unit assessment page with model answers and analytic rubrics. ERQ 5 is the integrative item, and its Diagnosis criterion is deliberately the hardest thing in the bank. The remark about group work admits two defensible readings, and the unit teaches both: Topic 5.1's cynicism dimension, and Topic 5.4's accurate judgement about the third region being used to excuse inaction in the first. Mr Bilal is the worked case of the second, and topic-04 says plainly that he "is not wrong about the numbers". Do not award the Strong band for naming cynicism alone, and do not withhold it from a candidate who argues for the Topic 5.4 reading. Award it for distinguishing the two and arguing from the text which the evidence supports. Telling an exhausted judgement apart from an accurate one is the discrimination this unit exists to teach; a candidate who reaches for the first label is doing to the described teacher exactly what the unit warns against. Two marking cautions specific to this unit. First, RRQ 2 asks where each burnout source was conducted; that is deliberate, and a candidate who cites the studies without their scope should lose the mark, because this unit is partly about citation discipline. Second, ERQ 4 and ERQ 5 both invite an answer that is really a complaint about the system. A complaint may be accurate and it is not an answer; the rubrics cap it.

This is the last unit of the course, and it is the one that decides whether the other five were worth your time. Unit 1 said a profession rests on specialised knowledge that keeps developing. Unit 3 described the teacher as a researcher of their own practice and a life-long learner. Unit 4 gave you a self-evaluation cycle. Unit 5 ended on what remains within your control when conditions are hard. Every one of those was a promissory note. This unit is where they are paid, or not. The honest position is that most teachers stop developing. Not through laziness: through the ordinary operation of a hard job in which nothing external requires it, the available development is often poor, and the first years are survived rather than examined. Knowing that is the beginning of not doing it.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Define continuous professional development, distinguish it from a training course and from an appraisal requirement, and explain why continuing development is not optional for a professional. State the principles that distinguish development which changes practice from development which does not. Describe the preservice, new teacher and experienced teacher stages, the characteristic difficulty of each, and the support each actually needs. Compare conferences, workshops, online platforms, professional learning communities and reflective tools against cost, reach and what each can and cannot deliver. Explain reflective practice as a structured professional method rather than as keeping a diary, and describe journals, portfolios, peer feedback and lesson study. Build a personal professional development plan and defend it against the conditions that ordinarily defeat one.

Units 1 to 5. This unit assumes Unit 3's researcher role, Unit 4's self-evaluation cycle and Unit 5's control-and-influence distinction, and its job is to turn those three into something you do deliberately across a career rather than once during training.

Topic 6.1 - What continuing development is, and why it is not optional - the concept, the need, and the principles that separate development that works from development that does not. Topic 6.2 - The stages of a teaching career - preservice, new teacher and experienced teacher, and what each stage actually needs. Topic 6.3 - The ways teachers actually develop - conferences, workshops, online platforms, professional learning communities, and reflective tools including lesson study. Topic 6.4 - Building a plan that survives the year - what a plan contains, and what usually destroys one by March.

Topic 6.4 is the point of the unit and the point of much of the course. Do not treat it as a summary. It asks you to produce something real, and the plan you write there is intended to outlive this course. Topic 6.3 is the longest and most practical. If you are choosing where to spend effort, spend it there and in 6.4. The question bank covers all four topics, and its final extended item asks you to build and defend a development plan drawing on the whole course. That item is the closest thing this course has to a final examination of whether any of it was understood.

textbook.com.pk Mr Naeem has taught Class 7 mathematics for five years. In that time he has attended eleven in-service workshops, because attendance is recorded and the district requires a minimum. He can tell you the titles. He has the certificates in a folder. Ask him what he does differently in a lesson because of any of them and he will, honestly, have no answer. He is not a bad teacher and he was not inattentive at the workshops. The eleven certificates are an accurate record of eleven days spent. They are not a record of any development, and the difference between those two things is what this topic is about.

Continuous professional development is the ongoing process by which a professional maintains and extends the knowledge, judgement and skill their work requires, across a whole career rather than at its start. The figure above sets it beside three things it is routinely confused with, and the distinctions matter practically. A training course is an event. It has a start, an end and a certificate. It may contribute to development and it is not development, in the same way that buying a textbook is not reading it. A qualification certifies that a threshold was met at a point in time. Unit 4's certification material applies: it answers "was this person prepared", past tense. An appraisal requirement is an obligation imposed by an employer. It may prompt development and its natural product is compliance, as Unit 4's account of mixed purposes explained. Continuing development differs from all three on the same axis: it is driven by the practitioner, it is continuous rather than episodic, and its measure is a change in what you actually do, not attendance, certification or compliance. That last point disposes of Mr Naeem's folder. Eleven certificates measure eleven attendances. Guskey (2000), writing about how professional development should be evaluated, argues that evaluation must reach beyond participants' satisfaction and even beyond what they learned, to whether their practice changed and whether pupils' outcomes changed. Most systems stop at the first level, because satisfaction is the easiest thing to measure. Unit 4's warning about indicators that are easy to check applies exactly here. A misconception to name at once: professional development means attending a workshop. It is the commonest belief in the field, it is what produces Mr Naeem's folder, and the rest of this unit is an argument against it.

Why is this obligatory rather than admirable? Four reasons, and the first two are the ones a sceptical trainee will accept. The knowledge base changes. What is known about how pupils learn, what the curriculum requires and what the examination demands all move. A teacher working from what they were taught in 2026 will, by 2040, be teaching from a settled picture that is no longer the picture. Your pupils change. The intake shifts, languages shift, what children arrive knowing shifts. Unit 5's multilingual and multi-grade material is a live example: a method that worked for one cohort does not transfer unexamined. Initial preparation cannot be sufficient, by construction. A B.Ed is three or four years against a career of thirty. No initial preparation in any profession attempts completeness; it attempts a foundation plus the capacity to keep learning. Unit 1's account of specialised knowledge as a mark of a profession implies this directly: a profession whose members stopped learning would have a static knowledge base, which is a trade rather than a profession. And the alternative is not stability but drift. This is the reason teachers underestimate. A practice that is not examined does not stay the same; it slowly adapts to convenience. Marking gets lighter, explanations get shorter, the same three pupils answer every question. Nobody decides any of it. Kwakman (2003) studied what makes teachers participate in professional learning activities, which is the right question: participation is not automatic even when opportunity exists, and understanding why is more useful than exhorting people to develop. Note that this unit cites that work only for the question it asks; its abstract was not available when this unit was written, so no finding from it is claimed here. Two things should be said plainly about the Pakistani context. Much available in-service provision is of the kind Mr Naeem attended: one-day, generic, delivered to a hall. And the structural supports that make development easy elsewhere, protected time, a subject specialist to ask, a library, are frequently absent, as Unit 5 described. Both are described here from the course guide and from ordinary observation rather than from a study; no verifiable source for the Pakistani picture was located. Neither removes the obligation, and Topic 6.3 is built around what is available rather than what should be.
documents.s: The need for continuous professional learning and development

documents.t: textbook.com.pk The figure above states the principles as branches and, more usefully, names what each one rules out. The international review literature on teacher development, including Villegas-Reimers' survey for UNESCO's International Institute for Educational Planning (2003), converges on a recognisable set. Sustained over time. Development that changes practice happens over months, not in a day. This rules out the one-day event as a complete intervention, which is most of what is offered. Embedded in your own classroom. The gap between knowing a technique and using it with your Class 7 on a Tuesday is where most development dies. This rules out development that never touches your actual room. Focused on specific content and specific pupils. "Improving questioning" is too general to act on; "getting the back three rows to answer in Class 7 mathematics" is not. This rules out the generic workshop. Collaborative. Development done alongside colleagues persists, because the colleagues remain after the event ends. This rules out the individual attending alone and returning to a staffroom with no shared vocabulary for what they learned. Supported by feedback on real practice. Someone has to see what you actually do. This rules out development that consists entirely of being told things. Chosen rather than assigned. A teacher developing something they identified will persist through difficulty; a teacher sent on a course will not. Unit 4's separation of development from appraisal is the same principle from the other side. Read those six against Mr Naeem's eleven workshops and the result is immediate: generic, one-day, off-site, individual, assigned, with no follow-up and no observation of his practice. His folder is not evidence of a lazy teacher. It is evidence of a provision that violates every principle at once, and it is what most in-service provision looks like. The practical consequence is not to refuse what is offered. It is to know what a given activity can and cannot do, which is Topic 6.3, and to supply the missing principles yourself where you can, which is Topic 6.4.

Work in groups of three. Take a real professional development activity that someone in the group has attended or heard described, in any subject. Score it against the six principles: for each, is it satisfied, partly satisfied, or absent? Then answer two questions. Which principles could have been added cheaply, without changing the activity itself? And which of those could a participating teacher have supplied for themselves, without anyone's permission? Allow 25 minutes. The second question is the one that matters, and it usually produces at least two answers nobody had considered.

Distinguish continuing professional development from a training course, a qualification and an appraisal requirement. (Understand) Explain why eleven certificates are not evidence of development, using what evaluation should reach beyond. (Apply) Give four reasons continuing development is an obligation rather than an optional extra. (Remember) Explain what is meant by saying the alternative to development is drift rather than stability. (Understand) Name the six principles, and for any three state what that principle rules out. (Remember) Score Mr Naeem's workshops against the principles and explain what his folder actually demonstrates. (Analyze)

Continuing professional development is the ongoing process by which a professional maintains and extends the knowledge, judgement and skill the work requires. It is not a training course, which is an event; not a qualification, which certifies a past threshold; and not an appraisal requirement, which produces compliance. It is driven by the practitioner, continuous, and measured by a change in practice rather than by attendance. It is obligatory rather than admirable for four reasons: the knowledge base changes, the pupils change, initial preparation cannot be complete by construction, and the alternative to examined practice is not stability but drift toward convenience. Development that changes practice is sustained, embedded in the teacher's own classroom, focused on specific content and pupils, collaborative, supported by feedback on real practice, and chosen rather than assigned. Most available provision violates all six at once, which explains a folder of certificates and no change in teaching.

I can distinguish development from training, qualification and appraisal. I can explain why attendance is a poor measure and say what a better one reaches. I can give four reasons development is obligatory, including drift. I can name the six principles and what each rules out. I can audit a real offering against the principles and say which I could supply myself.

Ask three teachers in your practicum school two questions: what professional development they have attended in the last two years, and what they do differently because of it. Write half a page on the gap between the two answers. Be careful with the framing: this is not an audit of whether they are good teachers, and if it is heard that way you will get defensive answers and learn nothing. The honest framing is that you are trying to find out what kind of development actually works, and their experience is your evidence.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Mr Naeem has eleven certificates and no change in practice. Diagnose why, and design a single development activity for him that satisfies as many of the six principles as a real Pakistani government school could support. Your answer must score his existing provision against the principles, identify which failures are the provider's and which are his, and design something specific. Address the objection that your design requires time and colleagues that his school does not have. textbook.com.pk Three teachers sit in the same in-service session on questioning technique. Sana is on practicum. She has taught nine lessons in her life and is still working out how to stand. The session's advice about wait time is interesting and she has no room in which to try it, because she is concentrating on getting through the material without losing the class. Imran is in his second month of employment. He knows about wait time. He also has a Class 8 that talks over him, and everything he has been given assumes a room that listens. Mrs Aslam has taught for nineteen years. She has heard this session, or something close to it, five times. She could deliver it. What she has not had in nineteen years is one person watching her teach and telling her something true. The same session. Three entirely different needs, one of which it meets.

The preservice stage covers initial teacher education up to qualification: your own position now. What changes at its end is responsibility. A trainee observes, assists, and teaches under supervision with someone else accountable for the class. A qualified teacher is accountable. The characteristic difficulty is that almost everything is new at once, so attention is consumed by mechanics: where to stand, how to start, how to get thirty books collected without losing ten minutes. Sana is not failing to apply wait time; she has no spare attention with which to apply it. What this stage needs is structured practice with feedback, in a real classroom, on a small number of things at a time. Not more content. Day (1999), writing about teacher development across a working life, situates initial preparation as the beginning of a long process rather than as a loading of everything required. What is usually offered instead is a heavy content curriculum and a short practicum, which is the pattern in most systems including this one. The practical response is to use your practicum deliberately: the transfer tasks in this course exist because a practicum used for observation alone teaches much less than one used for structured trials.

The new teacher stage covers roughly the first three to five years. What changes at its beginning is that you are alone with a class and responsible for what happens in it. This transition is abrupt in teaching in a way it is not in most professions: a new doctor is supervised for years; a new teacher frequently has the same load as a colleague of twenty years' standing from the first week. That comparison is offered as a widely observed contrast rather than a sourced finding, and no study is cited for it here. The characteristic difficulty is survival. The demands are immediate and continuous, and the teacher has not yet built the automatic routines that later make room for thought. Imran knows about wait time, and his problem is not knowledge. It is that he cannot use it in a room he cannot yet hold. This is where two of Unit 5's findings become concrete. New teachers absorb the elastic work because they do not yet know they may decline it, and burnout risk is high at this stage for exactly that reason. What this stage needs is a mentor, reduced load, and help with the specific thing that is actually blocking them, which is usually classroom management rather than technique. Ordinary survival help. What is usually offered instead is the same generic in-service programme given to everyone, plus, frequently, the hardest classes, on the reasoning that senior teachers have earned the better ones.

textbook.com.pk The experienced teacher stage covers the long remainder, and it is the least served. What changes is that the mechanics have become automatic. Attention is freed. A teacher at this stage can do things that were impossible earlier: notice an individual pupil mid-explanation, change course in a lesson, hold a class while thinking about something else. The characteristic difficulty is that nothing external requires any further change. The classes run, the results hold, nobody complains. This is where Topic 6.1's drift operates, and it is slow enough to be invisible from inside. What this stage needs is genuine challenge: someone who will observe and say something true, a problem worth solving, a role that requires learning something new, contact with practice outside the school. Mrs Aslam's nineteen years without a single honest observation is the common case, not an unlucky one. What is usually offered instead is the same generic session for the fifth time, or an administrative promotion that removes them from teaching altogether. A misconception belongs here: experienced teachers have finished developing. The stage model says the opposite. The experienced stage is the one with the most capacity for development, because attention is free, and the least external pressure toward it. Capacity and demand are inversely arranged, which is why development at this stage has to be self-driven or it does not happen. A caution about stage models generally. These stages describe a common pattern, not a law. Teachers move at different rates, a change of school or subject can return an experienced teacher to something like the new-teacher stage, and long service is not the same as being in the experienced stage in this sense. Use the model to locate what you need, not to categorise people.

Work in groups of three, taking one of Sana, Imran and Mrs Aslam each. For your teacher, write what the questioning session actually offered them, what they needed instead, and one thing the session's organiser could have done to make it useful for your teacher specifically without abandoning the other two. Read all three out. Then answer as a group: is a single session for all three stages salvageable, or is the mixed-stage room the fundamental problem? Give reasons. Allow 25 minutes.

Name the three stages and state what changes at each transition. (Remember) Explain why the new teacher transition is more abrupt in teaching than in most professions. (Understand) Sana and Imran both know about wait time and neither uses it. Explain why, and show that the reasons differ. (Apply) Explain why the experienced stage has the most capacity for development and the least pressure toward it. (Analyze) Give, for any two stages, the support that helps and the support usually offered instead. (Remember) Why should a stage model be used to locate a need rather than to categorise a teacher? (Understand)

A teaching career passes through three broad stages. The preservice stage ends when responsibility transfers; its difficulty is that everything is new at once, so attention goes to mechanics, and it needs structured practice with feedback rather than more content. The new teacher stage begins with an abrupt transition to full responsibility; its difficulty is survival, and it needs a mentor, a reduced load and help with what is actually blocking the teacher, usually classroom management. The experienced stage is the longest and least served. Mechanics have become automatic and attention is free, so capacity for development is at its highest, while external pressure toward it is at its lowest. Its difficulty is that nothing requires change, which is where drift operates. It needs genuine challenge and honest observation, and is usually offered a repeat session or an administrative promotion. At every stage the support offered tends to mismatch the support needed. Stage models describe a common pattern rather than a law, and are for locating a need, not for categorising a person.

I can name the three stages and what changes at each transition. I can state the characteristic difficulty of each stage. I can explain why two teachers who know the same technique may both be unable to use it. I can explain the inverse arrangement of capacity and pressure in the experienced stage. I can locate myself and a colleague on the model without treating it as a label.

Find a teacher at each stage in your practicum school if you can: someone in their first years and someone with long service. Ask each the same question: "What would actually help you get better at this?" Write half a page comparing the answers against what this topic says each stage needs. The answers are often more specific and more modest than the topic predicts, and where they differ from it, the teachers are the better evidence.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. A district has budget for one professional development intervention, for all teachers, once a year. Using the stage model, argue what it should spend it on. Your answer must use all three stages, acknowledge that one intervention cannot serve them equally, and reach a defended choice. Address the objection that spending on new teachers abandons the experienced majority, or that spending on the experienced abandons those most at risk of leaving. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Use of the stage model (Apply) Applies all three stages with their specific needs, not a general plea for more training Recognition of the constraint Accepts that one intervention cannot serve all three, rather than proposing three Defended choice (Evaluate) States the criterion the choice rests on and answers the objection from the group not chosen Realism The proposal is deliverable once a year on a district budget

textbook.com.pk A head teacher has a small budget and one question: what is the best way to help her twelve teachers get better? She can send two of them to a conference in Karachi. She can bring a trainer in for one day for all twelve. She can buy data for an online platform. She can protect one hour a fortnight in which her teachers talk to each other about teaching. Or she can do nothing formal and require each teacher to keep a journal. The honest answer is that these options are not ranked, they are suited to different things, and the cheapest of them is probably the most powerful. This topic is the comparison she needs.

The figure above is the summary. The sections below give the reasoning, and each route is judged against the six principles from Topic 6.1: sustained, embedded, focused, collaborative, feedback-supported and chosen.

A conference gathers a large number of practitioners for presentations, usually over one to three days, usually away from the school. What it suits. Exposure to what exists beyond your own school, contact with practice you would not otherwise meet, and the discovery that a problem you thought was yours is general. For an isolated teacher in a rural school, that last effect is not trivial. What it cannot do. Change your practice on its own. A conference satisfies almost none of the six principles: not sustained, not embedded, rarely focused on your pupils, and the collaboration is with people you will never see again. Cost and reach. The most expensive per teacher of all five routes and reaches the fewest. The head's two teachers in Karachi will cost more than a day's trainer for all twelve. The defensible use is as a source of ideas that something else then develops, never as the development itself.

A workshop is a shorter, more practical session, usually delivered to a group, often in or near the school. What it suits. Transmitting a specific technique or a curriculum change to many teachers at once. If a new assessment format arrives, a workshop is the right instrument. What it cannot do. Produce the practice. A workshop can put a technique in your hands and cannot make it survive contact with your Class 8 on Tuesday. Mr Naeem's eleven certificates in Topic 6.1 are eleven workshops that stopped at the first level. Making one work. This is the practical part, because workshops are what you will actually be sent to. Three things convert a workshop from an event into development, and all three are within a participant's control: decide before you leave which single thing you will try; agree with one colleague who attended that you will each try it and compare in a fortnight; and decide what you will look at to know whether it worked. Those three supply sustained, collaborative and feedback-supported, the principles the workshop format lacks.

Online platforms deliver courses, video and materials at a distance, and have expanded rapidly. What it suits. Reach and cost. A platform reaches teachers a trainer cannot, at low marginal cost, on the teacher's own schedule, which matters when the alternative is travel a teacher cannot afford. What the evidence says, carefully. Hennessy and colleagues (2022) reviewed technology use for teacher professional development in low- and middle-income countries. Note that scope: this is the right literature for this sub-topic, unlike a general claim about online learning. What they report is that development opportunities in such countries are limited, often unsustained and frequently not informed by research evidence, that technology has real potential to extend both formal programmes and informal peer learning, and that outcomes so far are mixed. Mixed deserves emphasis rather than hiding. The potential is real and the delivery so far has not reliably realised it, which is the same verdict Unit 5 reached about classroom technology. What it cannot do. Observe you. No platform sees your practice, which means it cannot supply the feedback principle. Completion of self-directed online courses without an external structure is widely reported to be poor; this unit's cited sources do not establish that, so treat it as a working expectation to design against rather than a finding you can quote. In Pakistani conditions add the obvious: data cost, device access and electricity are real constraints, and a platform that assumes reliable connectivity is not available to many of the teachers who most need development.

A professional learning community is a group of teachers in the same school who meet regularly to examine their own practice and their pupils' learning, with a shared focus and an expectation that what is discussed is acted on. This is the route the head should probably choose, and the argument is that it satisfies more of the six principles than any other: it is sustained by construction, embedded in the school, focused on the pupils actually present, collaborative by definition, and capable of supplying feedback on real practice. That is five of the six; only teacher choice is left to how the school sets it up. What it costs. Almost nothing in money and a great deal in protected time, which is the scarcest resource in a school and the reason such groups are rare. One hour a fortnight, defended against everything that will try to take it, is the whole requirement. What defeats it. Three predictable things. It becomes an administrative meeting about timetables. It becomes a complaint session, which is a real relief and is not development. Or it avoids the specific, because discussing what happened in your classroom on Tuesday means admitting what did not work, and Unit 4's point about honesty requiring safety from consequence applies exactly. What makes it work. A specific question rather than a general topic, evidence brought from real classrooms, and a norm that saying "this did not work" is the most valuable contribution anyone can make.

textbook.com.pk Reflective practice is the disciplined examination of your own teaching against evidence. Brookfield (2017) treats it as a professional method rather than a disposition: the point is to see your practice through more than your own eyes, including your pupils' experience of it and a colleague's view of it. The misconception to defeat: reflective practice means keeping a diary. A diary of feelings records that Tuesday was difficult. Reflection establishes what happened, against evidence, and what to do differently. Four tools, each with a different strength. Journals. Cheapest and most under-used. The discipline that makes a journal work is the one from Unit 3: three structured sentences about a specific decision, not a general account of the day. Portfolios. A collected body of evidence about your practice over time: plans, pupil work, observations, your own notes. Its strength is that it makes change over months visible, which no single observation can. Its weakness is that it becomes a compliance exercise the moment it is collected for appraisal, which Unit 4 explained. Peer feedback. A colleague watches you teach and tells you something true. The most valuable and most avoided of the four. Its difficulty is not technical: it requires a relationship in which an honest observation will not be heard as an attack, and it requires that the observer is not also writing your appraisal. Lesson study. A group plans one lesson together; one member teaches it while the others observe the pupils rather than the teacher; the group examines what pupils actually did and understood; the lesson is revised and taught again. The figure above gives the cycle. Lesson study is the most demanding of the four and is worth describing carefully, because the detail that makes it work is counter-intuitive. Observers watch the pupils. That single rule removes the defensiveness that makes ordinary observation hard, because nobody is being judged, and it directs attention to what a teacher cannot see while teaching.

Work in groups of four. You are advising the head teacher from the top of this topic. She has twelve teachers, a small budget, and the five options. Produce a recommendation. It must name what she should do, say what she gives up, and specify how she protects it from the three things that defeat a professional learning community. Then present to another group, whose job is to argue for a different option as strongly as they can. Allow 30 minutes.

Name the five development routes and, for each, one thing it cannot do. (Remember) Explain why a conference is the most expensive route per teacher and what it is nonetheless good for. (Understand) Give the three things a participant can do to convert a workshop into development, and say which principle each supplies. (Apply) State what the review of technology for teacher development in low- and middle-income countries reports, and what that literature does not cover. (Understand) Name the three things that defeat a professional learning community. (Remember) In lesson study, observers watch the pupils rather than the teacher. Explain what that rule achieves. (Analyze)

Five routes, suited to different things and not ranked. A conference buys exposure and contact at the highest cost per teacher and satisfies almost none of the six principles. A workshop transmits a specific technique to many at once and cannot produce the practice, though a participant can supply the missing principles by deciding in advance what to try, agreeing with a colleague, and deciding what evidence would show it worked. Online platforms buy reach and low marginal cost, and the review evidence for low- and middle-income countries reports real potential with mixed outcomes so far. No platform observes your practice, and data, devices and electricity are genuine constraints. A professional learning community satisfies more of the principles than any other route and costs almost nothing but protected time. It is defeated by becoming an administrative meeting, by becoming a complaint session, or by avoiding the specific. Reflective practice is disciplined examination against evidence, not a diary. Journals are cheapest, portfolios make change over time visible, peer feedback is the most valuable and most avoided, and lesson study is the most demanding, with observers watching pupils rather than the teacher.

I can compare the five routes on cost, reach and what each cannot do. I can convert a workshop I am sent to into something that changes my practice. I can state what the technology evidence covers and what it does not. I can name what defeats a professional learning community and how to protect one. I can explain the lesson study cycle and why observers watch the pupils.

Ask whether teachers in your practicum school ever watch each other teach. If they do, ask what happens afterwards. If they do not, ask why not, and listen for whether the reason is time, timetable, or something about how an observation would be received. Write half a page on what you learn. The answer to "why not" is usually the third reason, and it is the one this topic says matters most.

Then set out specifically how the arrangement is protected from whatever ordinarily destroys it. textbook.com.pk In September, Miss Hina writes a professional development plan because her school asks for one. It has six goals. It says she will improve her questioning, integrate technology, develop better assessment practices, build stronger parent relationships, read more widely in her subject, and attend a conference. By March she has done none of it, and she feels vaguely guilty about a document she has not reopened since September. Nothing is wrong with Miss Hina. The plan was defeated before it began, and the specific reasons are predictable enough to design against.

A professional development plan is a short written statement of what you intend to get better at, how, and how you will know. One page is the right length. Six blocks, shown in the figure above. The gap, stated specifically. Not "questioning" but "in Class 7, the same four pupils answer every question and I do not know what the other thirty-four understand". Unit 4's indicator discipline applies: a gap you cannot observe is a gap you cannot close. The evidence that the gap is real. Not a feeling. A tally, a set of pupil work, a colleague's observation. This block is what stops a plan being a list of virtues. One goal. One. This is the block Miss Hina's plan violated six times over, and it is the single most common reason plans fail. A teacher with one goal in a year is unusually ambitious. The activity. What you will actually do: a lesson study cycle with two colleagues, a term of structured trials, a specific reading, a fortnightly conversation. Chosen from Topic 6.3 against what that route can actually deliver. The evidence that would show change. Decided now, in September, not in March. Unit 3's researcher discipline and Unit 4's self-evaluation cycle are the same rule arriving for the third time, which is deliberate: it is the rule most often skipped and the one that makes the difference between a plan and an intention. The review date. A date, in the diary, in the middle of the year, at which you reopen the plan and decide whether it survived. One more thing that belongs on the page and is usually missing: what you will stop doing, or who will help. A goal with no room made for it competes with a full working week and loses.
documents.s: What a personal professional development plan contains

documents.t: textbook.com.pk Four things destroy a plan, and each has a design response. Too many goals. Miss Hina's six. The response is the one-goal rule, and it is harder than it sounds because writing one goal means explicitly not addressing five things you know are weak. That discomfort is the plan working. No time was made. A goal added to a full week is a goal that loses to the week. The response is the block above: name what you will stop doing, or who is helping, or when the hour comes from. Unit 5's demands-and-resources framing is exactly this: you are adding a demand, so you must add a resource or remove another demand. No evidence was decided in advance. Then in March there is nothing to look at, and the honest answer to "did it work" is that you cannot tell. The response is the fifth block. No review date. A plan nobody reopens is a document, not a plan. The response is a date in the diary in the middle of the year, not at the end, because the end is too late to act on. The figure above adds the part most plans omit entirely: what happens at the review. Three outcomes are legitimate. Continue unchanged, because it is working and not finished. Narrow the goal, because it turned out to be bigger than a year. This is the commonest and it is a success, not a retreat. Replace it, because the evidence showed the real gap was somewhere else. Also a success: you have learned something true about your own practice, which was the point. What is not legitimate is quiet abandonment, and the review date exists to make abandonment a decision rather than a drift. A misconception to name, because it determines whether any of this is worth doing: a development plan is a document you write for an appraiser. If that is what it is, it will be written to look good and it will be useless, for exactly the reasons Unit 4 gave about mixing development with judgement. The plan described here is yours. Where a school requires a copy, a summary can be provided; the working document, with its honest statement of a gap, does not have to be the same piece of paper.
documents.s: Making a plan that survives a school year

documents.t: This is the end of the course, and it is worth naming what has been built. Unit 1 argued that teaching is a profession because it rests on specialised knowledge, a code, and accountability. Unit 2 gave the ethical obligations and two models for deciding when they conflict. Unit 3 described what effective teaching consists of and the roles a teacher now plays. Unit 4 gave the written standards and how to use one on yourself. Unit 5 described the conditions honestly and ended on what remains in your control. Each of those ends in the same place. A profession's claim rests on its members continuing to develop; the ethical obligation to teach competently implies keeping competent; effectiveness components are not fixed; standards are used for self-evaluation; and conditions are hard, which makes the question of what is within your control urgent rather than academic. The one-page plan is where all five become a single action. If you take one thing from this course, take the page.
documents.s: Closing: what this course was for

documents.t: Work individually for twenty minutes, then in pairs. Write your own plan, all six blocks, on one page. Use a real gap from your practicum or from your own schooling if you have not yet taught. Then exchange with a partner, whose job is to attack it on four questions only: Is the gap specific enough to observe? Is there really only one goal? Where does the time come from? Could you tell in March whether it worked? Revise. Allow 35 minutes in total, and keep the page: it is the deliverable of this unit and, arguably, of the course.

Name the six blocks of a one-page development plan. (Remember) Explain why "improve my questioning" fails as a gap statement and rewrite it so it does not. (Apply) Give the four things that destroy a plan, with the design response to each. (Remember) Explain why narrowing a goal at the mid-year review is a success rather than a retreat. (Understand) Explain why a plan written for an appraiser will be useless, referring to the separation of development from judgement. (Analyze) Why is the review date set in the middle of the year rather than at the end? (Understand)

A personal development plan is one page with six blocks: the gap stated specifically, the evidence that it is real, one goal, the activity, the evidence that would show change, and a review date. A seventh element is usually missing and matters: what you will stop doing, or who is helping, or where the time comes from. Four things destroy a plan: too many goals, no time made for it, no evidence decided in advance, and no review date. Each has a design response, and the one-goal rule is the hardest because it means explicitly not addressing weaknesses you know about. At the mid-year review three outcomes are legitimate: continue, narrow the goal, or replace it because the real gap was elsewhere. Narrowing is the commonest and is a success. Quiet abandonment is what the review date exists to prevent. A plan written for an appraiser will be written to look good and will be useless. The working document is yours.

I can name the six blocks and explain what each prevents. I can state a gap specifically enough to observe it. I can hold myself to one goal. I can say where the time for my goal comes from. I can decide in advance what evidence would show change. I can treat a mid-year narrowing as a success rather than a failure.

Ask your mentor teacher whether they have a professional development plan, and if so, whether they have reopened it since writing it. Then ask a different question: "What are you trying to get better at this year?" Many teachers without a plan have a clear answer to the second question, and many with a plan do not. Write half a page on what that tells you about the relationship between the document and the intention.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 450 to 500 words. Submit your own one-page plan, and defend it. Include the plan itself, then justify each block: why this gap, what evidence establishes it, why one goal and not another, why this activity given what Topic 6.3 says it can deliver, what evidence you will collect and why it would be capable of showing you were wrong, and where the time comes from. Finish by naming which of the four destroyers your plan is most vulnerable to and what you have done about it. Guskey, T. R. (2000). Evaluating professional development. Corwin Press. Day, C. (1999). Developing teachers: The challenges of lifelong learning. Falmer Press. Brookfield, S. D. (2017). Becoming a critically reflective teacher (2nd ed.). Jossey-Bass.

Continuous professional development is the ongoing process by which a professional maintains and extends the knowledge, judgement and skill the work requires. It is not a training course, a qualification or an appraisal requirement: it is driven by the practitioner, continuous, and measured by changed practice rather than attendance. It is obligatory because the knowledge base changes, the pupils change, initial preparation cannot be complete by construction, and the alternative to examined practice is drift toward convenience rather than stability. Development that changes practice is sustained, embedded in the teacher's own classroom, focused on specific content and pupils, collaborative, supported by feedback on real practice, and chosen rather than assigned. Most available provision violates all six at once. A career passes through three stages. Preservice ends when responsibility transfers; its difficulty is that everything is new at once and it needs structured practice with feedback. The new teacher stage begins abruptly with full responsibility; its difficulty is survival and it needs a mentor, reduced load and help with what is actually blocking the teacher. The experienced stage is longest and least served: attention is free so capacity is highest, while external pressure is lowest, which is where drift operates. At every stage the support offered tends to mismatch the support needed. Five routes are suited to different things. Conferences buy exposure at the highest cost per teacher; workshops transmit a technique and cannot produce the practice, though a participant can supply the missing principles; online platforms buy reach with mixed evidence and cannot observe you; professional learning communities satisfy more principles than any other route and cost only protected time; reflective tools range from journals to lesson study, where observers watch the pupils rather than the teacher. A plan is one page with six blocks: the gap, the evidence for it, one goal, the activity, the evidence of change, and a review date. Four things destroy a plan: too many goals, no time made, no evidence decided in advance, and no review. At the review, continuing, narrowing or replacing the goal are all legitimate; quiet abandonment is not.

Continuing professional development differs from a training course chiefly in that development is: (Understand) a) driven by the practitioner, continuous, and measured by changed practice b) certified by an external body c) longer d) required by an employer Eleven attendance certificates and no change in teaching demonstrate: (Apply) a) that the teacher needs a qualification b) a lazy teacher c) that the workshops were on the wrong subject d) that evaluation stopped at attendance rather than reaching changed practice "The alternative to development is not stability but drift" means that unexamined practice: (Understand) a) stays the same indefinitely b) improves automatically with experience c) slowly adapts toward convenience without anyone deciding d) becomes more demanding over time A workshop lasts a single day. Which principle does that one fact directly violate? (Remember) a) chosen rather than assigned b) sustained over time c) collaborative d) supported by feedback on real practice The new teacher transition is described as unusually abrupt because a new teacher: (Understand) a) is not permitted to ask for help b) has less subject knowledge than a trainee c) frequently carries the same load as a colleague of twenty years from the first week d) has no qualification The experienced teacher stage is the least served because: (Understand) a) capacity for development is highest while external pressure toward it is lowest b) no suitable provision exists anywhere c) experienced teachers refuse development d) experienced teachers have finished learning Which route satisfies the largest number of the six principles? (Remember) a) a conference b) a workshop c) an online platform d) a professional learning community In lesson study, observers watch the pupils rather than the teacher chiefly because it: (Apply) a) is easier b) removes defensiveness and directs attention to what a teacher cannot see while teaching c) avoids the need for planning d) produces a record for appraisal The single most common reason a development plan fails is: (Remember) a) the school did not approve it b) the goal was too difficult c) there were too many goals d) the teacher changed schools At a mid-year review, narrowing the goal is best understood as: (Understand) a) a legitimate outcome and the commonest one b) grounds for abandoning the plan c) evidence the plan was written badly d) a failure of ambition

Distinguish continuing professional development from a training course, a qualification and an appraisal requirement, by what each is for and who drives it. (Understand) Give four reasons continuing development is obligatory rather than optional, and explain the drift argument in your own words. (Understand) Name the six principles of development that changes practice, state what any three of them rule out, and explain why a one-day workshop fails the first principle however good its content is. (Understand) Name the three career stages, state what changes at each transition, and explain why the new-teacher transition frees attention rather than adding knowledge. (Understand) Sana and Imran both know about wait time and neither uses it. Explain why, and show that the reasons differ by stage. (Analyze) Explain why capacity for development and pressure toward it are inversely arranged in the experienced stage, and what follows for how that stage must be served. (Analyze) Give the three things a participant can do to convert a workshop into development, naming the principle each supplies. (Apply) State what the review of technology for teacher development in low- and middle-income countries reports, and name two constraints on online platforms in Pakistani conditions. (Understand) Name the six blocks of a one-page development plan, state what each one prevents, and explain why fixing the evidence in September rather than March is what separates a plan from an intention. (Understand) Explain why a plan written for an appraiser will be useless, referring to the separation of development from judgement. (Analyze)

Mr Naeem has eleven certificates and no change in practice. Diagnose why against the six principles, separate the provider's failures from his own, and design one activity that a real Pakistani government school could support. (Create) A district has budget for one professional development intervention, for all teachers, once a year. Using the three stages, argue what it should spend it on and answer the objection from whichever group you do not serve. (Evaluate) A head teacher has twelve teachers and a small budget. Compare at least three routes on cost, reach and the six principles, make a recommendation, state what is given up, and specify how the arrangement is protected from what ordinarily destroys it. (Evaluate) In September, Miss Hina writes a plan with six goals: improve her questioning, integrate technology, develop better assessment practices, build stronger parent relationships, read more widely in her subject, and attend a conference. By March she has done none of it. Critique her plan against the six blocks of a one-page plan and the principles of Topic 6.1, and rewrite it as a plan that could survive a year. Your rewrite must name what evidence you would look at in March, and say why you chose the goal you kept. (Analyze) Integrative, and the closing task of the course. Write your own one-page professional development plan and defend it. Justify each block: why this gap and what evidence establishes it, why one goal, why this activity given what it can actually deliver, what evidence you will collect and why it could show you were wrong, and where the time comes from. Draw on at least three earlier units of this course, and finish by naming the plan's own weakest point. (Create)

a - all three features together; length alone does not distinguish it. d - the certificates are an accurate record of attendance and evaluation never reached practice. c - drift is unchosen adaptation toward convenience, which is why it is invisible from inside. b - one day is the direct contradiction of sustained over time. Whether a workshop is also unchosen, solitary or unsupported by feedback depends on facts the stem does not give. c - the abruptness is about load and accountability, not knowledge. a - the inverse arrangement of capacity and pressure is the topic's analytical claim. d - sustained, embedded, focused, collaborative and capable of supplying feedback. b - the rule removes judgement of the teacher and directs attention to the pupils. c - too many goals; Miss Hina's six. a - narrowing means the goal met reality, which is the plan working.

1. (8 marks) Two marks per instrument: what it is for and who drives it. Development: maintaining and extending capability, driven by the practitioner. Course: an event, driven by a provider. Qualification: certifying a past threshold, driven by an awarding body. Appraisal requirement: an employer obligation, driven by the employer. 2. (6 marks) Knowledge base changes (1); pupils change (1); initial preparation cannot be complete by construction (1); drift (1); drift explained as unchosen adaptation toward convenience (2). 3. (8 marks) Six principles named (4); three "rules out" statements (2); explains that a one-day workshop fails the sustained-over-time principle however good its content, because a change in practice happens over months rather than in a day (2). 4. (6 marks) Preservice, new teacher, experienced (2); transitions: responsibility transfers; mechanics become automatic and attention is freed (2); explains that the new teacher already knows the technique and lacks the spare attention to apply it, so what the transition frees is attention, not knowledge (2). 5. (5 marks) Sana's attention is consumed by mechanics, so there is no spare capacity (2); Imran's block is a class he cannot yet hold, not knowledge (2); concludes that identical knowledge gaps can have different stage-specific causes (1). 6. (5 marks) Mechanics automatic so attention is free, giving highest capacity (2); nothing external requires change, giving lowest pressure (2); therefore development at this stage must be self-driven or it does not occur (1). 7. (6 marks) Decide before leaving which single thing you will try (1, and with the fortnight comparison below it supplies sustained); agree with one colleague who attended that you will each try it and compare in a fortnight (2, supplies collaborative); decide what you will look at to know whether it worked (2, supplies feedback-supported); one mark for correctly pairing principles to actions. Award the pairing mark for any answer matching topic-03's three principles, which are the ones the workshop format lacks. 8. (5 marks) Limited, often unsustained provision, not always research-informed; real potential to extend formal and peer learning; outcomes mixed (3); two constraints from data cost, device access, electricity, connectivity (2). 9. (10 marks) Six blocks named (4); what each prevents (4): vagueness, a list of virtues, dilution across many goals, an unchosen activity, a March with nothing to look at, quiet abandonment; explains that evidence chosen after the fact confirms whatever was hoped, so a measure fixed in September is what makes the review capable of surprising you (2). 10. (4 marks) A plan feeding judgement is written to look good (1); honest gaps disappear (1); Unit 4's mixed-purpose degradation (1); the remedy that the working document is the teacher's own and a summary can be supplied (1).
