documents.t: Each ERQ is marked out of 20 across four criteria. A response not reaching "Adequate" on the analysis, evaluation or creation criterion cannot exceed 10 overall. ERQ 1 - Mr Naeem's eleven certificates Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) Use of the principles Two or three applied All six applied Applied to the actual provision described, not to workshops in general Attribution Blames the teacher Separates provider from teacher Identifies what he could have supplied himself without permission Design (Create) Generic proposal Specific activity Startable on Monday and supplies the principles the provision violated Constraint (Evaluate) Assumes resources Notes constraints Designs within the absence of time and colleagues rather than around it ERQ 2 - One intervention, three stages Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) Use of the stages One or two stages All three with their needs Needs stated specifically rather than as "more support" Recognition of constraint Proposes three interventions Accepts one Explains what makes the choice genuinely exclusive Defended choice (Evaluate) Preference stated Choice with reasons States the criterion and answers the group not served Realism Not deliverable Deliverable Deliverable once a year on a district budget ERQ 3 - The head's twelve teachers Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) Comparison One route Three routes on some criteria Three or more on cost, reach and principles What is given up Not stated Stated Stated precisely, including who loses Protection (Create) None General intent Concrete defences against the three named failure modes Constraint (Evaluate) Assumes protected time Notes the difficulty Argues whether a head in an understaffed school can actually defend it ERQ 4 - Miss Hina's six goals, critiqued and rewritten Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) Diagnosis Says six is too many Names the one-goal rule Explains why six goals defeat a plan before March, not merely that they do Against the six blocks Names one or two missing blocks Names the missing blocks Identifies that the gap and its evidence were never stated, so nothing could be reviewed Critique against the principles (Analyze) Asserts the plan is weak Applies the principles of Topic 6.1 Shows which principles the plan could not have satisfied, and why that follows from its structure The rewrite One goal, no evidence One goal with evidence named Evidence chosen in September that could be compared in March, with the choice of goal justified ERQ 5 - Your own plan, defended (integrative) Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) The plan itself Blocks missing All six present The gap is stated so an observer could confirm or disconfirm it Fit of the activity Chosen by preference Justified Justified against what that route can actually deliver Evidence design (Create) Vague or retrospective Decided in advance Capable of showing the goal was not met, and the candidate says so Use of the course and self-diagnosis (Evaluate) No earlier units used Draws on three units Uses them substantively and names the plan's own weakest point honestly

This is the last unit of the course and the one that determines whether the previous five leave anything behind. Every earlier unit ends in a promise that only continuing development keeps: a profession rests on developing knowledge, competence is an ethical obligation, effectiveness components are not fixed, standards are for self-evaluation, and conditions are hard so what is within your control matters. The deliverable is Topic 6.4's one-page plan. If the block runs short, protect that session above everything else, including the assessment. A cohort that leaves with a real plan has got more from this course than one that leaves with a good examination mark and no page.

Four topics over three weeks: 6.1 in Week 14, 6.2 and the first half of 6.3 in Week 15, the rest of 6.3 and 6.4 in Week 16. Topic 6.3 is the longest in the unit and 6.4 must not be squeezed by it. If you are behind, cut the conference and online-platform sections of 6.3 to a brief treatment, and keep professional learning communities and lesson study, which are the two routes trainees can actually use. Teach 6.1 before anything else and teach the six principles properly. Every later topic is scored against them, and a cohort that has not internalised them will read 6.3 as a list of options rather than as a comparison.

"Professional development means attending a workshop." The commonest belief in the field and the one the whole unit argues against. Mr Naeem's folder is the intervention; let the class reach the diagnosis rather than stating it. "Development is what a system provides, so if none is provided none happens." Common and understandable in cohorts who have seen poor provision. The response is Topic 6.3's professional learning communities and reflective tools, which cost almost nothing, and Unit 5's control distinction. "Experienced teachers have finished developing." Trainees hold this and so, quietly, do many serving teachers. The inverse arrangement of capacity and pressure in Topic 6.2 is the repair. "A development plan is a document you write for an appraiser." If this survives, Topic 6.4 produces a page written to look good and the unit fails. Address it directly, and connect it to Unit 4's argument about mixing development with judgement, which the cohort has already accepted in another context. "Reflective practice means keeping a diary." Correct with the three-sentence structure from Unit 3 rather than by argument: show them what a reflective entry looks like beside a diary entry.

Topic 6.4's activity is the most important thirty-five minutes in the unit, and it fails in three predictable ways. Trainees write six goals. They will, despite the one-goal rule, because narrowing feels like admitting defeat. Enforce it during the session rather than in marking. Ask each person to read their goal aloud; a six-goal plan cannot be read aloud as one sentence and the exercise exposes itself. Gaps are stated as virtues. "I want to be more patient" is not a gap. Require that every gap names something an observer could see, and be prepared to send several people back to this block. The time question is skipped. "Where does the hour come from" is the block trainees leave blank and the one that decides whether anything happens. Do not accept a plan without it. Have trainees keep the page. Ask them to photograph it. A plan collected by you and filed becomes exactly the appraiser's document the topic warns against.

Development audit (Week 14). The Topic 6.1 task asks three teachers what development they have attended and what they do differently. Brief the framing carefully: this is not an audit of whether those teachers are good, and if it is heard that way the answers will be defensive and useless. Stage interviews (Week 15). The Topic 6.2 task asks a new and an experienced teacher what would actually help them. The answers are usually more modest and more specific than the topic predicts, and where they differ from the text, say plainly in the debrief that the teachers are the better evidence. Observation question (Week 16). The Topic 6.3 task asks whether teachers in the school ever watch each other teach, and why not. The third reason, about how an observation would be received, is the one worth drawing out. The plan (Week 16). Topic 6.4, described above.

ERQ 5 is the integrative item and the closing task of the whole course. It requires a real plan, a defence of each block, substantive use of at least three earlier units, and an honest naming of the plan's own weakest point. It is the best single indicator of whether the course was understood, because it cannot be answered from Unit 6 alone. Two marking notes. The rubric rewards a candidate who names their plan's vulnerability; a plan presented as having no weak point should not reach the top band, because the self-diagnosis is the skill being assessed. And a gap that an observer could not confirm or disconfirm caps the first criterion however well the rest is written. If you have time in the final session, do one thing: ask how many trainees expect to reopen their page in March. Take the honest count rather than the polite one, and say plainly that the count is what the course was for.
documents.s: Marking the unit assessment, and closing the course

documents.t: This course develops prospective teachers' quantitative reasoning skills required for academic study, professional practice, and everyday problem solving. It emphasizes logical thinking, numerical sense, data interpretation, and the application of mathematical concepts in real-life contexts. The course strengthens foundational mathematical understanding and prepares future teachers to model quantitative reasoning skills for their students.

On completing this course, you should be able to: Demonstrate numerical and algebraic reasoning. Solve real-world quantitative problems. Apply proportional and logical reasoning. Communicate mathematical ideas clearly. Interpret tables, graphs, and statistical information. These outcomes are referenced throughout the course as SLO:GQUR-300-1-1 through SLO:GQUR-300-5-5 (course outcome, then unit).

Unit Title Focus 1 Foundations of Quantitative Reasoning what QR is, number sense, estimation, logical reasoning, problem-solving strategies 2 Numbers and Operations the number system, ratios, proportions, percentages, powers and roots in daily life 3 Algebraic Reasoning patterns to expressions, linear equations and inequalities, algebra in problem solving 4 Measurement and Geometry metric units, perimeter, area, volume, basic shapes, real measurement tasks 5 Data Analysis and Statistics the data cycle, displays, averages, reading published statistics 6 Quantitative Reasoning in Everyday Life financial literacy, media claims, decision-making with data

Assessment follows the GECE default: 60% summative / 40% formative (Constitution Art. III.7). Each unit ends with a bank of 10 multiple-choice, 10 restricted-response and 5 extended-response items with marking guidance, and each topic carries its own check-your-understanding and summative task.
Recommended sources from the course guide are listed for scope and further reading only; they are never reproduced as content.

This unit lays the foundation for the whole course. Quantitative reasoning is not a bag of formulas; it is a way of thinking with numbers, data, and logic that you will use in every later unit, and every day as a teacher. Here you learn what it is, how to estimate when exactness is unnecessary, and how to reason and solve problems in checkable steps.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain what quantitative reasoning is and why it matters for a teacher. Apply number sense to judge the size and reasonableness of quantities. Estimate and approximate using grouping, rounding, front-end digits, and compatible numbers, and judge when an estimate is good enough. Use the logical-reasoning moves (pattern, if-then, deduction, elimination) and the four-step problem-solving strategy on real school problems.
No prior course is assumed. The unit starts from the level of a student who has completed higher secondary education in Pakistan and uses everyday arithmetic comfortably.

Topic 1.1 - What is quantitative reasoning and why does it matter? - the nature and importance of quantitative reasoning. Topic 1.2 - Number sense, estimation and approximation - numeracy, number sense, and the estimation strategies. Topic 1.3 - Logical reasoning and problem-solving strategies - the reasoning moves and the four-step strategy.

Work through the three topics in order; each builds on the last. In every topic, read the classroom situation first, then work through the explanation with a pencil and paper, and do the activity with your classmates rather than alone. The "Try this at your practicum school" tasks collect real material you will use in the unit assessment, so keep your notes. Glossary terms are underlined; hover or tap them for the Urdu definition.

textbook.com.pk Miss Saima teaches Class 5 in a government primary school near Hyderabad. One morning her headteacher asks a simple question: "We have 240 pupils and 6 teachers this year. Can we run the reading programme in mixed groups of 15?" Miss Saima does not reach for a calculator. She thinks: 240 divided by 15 is 16 groups; 16 groups across 6 teachers is nearly 3 groups each; each group meets for one period, so the timetable can carry it. She has just used quantitative reasoning. Notice what she did not do: she did not only compute. She judged what the numbers meant for a real decision in her school.

Quantitative reasoning is the habit of using numbers, data, and logical thinking to understand situations and make sound decisions. It is bigger than arithmetic. Arithmetic asks "what is 240 divided by 15?" Quantitative reasoning asks "what does 240 divided by 15 tell me about my reading programme?" Steen (2001) argues that quantitative literacy, which he treats as the same family of skills, is a requirement of citizenship in a modern democracy, not only a tool for scientists. His argument is simple: elections, budgets, health advice, and news reports all arrive as numbers. A citizen who cannot question them must simply believe them. A teacher carries an extra duty, because pupils learn their attitude towards numbers from their teacher. The OECD's PISA framework makes the same point in a classroom-friendly way: it defines mathematical literacy as a person's capacity to reason mathematically and to formulate, employ, and interpret mathematics in real-world situations (OECD, n.d.). What quantitative reasoning is not. It is not speed in calculation, and it is not memorising formulas. Sikko (2023) reviews the cluster of overlapping terms - mathematical literacy, quantitative literacy, numeracy - and shows their meanings are imprecise and sometimes used interchangeably; what they all describe, though, is mathematics used in everyday life and society rather than mathematics for its own sake. A quick test: if a task could be done by a calculator alone, with no human judgement about what the numbers mean, it is probably not quantitative reasoning.

textbook.com.pk A teacher meets quantities all day, often without noticing. The table above sorts some everyday school tasks by whether they need quantitative reasoning. Read it and notice two things. First, the tasks that need reasoning are the ones with consequences: grouping pupils, spending a budget, spotting a pupil who is falling behind. Second, the reasoning is always about a decision, never about the calculation alone. The National Professional Standards for Teachers (HEC, 2009) expect a teacher to manage the classroom, plan lessons, and assess learning - and each of those standards quietly rests on numbers: attendance registers, mark records, and time plans (the standards document could not be retrieved on this host; cited at bibliographic level under D-2026-0001). Grawe (2012) argues that quantitative literacy differs from traditional mathematics in exactly the way this course cares about: mathematics is deliberately abstract, while quantitative literacy pushes toward the concrete setting of a problem, and its demand runs across citizenship, work, personal finance and health. A teacher who reasons that way in front of pupils gives them a gift that outlasts the syllabus. A common misconception to correct. Many trainees arrive believing "quantitative reasoning means doing hard calculations". The opposite is closer to the truth. The hard part is deciding what to calculate, what the result means, and how confident to be in it. A calculator can divide 240 by 15 in an instant; only a reasoning human can decide that 16 groups of 15 is a workable plan for 6 teachers.
documents.s: The importance of quantitative reasoning for a teacher

documents.t: Work in pairs. Your tutor will give each pair twelve slips of paper, each describing one task from a normal school day (take attendance, order chalk for the month, decide how many exam papers to print, comfort a crying child, and so on). Sort the slips into two piles: "needs quantitative reasoning" and "does not". For each slip in the first pile, write one sentence naming the decision the numbers serve. Then compare your piles with another pair and argue about any slips you placed differently. About 20 minutes.

Define quantitative reasoning in one sentence of your own, without using the words "calculate" or "mathematics". (Understand) A headteacher says: "Our school's electricity bill was 18,400 rupees this month, up from 16,000 last month." State two different questions a quantitatively reasoning teacher could ask before deciding what to do about the bill. (Apply) Give one example from your own school days of a teacher who used numbers to make a decision, and name the decision the numbers served. (Understand)

Quantitative reasoning is reasoning with numbers and data in context, for a purpose. It is not speed in calculation: the thinking is in deciding what to calculate and what the result means. Teachers meet it constantly, because grouping pupils, reading marksheets, and spending budgets are all quantitative decisions, and pupils learn their number attitude from their teacher.

I can define quantitative reasoning in one plain sentence. I can classify a school task as needing or not needing quantitative reasoning, with a reason. I can name the decision that a given set of numbers serves in a school situation.

Ask your cooperating teacher for one decision they made this month that involved a number of any kind (a mark list, a budget line, an attendance count, a group size). Write down the decision, the number, and what the teacher concluded from it. Bring the note to your next class; you will use it in the unit assessment.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Your headteacher announces: "Next month we will combine Classes 4 and 5 for games period because 63 pupils have signed up and the ground fits 80." Write a short note (about half a page) to the headteacher that (a) checks the arithmetic claim, (b) names one further quantity the decision ignores, and (c) recommends whether to go ahead, with a reason. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Arithmetic checked: the note verifies or corrects the enrolment-vs-capacity comparison. Missing quantity identified: the note names a real ignored quantity (e.g. equipment count, supervision ratio) and explains why it matters. (Analyze) Recommendation justified: the recommendation follows from the two checks, not from the announcement alone.

Steen, L. A. (Ed.). (2001). Mathematics and Democracy: The Case for Quantitative Literacy. National Council on Education and the Disciplines. https://archive.org/details/mathematicsdemoc0000unse (cited at bibliographic level; the scan is controlled-lending) Grawe, N. D. (2012). Achieving a quantitatively literate citizenry: Resources and community to support national change. Liberal Education, 98(2), 30-35. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ981327 Higher Education Commission, Pakistan. (2009). National Professional Standards for Teachers. textbook.com.pk It is the annual sports day at a primary school in Sukkur. The headteacher turns to Miss Farzana, the Class 6 teacher: "Roughly how many people are on the ground now? The water contractor wants to know." Miss Farzana cannot count 800 people one by one. She looks at one crowded section, counts about 40 people there, counts 20 similar sections by eye, and says "about 800, maybe a few more". The contractor fills the water cooler accordingly, and there is enough. Nobody needed the exact number 817. What Miss Farzana used is estimation, and the judgement of when it is good enough is part of number sense.

Numeracy is the ability to use mathematics in daily life. Number sense is its foundation: a feel for what numbers mean, how big they are, and how they relate to each other. A person with number sense is not surprised that a class of 40 pupils cannot share 5 books fairly, or that a 10 percent fee rise on a 2,000-rupee fee is 200 rupees, not 2,000. Number sense shows itself in small, fast judgements: Size judgement: knowing that 0.5 kg of tomatoes at 120 rupees a kg costs about 60 rupees, before the shopkeeper weighs it. Relationship sense: knowing that doubling a group doubles its cost, and that a third as many pupils needs a third as many worksheets. Reasonableness checking: looking at any answer and asking "could this possibly be right?" If a trainee computes that a school of 300 pupils needs 3,000 chairs, number sense sounds the alarm. Gula and Lovric (2025) argue that numeracy tasks are their own category of mathematics task, distinct both from word problems and from mathematical modelling, and that a quality numeracy task "inspire[s] transfer between concrete and abstract thinking spaces". That is exactly the movement this topic asks of you: from a ground full of people (concrete) to a defensible estimate (abstract), and back to the decision the estimate serves.

textbook.com.pk An estimation is a deliberate, reasoned guess that is close enough for the purpose. An approximation is a value used in place of an exact one to make work easier, like taking 398 as 400. The two often travel together: Miss Farzana approximated each section as 40 people, then estimated the total. The table above shows the four estimation strategies you will use most. Study the examples before trying the practice below. Gula and Lovric (2025) put exactly this habit at the heart of a quality numeracy task: the estimate is the abstract answer that the concrete situation must be able to carry, and checking it against the situation is the transfer back. Worked example. A school function needs biscuits for the pupils. A packet serves about 10 pupils. The school has 348 pupils in Classes 1 to 5, plus about 30 parents. Round 348 up to 350 (we do not want to run short), add 30 parents to get 380 people, and divide by 10: about 38 packets. Buy 40 to be safe. Notice the reasoning moves: round for ease, round up when shortage is worse than surplus, and check the size of the answer at the end. A common misconception to correct. Many trainees believe "estimation is just guessing". A guess has no method; an estimate has a method and a purpose. A good estimate can be defended: "I counted one section and multiplied" is an argument, not a shrug. Equally, estimation has limits: when the headteacher files the official enrolment return, an estimate is wrong even if it is close - the register must be counted exactly. Part of quantitative reasoning is knowing which situations demand exactness and which reward a fast, defensible estimate.

Work in groups of four. Your tutor will show five quick prompts one at a time, for exactly one minute each (for example: how many bricks are in the front wall of the classroom, how many litres does the water cooler hold, what is the monthly chalk cost for the school). Each group writes an estimate plus one sentence naming its method. After all five prompts, each group reveals its methods. The tutor awards a point for a sensible method, not for closeness to the true figure. About 25 minutes.

In your own words, state the difference between an estimate and an approximation, with one example of each. (Understand) A trainee estimates 47 x 52 as 50 x 50 = 2,500. Name the strategy used, and say whether the true answer is above or below the estimate, with a reason. (Apply) For each situation, say whether an estimate or an exact count is appropriate, and why: (a) ordering exam papers for the class, (b) deciding whether the school van can carry all pupils in one trip. (Apply)

Number sense is a feel for the size and meaning of numbers; it powers the reasonableness check on every answer. Estimation is a reasoned, defensible guess with a method and a purpose, built from strategies like grouping, rounding, front-end digits, and compatible numbers. Knowing when an estimate is good enough, and when exactness is required, is itself a quantitative judgement.

I can explain the difference between a guess, an estimate, and an approximation. I can apply at least two estimation strategies to a school situation and name my method. I can judge whether a given situation needs an estimate or an exact count, with a reason.

Estimate one quantity at your practicum school without counting it fully (for example, the number of books on the class shelf, or the pupils on the ground at break). Write down your estimate, your method, and then, with permission, find the true figure. Note how far off you were and what you would change about your method. Bring the note to class.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: The Parent Teacher Association can spend 25,000 rupees on prizes for a school of 512 pupils. The president plans to buy 100 prizes at about 250 rupees each. In a short written answer: (a) estimate whether the plan fits the budget, naming your strategy, (b) identify one quantity the plan ignores that could change the conclusion, and (c) recommend the plan or a change to it, with reasons. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Estimate with a named strategy: the budget check uses a stated estimation strategy, not a bare number. Ignored quantity identified: the answer names a real factor (prize quality tiers, transport cost, number of prize categories) and shows how it could change the result. (Analyze) Recommendation follows: the final recommendation follows from (a) and (b) together.

Gula, T., & Lovric, M. (2025). Promoting mathematical thinking of university students: The case of a numeracy course. Canadian Journal of Science, Mathematics and Technology Education, 25(1), 171-184. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42330-024-00342-0 OECD. PISA mathematics framework. https://www.oecd.org/pisa/

textbook.com.pk Mr. Danish is the timetable in-charge at a middle school in Larkana. The headteacher says: "Three teachers are on leave every Friday, and Classes 6, 7 and 8 still need their math periods. Fix it." Mr. Danish does not panic. He writes down what is asked (every class gets its math period on Friday) and what is given (6 math periods to cover, 3 teachers short). He tries a plan: combine two classes for a games-plus-math activity so one teacher covers both. He carries it out on paper, then looks back: Class 8's math period now clashes with the science lab slot. He returns to step one and adjusts. By the third loop, the timetable works. His method matters more than his arithmetic, and the method is what this topic teaches.

textbook.com.pk Logical reasoning is thinking in ordered, checkable steps: each conclusion follows from what came before, so another person can retrace your path. The table above shows the four moves you will use most often. Two of them deserve a closer look. If-then reasoning. "If the van seats 30, and 34 pupils signed up, then one trip cannot carry everyone." The conclusion is forced by the two facts. Quantitative reasoning leans heavily on this move, because numbers make the "if" precise. If the school's water tank holds 500 litres and the school uses about 100 litres a day, then a full tank lasts about five days. Notice that if-then reasoning is only as good as its starting facts: if the tank actually holds 400 litres, the five-day conclusion collapses even though the logic was perfect. Elimination. "The missing book is not in the cupboard (checked), not on the shelf (checked), not borrowed by anyone (register says so); therefore it is lost." Elimination rules out options until one remains. It is how a teacher narrows down why a class's average fell: not the syllabus (same as last term), not absenteeism (attendance was normal), so most likely the test's hardest chapter fell in the exam week. A common misconception to correct. Some trainees believe "there is one correct method for every problem". Real problems have many defensible routes. What makes a route correct is that each step follows from the last and the final answer survives the look-back check, not that it matches the textbook's method. Steen (2001) makes this point at the level of a whole society: the value of quantitative reasoning is not in ritual procedures but in sound judgement.

A problem-solving strategy is an ordered way through a problem you have not met before. The flowchart above shows the classic four steps, often traced to the mathematician George Polya: understand the problem, make a plan, carry out the plan, and look back. Worked example. Problem: a school of 240 pupils must seat 4 pupils per bench in the hall for a function; how many benches are needed? Understand: we need the number of benches; given 240 pupils and 4 per bench. Plan: divide total pupils by pupils per bench. Carry out: 240 divided by 4 is 60 benches. Look back: does 60 make sense? 60 benches of 4 give exactly 240 seats. But the chief guest and two teachers also need seats, so 62 is safer. The look-back step is where the real-world answer separates from the bare arithmetic answer. The four steps are also a teaching tool. When a pupil says "I don't know how to start", they are stuck at step one, not at the arithmetic. Asking "what is asked, what is given?" is usually enough to unstick them, and it models the strategy in front of the whole class. Steen (2001) frames the whole enterprise this way: quantitative literacy is sound judgement in the face of real problems, and a named strategy is what makes that judgement teachable.

Work in pairs. Your tutor will show three short pieces of school reasoning, each with one flawed step (for example: "Attendance was 90 percent on Monday and 90 percent on Tuesday, so the same pupils were absent both days"). For each one, identify which logical move is being misused, name the broken step, and write the corrected version in two sentences. Then join another pair and compare repairs. About 20 minutes.

Name the four steps of the problem-solving strategy in order, in your own words. (Remember) A teacher reasons: "If every pupil brings 50 rupees, and 40 pupils promise to bring it, we will collect 2,000 rupees." State the two facts this if-then conclusion depends on, and one way the conclusion could fail. (Apply) Use elimination in two sentences to narrow down why a class's water bill doubled this month, given: no new taps installed, same number of pupils, and the meter was read correctly. (Analyze)

Logical reasoning moves in checkable steps: spotting patterns, if-then chains, deduction, and elimination. Its strength depends on the truth of its starting facts. The four-step problem-solving strategy (understand, plan, carry out, look back) turns reasoning into a repeatable method, and the look-back step is where a bare answer becomes a real-world decision.

I can name and use the four logical-reasoning moves with everyday examples. I can apply the four-step problem-solving strategy to a problem I have not seen before. I can find the broken step in a flawed piece of reasoning and repair it.

Take one real problem your cooperating teacher solved this week (a seating plan, a worksheet count, a duty roster). Reconstruct their solution as the four steps: understand, plan, carry out, look back. Note which step took them the longest, and ask them whether they agree with your reconstruction.

documents.t: A school notice says: "Last year 20 pupils failed the Class 8 math exam. This year we bought a new workbook series, and only 10 pupils failed. Therefore the new workbooks halved our failure rate." Write a short analysis that (a) names the reasoning move used, (b) identifies at least two other quantities that changed between the two years and could explain the drop, and (c) states what evidence would be needed before crediting the workbooks. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Move named: the analysis correctly identifies the if-then (cause-effect) structure. Alternative explanations: at least two real alternative quantities are named with a sentence each on how they could produce the same drop. (Analyze) Evidence standard: the analysis states what comparison or data would isolate the workbook effect.

Steen, L. A. (Ed.). (2001). Mathematics and Democracy: The Case for Quantitative Literacy. National Council on Education and the Disciplines. https://archive.org/details/mathematicsdemoc0000unse (cited at bibliographic level; the scan is controlled-lending) Sikko, S. A. (2023). What can we learn from the different understandings of mathematical literacy? Numeracy, 16(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1450768

Quantitative reasoning is reasoning with numbers, data, and logic in context, for a purpose; the thinking lies in deciding what to calculate and what the result means, not in the calculation itself. Number sense is a feel for the size and meaning of numbers, and it powers the reasonableness check on every answer. Estimation is a reasoned, defensible guess built from strategies (grouping, rounding, front-end digits, compatible numbers), and knowing when an estimate is good enough is itself a quantitative judgement. Logical reasoning moves in checkable steps (pattern, if-then, deduction, elimination), and the four-step problem-solving strategy (understand, plan, carry out, look back) turns that reasoning into a repeatable method whose look-back step converts a bare answer into a real-world decision.

Quantitative reasoning is best described as: (Remember) a) fast mental arithmetic b) memorising mathematical formulas c) reasoning with numbers and data in context to make decisions d) using a calculator accurately Which school task needs quantitative reasoning rather than bare calculation? (Understand) a) deciding how many exam papers to print when absentee patterns are known b) typing marks into a register c) adding a column of marks d) writing a pupil's name on a certificate A headteacher says: "63 pupils signed up for games period and the ground fits 80." A quantitatively reasoning teacher should first: (Apply) a) accept the plan because 63 is less than 80 b) check the arithmetic and ask what other quantities the decision ignores c) refuse the plan until a calculator is available d) ask the pupils to count themselves Steen's argument for quantitative literacy rests mainly on: (Understand) a) employers demanding faster clerks b) mathematics examinations becoming harder c) universities needing more mathematicians d) democratic life arriving as numbers that citizens must be able to question Number sense is best described as: (Remember) a) memorising number facts up to twenty b) writing numbers neatly and correctly c) a feel for the size, meaning, and relationships of numbers d) counting objects quickly A trainee estimates 47 x 52 as 50 x 50 = 2,500. The strategy used is: (Apply) a) rounding to compatible numbers b) front-end digits c) grouping d) order-of-magnitude The school must file its official enrolment return to the district office. The appropriate approach is: (Apply) a) an estimate based on last year's figure b) an exact count from the attendance register c) an approximation to the nearest ten d) a count of one class multiplied by the number of classes The four steps of the problem-solving strategy, in order, are: (Remember) a) plan, understand, check, compute b) understand, compute, plan, look back c) compute, check, plan, understand d) understand, plan, carry out, look back "If the van seats 30, and 34 pupils signed up, then one trip cannot carry everyone." This sentence is an example of: (Apply) a) elimination b) pattern spotting c) if-then reasoning d) approximation In the bench problem, the look-back step changed the answer from 60 benches to 62 because: (Apply) a) real-world needs (chief guest and teachers) were missing from the bare computation b) the division 240 by 4 had been done wrongly c) benches sometimes break and spares are required by rule d) 60 is an unlucky number for functions

Define quantitative reasoning in one sentence of your own, and give one example from school life. (Understand) Explain in two sentences why a teacher's attitude towards numbers matters for pupils. (Understand) A colleague says: "Quantitative reasoning means doing hard calculations." Correct the claim in two sentences, using the idea that reasoning serves a decision. (Analyze) State the difference between an estimate and an approximation, with one example of each. (Understand) A school has 348 pupils and each pupil needs 2 worksheets; worksheets come 10 to a packet. Estimate the number of packets needed, and name the strategy you used. (Apply) For each situation, say whether an exact figure or an estimate is appropriate, and why: (a) ordering exam papers for Class 8; (b) deciding whether the school van can carry all pupils in one trip. (Analyze) Explain in two sentences why "about 800 people" was good enough for the water contractor at sports day, but the official enrolment return must be an exact count. (Understand) Name the four logical-reasoning moves, and give a one-line example of any two of them. (Understand) A water tank holds 500 litres and the school uses about 100 litres a day. State the if-then conclusion, and name one condition that would break it. (Apply) "Attendance was 90 percent on Monday and 90 percent on Tuesday, so the same pupils were absent on both days." Identify the flaw in this reasoning in two sentences. (Analyze)

Your headteacher announces: "Next month we will combine Classes 4 and 5 for games period because 63 pupils have signed up and the ground fits 80." Write a short note to the headteacher that checks the arithmetic claim, names one further quantity the decision ignores, and recommends whether to go ahead, with reasons. (Analyze) The Parent Teacher Association can spend 25,000 rupees on prizes for a school of 512 pupils, and the president plans 100 prizes at about 250 rupees each. Estimate whether the plan fits the budget, identify one quantity the plan ignores that could change the conclusion, and recommend the plan or a change to it, with reasons. (Analyze) A school notice says: "Last year 20 pupils failed the Class 8 math exam. This year we bought a new workbook series, and only 10 pupils failed. Therefore the new workbooks halved our failure rate." Analyse the claim: name the reasoning move used, identify at least two other quantities that changed between the years and could explain the drop, and state what evidence would be needed before crediting the workbooks. (Analyze) At sports day, Miss Farzana estimated the crowd by counting one section (about 40 people) and multiplying by the 20 sections she could see. Reconstruct her estimate as the four-step problem-solving strategy, name the estimation strategy she used, and explain in what situation her method would not be good enough. (Analyze) Using a real decision you observed at your practicum school that involved a number (from your Topic 1.1 practicum task or another), describe the decision, then analyse it with this unit's tools: what was asked and given, which reasoning moves were used, whether an estimate or an exact figure was appropriate, and whether the look-back step happened. Evaluate the quality of the decision and name one thing you would do differently. (Evaluate)

c - quantitative reasoning is reasoning with numbers in context for a decision; arithmetic speed is only a component. a - printing decisions must weigh absentee patterns; the other tasks are pure procedure. b - checking the claim and asking what else matters is exactly the two-part habit the unit teaches. d - Steen's case is about citizenship: numbers arrive in public life and must be questionable. c - number sense is the feel for size and meaning, not memorised facts. a - 47 and 52 were rounded to the compatible numbers 50 and 50. b - an official return is a legal record; only the register count is appropriate. d - understand, plan, carry out, look back. c - two stated facts force a conclusion; that is if-then reasoning. a - the look-back step adds real-world requirements the bare computation omitted.

Model: quantitative reasoning is using numbers, data, and logic to understand a situation and make a sound decision; example: grouping 240 pupils into groups of 15 to plan a reading programme. Marks (2): 1 - definition in the learner's own words naming reasoning and purpose; 1 - a genuine school example. Model: pupils copy their teacher's confidence or fear with numbers; a teacher who reasons aloud shows pupils that numbers serve decisions. Marks (2): 1 - the modelling idea; 1 - a concrete consequence for pupils. Model: the correction should move the centre of gravity from calculation to judgement: the hard part is deciding what to calculate and what the result means for a decision; calculation is only a tool inside that judgement. Marks (2): 1 - names the decision focus; 1 - gives a contrasting example or a clear restatement. Model: an estimate is a reasoned guess at a value (crowd at the mela, about 800); an approximation is a deliberately simplified value used in place of an exact one to make work easier (taking 398 as 400). Marks (2): 1 - the distinction; 1 - one example of each. Model: 348 x 2 = 696 sheets; 696 / 10 = 69.6, so about 70 packets (buy 70; some add a spare packet). Strategy: rounding (348 to 350) or direct computation with a named strategy; any defensible named strategy earns the mark. Marks (2): 1 - a correct estimate near 70 packets; 1 - a named strategy. Model: (a) exact - each candidate needs a paper, and shortage blocks the exam; (b) an estimate can suffice for a one-trip decision if there is a clear margin, but an exact count is safer when the number is near the van's capacity. Full marks require linking the choice to the consequence of being wrong. Marks (4): 1 - (a) exact; 1 - reason tied to consequence; 1 - (b) either defensible choice; 1 - reason tied to margin or consequence. Model: the water decision only needed the right order of size (a few hundred), so an estimate served the purpose; the enrolment return is an official record where an error has consequences regardless of size. Marks (2): 1 - purpose-relative accuracy; 1 - the official-record point. Model: pattern, if-then, deduction, elimination (order not required); examples such as "if the tank holds 500 litres and we use 100 a day, it lasts 5 days" (if-then) or "the book is not in the cupboard, not on the shelf, not borrowed; it is lost" (elimination). Marks (3): 1 - all four moves named; 2 - two correct one-line examples (1 each). Model: if the tank is full and use is 100 litres a day, the water lasts about 5 days; the conclusion breaks if the tank is not full, if daily use is higher, or if the tank leaks. Marks (2): 1 - the if-then conclusion; 1 - one breaking condition. Model: the two percentages describe different days and do not identify anyone; the same 90 percent could be produced by entirely different absentees, so the conclusion about "the same pupils" is not forced. Marks (2): 1 - identifies the unsupported identity claim; 1 - explains why equal percentages do not imply the same pupils.

documents.t: Games-period note. Analytic rubric: Arithmetic checked (0-2: verifies 63 < 80 and probes what the claim assumes); Missing quantity identified (0-2, Analyze: names a real ignored quantity such as supervision ratio or equipment and explains its effect); Recommendation justified (0-2: the recommendation follows from both checks); Clarity and register (0-2: a respectful, plain note a headteacher would act on). Total 8. PTA prize budget. Analytic rubric: Estimate with named strategy (0-2: 100 x 250 = 25,000 fits exactly, shown with a stated strategy); Ignored quantity (0-2, Analyze: names a real factor, e.g. prize tiers, transport, or that 100 prizes for 512 pupils means most pupils get nothing, and shows its effect); Recommendation (0-2: follows from the analysis); Clarity (0-2). Total 8. Workbook claim. Analytic rubric: Move named (0-2: identifies the if-then cause-effect structure); Alternative explanations (0-3, Analyze: two or more real changed quantities, e.g. a different cohort, a different exam, extra coaching, each with a sentence of mechanism); Evidence standard (0-2: names a comparison that would isolate the workbook effect, e.g. a comparable school without the workbooks); Clarity (0-1). Total 8. Sports-day reconstruction. Analytic rubric: Four-step reconstruction (0-3: understand, plan, carry out, look back each correctly mapped to her actions); Strategy named (0-2: grouping / section-and-multiply); Limit of the method (0-3, Analyze: names a situation where it fails, e.g. unevenly filled sections, moving crowds, or a safety decision needing an exact figure, with a reason). Total 8. Practicum decision analysis. Analytic rubric: Decision described (0-2: a real, specific school decision with its number); Tool application (0-3: asked/given, reasoning move, estimate-vs-exact all applied to the case); Look-back evaluation (0-2, Analyze: judges whether the decision survived its look-back and why); Improvement named (0-2: one concrete thing the learner would do differently); Clarity (0-1). Total 10.

The three topics form one arc. Topic 1.1 changes what trainees think quantitative reasoning is. Topic 1.2 gives them the first practical tools (number sense and estimation). Topic 1.3 gives them a method for unfamiliar problems. Teach them in order across the three weeks the content-spec allows, and keep returning to Topic 1.1's definition: every later skill should be introduced as an instance of "reasoning with numbers for a decision".

The course guide names interactive lectures, problem-solving sessions, group activities, real-life case studies, guided practice and discussions, plus lecture, discussion, question-answer and brainstorming. In this unit: Use the interactive lecture shape for Topic 1.1: present the classroom situation, then question-and-answer your way to the definition rather than dictating it. Run Topic 1.2's "one-minute estimate challenge" exactly as timed: the time pressure is what forces estimation instead of counting. Use the guide's brainstorming mode for Topic 1.3's activity: collect the pairs' repairs on the board and let the group argue for the best one.

"Quantitative reasoning means doing hard calculations." Probe with a task that needs no calculation at all: "The ground fits 80 and 63 signed up - what else do you want to know before deciding?" Trainees who reach for a formula are stuck in the old frame. "Estimation is just guessing." Ask for the method behind an estimate. If a trainee cannot name a strategy, it was a guess; make the class supply the missing strategy. "There is one correct method for every problem." Deliberately solve one problem two ways on the board and ask the class to check both; when both survive the look-back, the misconception is refuted by demonstration.

Sort the school day (Topic 1.1): prepare the twelve slips in advance and include at least two ambiguous ones (ordering chalk for the month) so the pairs have something to argue about. Debrief by asking for the decision each quantitative task serves. The one-minute estimate challenge (Topic 1.2): award points for method, never for closeness, or the activity collapses into guessing. Keep the true figures hidden until the debrief. Spot the broken step (Topic 1.3): the three flawed reasonings should each break a different move (a false if-then, a pattern over-read, a bad elimination). Ask pairs to name the move, not just the flaw.

The guide's practical work (group work, group assignments, individual assignment, presentations) maps onto this unit as: group work in the three topic activities; a group assignment collecting the class's practicum notes into one "school decisions" wall; an individual assignment in the Topic 1.2 practicum task; and presentations in the unit's debrief, where each group presents one reconstructed decision.

The unit-end bank samples all three topics. When marking the ERQs, resist the temptation to reward arithmetic alone: the rubrics weight the Analyze criteria (missing quantity, alternative explanations, limit of the method) precisely because the unit's claim is that reasoning outranks calculation. A note that checks the arithmetic but names no missing quantity is a pass at best; the distinction goes to the trainee who asks what the numbers leave out.

Trainees collect two artefacts this unit: a teacher's real numeric decision (Topic 1.1) and an estimate with its true figure (Topic 1.2). Both feed ERQ-5. Warn trainees to seek permission before counting anything, and to anonymise names in anything they write up.

This unit builds the working toolkit. Unit 1 established what quantitative reasoning is; here you sharpen the number skills it runs on: the number system from whole numbers to decimals, the proportional reasoning that connects recipes, marksheets and discounts, and the powers and roots behind areas and tiling. Every skill is met first in a Pakistani bazaar, kitchen or classroom, because that is where you will use it.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Place whole numbers, integers, fractions and decimals on one number line and compute across the system. Scale quantities with ratios and proportions, and handle all four percentage situations including the reverse case. Compute squares and square roots, and bracket a root between neighbouring squares. Choose the right operation for a daily-life problem by asking what the total does, and check the answer for reasonableness.
Unit 1 (especially the four-step problem-solving strategy and the reasonableness check), plus comfortable everyday arithmetic.

Topic 2.1 - The number system: whole numbers, integers, fractions and decimals - the number family tree and computing across it. Topic 2.2 - Ratios, proportions and percentages - proportional reasoning and the four percentage situations. Topic 2.3 - Powers, roots and daily-life applications - squares as areas, and choosing the operation.

Work through the topics in order; each assumes the previous. Do every worked example with a pencil before reading its conclusion, and keep your Unit 1 practicum notes at hand: the reasonableness habit from Unit 1 is used in every topic here. Glossary terms are underlined; hover or tap them for the Urdu definition.

textbook.com.pk Mr. Rashid keeps the accounts for his brother's cloth shop in Karachi's Jodia Bazaar. One morning the shop ledger shows four entries: 12 metres sold, a debt of 3,500 rupees, three quarter metres cut for a customer, and 0.75 in the decimal column of the same sale. His new assistant is confused: "Are these all numbers? One has a minus, one has a bar, one has a dot." Mr. Rashid laughs and draws a picture on the back of an invoice: the number family tree. All four entries are numbers; they simply live in different rooms of the same house. By the end of this topic you will be able to draw that picture yourself, and more importantly, compute across it.

Whole numbers are the counting numbers and zero: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on. They answer "how many?" when the answer cannot be negative: 240 pupils, 16 groups, 5 books. Integers extend whole numbers below zero: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... The negative side is not strange; it is bookkeeping made honest. A debt of 3,500 rupees is written -3,500 so that adding it to the cash box gives the true position. Temperature in Skardu in December, floors below ground level, marks deducted for wrong answers: all are natural uses of negative numbers. Two everyday situations build integer sense: Debt and credit: cash box 8,000 rupees, debt 3,500 rupees; the position is 8,000 + (-3,500) = 4,500 rupees. Change and difference: the temperature rose from -2 to 6 degrees; the change is 6 - (-2) = 8 degrees, not 4. The National Curriculum Council publishes the national mathematics curriculum for Grades 1-12 (NCC, n.d.); whole numbers and integers sit at its foundation, as they do in every school curriculum, because everyday bookkeeping demands them.

textbook.com.pk A fraction names a part of a whole or a share of a group: three quarters means 3 of 4 equal parts. The bottom number (the denominator) counts the equal parts; the top number (the numerator) counts the parts taken. A decimal is the same idea written in place value: 0.75 says 7 tenths and 5 hundredths. Every fraction has a decimal name and almost every decimal in daily life is a fraction in disguise; the shop's "three quarter metres" and "0.75" were the same quantity twice. The table above shows the four operations with fractions and decimals side by side, each with a metre-and-rupee example. Study one row at a time, then cover the answers and reproduce it. Worked example. A tailor has 5.5 metres of cloth. A shalwar kameez suit needs 2.75 metres. How many suits, and what remains? Plan: divide. Carry out: 5.5 divided by 2.75 is exactly 2. Look back: 2 suits use 5.5 metres, so nothing remains - and the answer is reasonable because 5.5 is a bit more than two lots of 2.5. Notice how Unit 1's four-step strategy carries straight into computation. A common misconception to correct. Many trainees believe "multiplying always makes bigger". With whole numbers it usually does, but 12 x 1/2 is 6 (smaller), and 12 x 0.1 is 1.2 (much smaller). Multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 shrinks. This one idea explains dozens of daily errors, from fabric orders to electricity unit calculations. Test every answer against your number sense: could this result be sensible?

Work in pairs. Your tutor gives each pair a mock shop ledger with six entries mixing whole numbers, signed amounts, fractions and decimals (for example: sold 3.25 kg sugar; loan repaid -1,200 rupees; 1/2 kg tea received). First, place every entry on a number line drawn on paper. Then compute the shop's closing position. Finally, convert each fraction entry to its decimal form and check that your closing position does not change. Compare ledgers with the pair beside you. About 25 minutes.

Place these on a number line and order them from smallest to largest: 2, -3, 1/2, 0.75, -0.5. (Apply) A shop's cash box holds 9,000 rupees and its debts total 4,500 rupees. Write the shop's position using integers and compute it. (Apply) A recipe needs 3/4 kg of flour and you have 1.5 kg. How many full recipes can you make, and what is left over? Show the division. (Apply) In your own words, explain why 12 x 0.1 is smaller than 12, using the idea of "part of a whole". (Understand)

Whole numbers count what cannot be negative; integers add the negative side and make bookkeeping honest; fractions and decimals are two notations for parts of wholes, and every fraction has a decimal name. Operations work the same across the system, and the reasonableness check from Unit 1 applies to every result: multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 shrinks, and a negative result must mean something real in the situation.

I can place whole numbers, integers, fractions and decimals on one number line and order them. I can compute with integers in debt-and-credit situations. I can add, subtract, multiply and divide with fractions and decimals in daily-life examples, and convert between the two notations.

Ask the school clerk (or your cooperating teacher) how the stationery register records part-used items (half reams of paper, part boxes of chalk). Note two entries that use fractions or decimals, copy them exactly, and convert each to the other notation. Bring the note to class.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: A school canteen buys flour in 5.5 kg bags at 1,200 rupees per bag. One batch of parathas uses 0.75 kg. In a short written answer: (a) compute how many full batches one bag gives and the flour left over, (b) compute the flour cost per batch to the nearest rupee, and (c) check both answers for reasonableness using estimation, showing your check. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Division correct: full batches and remainder from 5.5 divided by 0.75 (7 batches, 0.25 kg left). Cost per batch: cost per batch computed with clear working (1,200 divided by 7.33 batches gives about 164 rupees; 1,200 divided by 7 full batches gives about 171 rupees treating the leftover as waste; either defensible computation earns the mark). Reasonableness check: an explicit estimation check of at least one answer, not a bare restatement. (Analyze)

textbook.com.pk The school function is tomorrow, and the cook must scale up her tea recipe. For 20 people she uses 6 spoons of sugar to 4 spoons of tea leaves. The headteacher says 60 people are coming. "Then triple everything," says the cook instantly: 18 spoons of sugar, 12 spoons of tea. She has never studied algebra, but she has flawless proportional reasoning: she knows that 18 to 12 is the same ratio as 6 to 4, because both simplify to 3 to 2. This topic takes the reasoning the cook already owns, names it, and connects it to the percentage table that will follow, so you can use it deliberately and teach it explicitly.

A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind: 6 spoons of sugar to 4 spoons of tea leaves, 40 girls to 20 boys in a school. A proportion is a statement that two ratios are equal: 6 to 4 equals 18 to 12, because both are 3 to 2. The cross-products check makes a proportion verifiable without trusting the eye: 6 x 12 = 72 and 4 x 18 = 72, so the proportion holds. Worked example (scaling up). The recipe serves 20 people with 6 spoons of sugar. For 60 people: the crowd is 3 times as large, so every ingredient is 3 times as large: 18 spoons. For 50 people: the crowd is 2.5 times as large, so 15 spoons. The reasoning move is always the same: find the multiplier between the situations and apply it to every quantity. Worked example (finding the multiplier). A school has 40 girls and 20 boys. The ratio of girls to boys is 40 to 20, which simplifies to 2 to 1: two girls for every boy. If the next school year admits 30 more pupils in the same ratio, expect 20 girls and 10 boys. A common misconception to correct. Trainees often add instead of multiplying when scaling: "30 more people, so add one more batch of 6 spoons of sugar and 4 of tea." Adding one original batch happens to feed exactly 20 more people, so the rule works only when the extra crowd is exactly 20. The 50-person function needs 2.5 times the recipe - 15 spoons of sugar and 10 of tea - while the friend's addition cooks for only 40, and ten guests go hungry. The test is to ask what must stay the same: the amount per person, so multiply every ingredient by the crowd multiplier, never add a fixed batch.

textbook.com.pk A percentage is a ratio expressed out of 100: "per cent" literally means "by the hundred". Percentages matter because so many daily quantities are quoted in them: fee rises, discounts, exam marks, battery levels, tax. The table above sorts the four situations you will meet, each with a rupee example. The fourth row deserves special care: finding the original after a rise is the classic trap, because the rise acts on the original, not on the final figure. Worked example (marks). A pupil scores 36 out of 45 in a math test. As a percentage: 36 divided by 45 is 0.8, which is 80 percent. The reasoning: the fraction 36/45 tells what share of the marks was earned; multiplying by 100 renames that share per hundred. Worked example (discount). A bookshop offers 25 percent off a 640-rupee atlas. The discount is 25/100 x 640 = 160 rupees, so the sale price is 640 - 160 = 480 rupees. A faster route: paying 75 percent of the price is 0.75 x 640 = 480; both routes must agree, and checking that they do is the look-back habit from Unit 1.

Work in groups of four. Your tutor gives each group five anonymised test results in different totals (for example 36/45, 42/60, 55/75, 18/25, 27/30). Each member converts two results to percentages by hand (no calculator), then the group ranks all five pupils from best to worst percentage. The debrief question: which raw scores looked biggest but were not best, and why the total matters. About 20 minutes.

Write the ratio 40 girls to 20 boys in its simplest form, and state what it means in one sentence. (Understand) A recipe for 12 people uses 4 eggs. How many eggs for 30 people? Show the multiplier you used. (Apply) Compute 15 percent of a 2,000-rupee fee, and state the new fee after a 15 percent rise. (Apply) After a 10 percent rise, a school's monthly electricity bill is 17,600 rupees. What was the bill before the rise? Show your reasoning. (Apply) A friend scales a recipe by adding: "30 more people, so add one more batch of 6 spoons of sugar and 4 of tea." Explain in two sentences why this leaves the function short and what to do instead. (Analyze)

Ratio compares, proportion states that two ratios are equal, and percentage is a ratio out of 100; they are one idea in three notations. Scaling multiplies every ingredient by the same multiplier - it never adds. The four percentage situations (of, increase, decrease, reverse) each need their own setup, and the reverse case is the classic trap because the rise acts on the original.

I can simplify a ratio and explain what it means in one sentence. I can scale a recipe or a plan by finding and applying the multiplier. I can handle all four percentage situations with rupee examples, including the reverse case.

Take one class's latest test (anonymised, with permission). Convert any five pupils' raw scores to percentages. Then ask the teacher one question: does the school report raw scores or percentages to parents, and why? Note the answer with one example.

documents.t: A stationery supplier offers two deals on notebooks costing 80 rupees each: Deal A gives "20 percent off", Deal B gives "5 notebooks free with every 20 bought". The school needs 100 notebooks. In a short written answer: (a) compute the total cost under each deal, (b) state which deal is cheaper and by how much, and (c) identify one circumstance (a different quantity, budget timing, or storage) under which the school might still prefer the other deal, with a reason. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Both totals correct: Deal A costs 6,400 rupees (80 x 100 x 0.8); Deal B costs 6,400 rupees (pay 80, receive 100) - or the equivalent correct computation shown. Comparison stated: the cheaper deal named with the difference (here they tie, and noticing the tie earns the mark). Circumstance analysed: a real non-price factor is identified and argued, not merely named. (Analyze)

textbook.com.pk The school in Nawabshah is re-tiling its verandah with square tiles. The mason lays one tile and says "one". He makes a 2 by 2 square: "four tiles". A 3 by 3 square: "nine". The headteacher asks: "I have 64 tiles. How wide a square can I lay?" The mason answers at once: "8 by 8." He has never written 8 squared or the square root of 64, but he owns both ideas. This topic gives you the notation for what the mason already knows, and then a wider tool: a flowchart for choosing the right operation when a daily problem does not tell you which one to use.

A power is repeated multiplication: 8 squared (written 8^2) means 8 x 8 = 64, and 2 cubed (2^3) means 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. The number being multiplied is the base; the small raised number, the exponent, counts the multiplications. The square of a number is its second power, and it is genuinely a square: a square floor 8 tiles on a side holds exactly 8 x 8 = 64 tiles. The diagram above shows the square numbers growing as tile grids; the "squared" arrow climbs from side to area, and the square root arrow climbs back down. The square root of 64, written sqrt(64), is 8: the side of the square that holds 64 tiles. Worked example. A store room has a square floor of 50 square metres. What is the length of one side, to the nearest metre? The side is sqrt(50). Since 7 x 7 = 49 and 8 x 8 = 64, sqrt(50) sits between 7 and 8, much closer to 7: about 7.1 metres. Estimation first (Unit 1), exactness when needed: 7.07 metres if the carpenter must cut a skirting board. A common misconception to correct. Trainees sometimes read 8^2 as 8 x 2 = 16. The exponent counts multiplications of the base, not a multiplication by itself. The tile picture is the cure: 8 squared is an 8-by-8 floor, not an 8-by-2 corridor. The same picture prevents the twin error of thinking squaring doubles: 8 squared is 64, not 16.

textbook.com.pk Most daily-life arithmetic fails before any number is touched: the wrong operation is chosen. Gula and Lovric (2025) make exactly this the mark of a genuine numeracy task: the work lies in reading the situation, not in the arithmetic that follows. The flowchart above is a repair. Its core question is: what does the total do? If the total combines equal groups (20 boxes of 12 chalks each), multiply. If the total breaks into equal groups (240 pupils into groups of 15), divide. If the total grows or shrinks by a change (a fee of 2,000 rises by 200), add or subtract. Worked example. A school orders transport for 187 pupils; each van carries 26. How many vans? The total (pupils) breaks into equal groups (vanloads), so divide: 187 divided by 26 is 7 with remainder 5. Look back: 7 vans carry 182 pupils, but 5 pupils remain, so the real-world answer is 8 vans. The look-back step is not decoration; it changes the answer. Choosing units as part of choosing the operation. Daily problems arrive wearing units: rupees, metres, pupils per van, rupees per notebook. A rate (rupees per notebook) multiplies a count (notebooks) to give a total (rupees). Keeping the units attached through the computation - 80 rupees/notebook x 100 notebooks = 8,000 rupees - makes the operation choice almost automatic and errors visible.
documents.s: Applications of numbers and operations in daily life

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Your tutor gives each group a courtyard plan (a rectangle, say 12 metres by 9 metres) and a choice of square tile sizes (0.5 m, 1 m, 1.5 m). For each tile size, compute how many tiles fill the courtyard and how many full tiles a 64-tile budget would cover. Then decide which tile size wastes the least cutting, and defend the choice in two sentences. About 25 minutes.

Compute: 6 squared, 9 squared, and the square roots of 81 and 100. (Remember) A square classroom floor has an area of 36 square metres. What is the length of each wall, and how do you know? (Apply) Between which two whole numbers does the square root of 40 lie? Justify in one sentence. (Apply) For each situation, name the operation and the reason: (a) 15 boxes of 40 books each; (b) 300 pupils into classes of 30; (c) a 5,600-rupee bill paid with 6,000 rupees. (Apply) A trainee computes 187 pupils divided by 26-pupil vans as 7 and orders 7 vans. Identify the error in one sentence using the look-back idea. (Analyze)

Powers are repeated multiplication, and squares are genuinely areas: an 8-by-8 floor holds 64 tiles, which is why the square root of 64 is 8. Estimation brackets a root between neighbouring squares before any exact work. When a daily problem does not name its operation, ask what the total does: combine equal groups (multiply), break into equal groups (divide), or change by an amount (add or subtract) - then check the answer for reasonableness, because the real-world answer may need the remainder you were about to discard.

I can compute squares and square roots of perfect squares, and bracket other roots between neighbouring squares. I can name the correct operation for a daily-life problem by asking what the total does. I keep units attached through a computation and use them to check the operation.

Find one tiled or bricked area (verandah, courtyard, walkway). Estimate its dimensions, compute its area, and work out how many square tiles of one size would cover it. Ask the caretaker how many tiles were actually used, and note any difference and its likely cause.

documents.t: The school wants a square mosaic of 225 small tiles on a corridor wall, and the wall space is a square of side 20 tiles. In a short written answer: (a) state how wide the mosaic is (the square root of 225) and whether it fits the wall, (b) the school has only these 225 tiles in stock: compute how many more tiles a full 20-by-20 design would need, and (c) propose one real reason a school might prefer the smaller mosaic, with a computation that supports it. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Root and fit: the mosaic is 15 by 15 and fits inside 20 by 20, with reasoning shown. Tile count: a 20-by-20 design uses 400 tiles, so 175 more tiles would be needed; the comparison with 225 is computed correctly. Supported proposal: the reason is argued with a computation (for example, cost per tile or leftover tiles for repairs), not merely asserted. (Analyze)

Whole numbers count what cannot be negative; integers add the negative side and make bookkeeping honest; fractions and decimals are two notations for parts of wholes. Ratio compares, proportion states two ratios are equal, and percentage is a ratio out of 100; scaling multiplies every quantity by the same multiplier and never adds. The four percentage situations (of, increase, decrease, reverse) each need their own setup, and the reverse case is the classic trap. Powers are repeated multiplication, squares are genuinely areas, and square roots return from area to side. When a problem does not name its operation, ask what the total does - combine equal groups (multiply), break into equal groups (divide), or change by an amount (add or subtract) - then check reasonableness.

Which list contains only whole numbers? (Remember) a) 0, 1, 5, 12 b) -3, 0, 5, 12 c) 1/2, 3, 7, 12 d) 0.5, 2, 9, 12 A shop ledger records a debt of 3,500 rupees as -3,500. The minus sign means: (Understand) a) the number was entered wrongly b) the amount counts against the shop's position c) the amount is a fraction of the takings d) the amount is a discount 5.5 metres of cloth divided into lengths of 2.75 metres gives: (Apply) a) 2 lengths b) 2.25 lengths c) 2.75 lengths d) 3 lengths 12 x 0.1 equals: (Apply) a) 120 b) 12 c) 1.2 d) 0.12 The ratio 40 girls to 20 boys in its simplest form is: (Understand) a) 40 to 20 b) 2 to 1 c) 1 to 2 d) 20 to 40 A recipe for 12 people uses 4 eggs. For 30 people the recipe needs: (Apply) a) 8 eggs b) 10 eggs c) 12 eggs d) 16 eggs After a 10 percent rise, a school's electricity bill is 17,600 rupees. The bill before the rise was: (Apply) a) 15,840 rupees b) 16,000 rupees c) 17,390 rupees d) 19,360 rupees 8 squared equals: (Remember) a) 16 b) 64 c) 82 d) 512 The square root of 81 is: (Apply) a) 8 b) 9 c) 40.5 d) 41 187 pupils must travel in vans of 26 seats. Since 187 divided by 26 is 7 with remainder 5, the school needs: (Apply) a) 7 vans b) 8 vans c) 5 vans d) 26 vans

Order these from smallest to largest: 2, -3, 1/2, 0.75, -0.5. (Apply) A shop's cash box holds 9,000 rupees and its debts total 4,500 rupees. Write the shop's position using integers and compute it. (Apply) Explain in two sentences why 12 x 0.1 is smaller than 12, using the idea of a part of a whole. (Understand) A recipe for 20 people uses 6 spoons of sugar. How much sugar for 50 people? Name the multiplier you used. (Apply) Compute 25 percent off a 640-rupee atlas in two ways (subtract the discount; pay 75 percent directly) and confirm the two answers agree. (Apply) A friend scales a recipe by adding: "30 more people, so add one more batch of 6 spoons of sugar and 4 of tea." Explain the error in two sentences and state what to do instead. (Analyze) Between which two whole numbers does the square root of 50 lie? Justify your answer in one sentence. (Apply) For each situation, name the operation and give your reason: (a) 15 boxes of 40 books each; (b) 300 pupils placed into classes of 30. (Apply) Compute 7 squared and the square root of 100, then explain in one sentence how the tile picture connects squaring and square roots. (Understand) A trainee computes 187 divided by 26 as 7 and orders 7 vans. Identify the error in one sentence using the look-back idea. (Analyze)

A school canteen buys flour in 5.5 kg bags at 1,200 rupees per bag. One batch of parathas uses 0.75 kg. Compute how many full batches one bag gives and the flour left over, compute the flour cost per batch to the nearest rupee, and check both answers for reasonableness using estimation, showing your check. (Analyze) A stationery supplier offers two deals on notebooks costing 80 rupees each: Deal A gives "20 percent off", Deal B gives "5 notebooks free with every 20 bought". The school needs 100 notebooks. Compute the total cost under each deal, state which is cheaper and by how much, and identify one circumstance under which the school might still prefer the other deal, with a reason. (Analyze) The school wants a square mosaic of 225 small tiles on a corridor wall, and the wall space is a square of side 20 tiles. State how wide the mosaic is and whether it fits; the school has only these 225 tiles in stock, so compute how many more tiles a full 20-by-20 design would need; and propose one real reason a school might prefer the smaller mosaic, with a computation that supports it. (Analyze) Five pupils scored 36/45, 42/60, 55/75, 18/25 and 27/30 on different tests. Convert each to a percentage, rank the pupils, and analyse which raw score looked most impressive but performed worst, explaining why the total matters when comparing results. (Analyze) A school must transport 187 pupils to an event. Each van carries 26 passengers and costs 3,000 rupees; the transport budget is 25,000 rupees. Compute the vans needed (with your look-back check), the total cost, and whether the budget fits. Then evaluate one alternative (for example, a larger 40-seat bus at 4,500 rupees) and recommend a plan with reasons. (Evaluate)

a - whole numbers are 0 and the counting numbers; the other lists contain a negative, a fraction, or a decimal. b - the negative sign records that the amount reduces the shop's position; that is bookkeeping made honest. a - 5.5 divided by 2.75 is exactly 2. c - multiplying by 0.1 takes one tenth of 12: 1.2. b - 40 to 20 simplifies by dividing both by 20: 2 to 1. b - the multiplier is 30/12 = 2.5, and 4 x 2.5 = 10. b - the rise acted on the original, so divide: 17,600 / 1.1 = 16,000. b - 8 x 8 = 64. b - 9 x 9 = 81. b - 7 vans carry 182 pupils and 5 remain; the real-world answer rounds up.

Model: -3, -0.5, 1/2, 0.75, 2. Marks (2): 1 - negatives placed before positives; 1 - full correct order. Model: position = 9,000 + (-4,500) = 4,500 rupees. Marks (2): 1 - correct integer expression; 1 - correct value. Model: 0.1 is one tenth, so the product takes one tenth of 12, and taking a part gives less than the whole. Marks (2): 1 - names 0.1 as a part (tenth); 1 - connects part to shrinking. Model: multiplier 50/20 = 2.5; sugar = 6 x 2.5 = 15 spoons. Marks (2): 1 - correct amount; 1 - multiplier named. Model: discount = 0.25 x 640 = 160; price = 640 - 160 = 480. Direct: 0.75 x 640 = 480. Both give 480 rupees. Marks (2): 1 - both routes computed; 1 - agreement confirmed. Model: one added batch feeds only 20 more people, so the 50-person function (multiplier 50/20 = 2.5) is left ten servings short; the fix is to multiply every ingredient by the crowd multiplier (15 spoons of sugar, 10 of tea). Marks (2): 1 - the shortfall or per-person point; 1 - the multiply fix. Model: between 7 and 8, because 7 x 7 = 49 < 50 < 64 = 8 x 8. Marks (2): 1 - correct pair; 1 - justification via neighbouring squares. Model: (a) multiply - the total combines 15 equal groups of 40; (b) divide - the total breaks into equal groups of 30. Marks (4): 1 - (a) multiply; 1 - reason; 1 - (b) divide; 1 - reason. Model: 7 squared = 49; sqrt(100) = 10. The tile picture: a square floor of side 7 holds 49 tiles (squaring climbs from side to area), and the root climbs back from area to side. Marks (3): 1 - both values; 2 - the connection explained (1 for direction, 1 for the side-area idea). Model: the look-back check shows 7 vans carry only 182 of 187 pupils, so the discarded remainder of 5 pupils forces an 8th van. Marks (2): 1 - identifies the discarded remainder; 1 - states the corrected answer.
