textbook.com.pk Two teachers compare their classes' test results. Miss Farhana's class of 11 scored: 20, 45, 50, 55, 60, 62, 62, 70, 70, 70, 96. Mr. Qurban's class also averaged "about 60". The headteacher, who has this topic, asks one question of each marksheet: "Which average are you quoting?" Miss Farhana's mean is 60 (the total 660 divided by 11); her median is 62 (the sixth mark when sorted); her mode is 70 (the only mark appearing three times). Three honest averages of one class, three different stories - and the diagram above shows all three living in different places on the same data. A class where the mean sits below the mode is a class with a long tail of low scorers pulling the mean down: that is a teaching fact, not just an arithmetic one.

The three measures of central tendency each answer "what is typical?" differently, and introductory statistics texts teach all three side by side for exactly this reason (Marecek, Anthony-Smith and Mathis, 2020, Section 5.5). The mean is the fair-share value: add all values, divide by how many. It uses every value, so one extreme mark can drag it - the 20 and the 96 in Miss Farhana's class pull in opposite directions. The median is the middle value when the data are sorted. Half the class scored at or below 62, half at or above. The median ignores how far the extremes sit, so it is the honest average for data with outliers - incomes, house prices, marks with one disaster. The mode is the most frequent value: 70, the mark the class "decided" to get. It is the only average that works for categories too - the modal travel mode, the modal shoe size. Worked example. A shop's five daily takings are 4,000, 4,200, 4,100, 4,300 and 39,000 rupees (one wedding order). Mean = 55,600 / 5 = 11,120 rupees - a figure no ordinary day resembled. Median = 4,200 rupees - the honest "typical day". When a headteacher reports "average class size", the same choice applies: a few tiny sections can make the mean flatter the reality most pupils live.

textbook.com.pk Published statistics arrive ready-dressed, and reading them is a skill of questions. The table above lists the five that carry most of the weight. Apply them to a real figure: the 2023 census counted Sindh's literacy rate (10 years and above) at 57.54 percent - 64.23 percent for males and 50.21 percent for females (PBS, 2023). Who collected it? The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, the national statistical office, in the country's first digital census - a strong provenance. How? Door-to-door enumeration on tablets, March to May 2023, approved by the Council of Common Interests. Compared to what? The same measure in 2017 was 54.57 percent - so the rise is about 3 percentage points, small and slow. What is the base? "10 years and above" - a child of nine who cannot read is not counted in this rate at all; a different base (say, 15 and above) gives a different number. What is missing? The gap: about 14 percentage points between male and female literacy (64.23 minus 50.21), and an out-of-school rate (ages 5 to 16) of 46.29 percent - almost half of Sindh's school-age children. The single headline number hides both. Tout (2020) traces how international assessments learned the same lesson: what counts as "literacy" or "numerate" depends on the tasks asked, and cross-comparing numbers without reading their construction misleads. A teacher who can read a statistic this way - base, comparison, collector, missing gap - is a teacher a parent can trust with a marksheet.

Work in groups of three. Your tutor gives each group two anonymised marksheets of 11 scores each (one with an outlier, one without). Each group computes the mean, median and mode of both, then writes three sentences: which average each teacher should quote to parents and why. The debrief question: what does the gap between mean and median say about a class? About 25 minutes.

Compute the mean, median and mode of: 20, 45, 50, 55, 60, 62, 62, 70, 70, 70, 96. (Apply) A shop's takings are 4,000, 4,200, 4,100, 4,300, 39,000 rupees. Which average describes the typical day, and why is the other one misleading here? (Apply) Sindh's literacy rate (10 years and above) is 57.54 percent. State what changes if the base were "15 years and above", and why the base must be read with the number. (Analyze) Name the only average that works for categories, with one example. (Understand) A news report says "literacy rose to 57.54 percent". Write the two questions you would ask before repeating the claim, and what each guards against. (Analyze)

The mean is the fair share that outliers can drag, the median is the middle that ignores them, and the mode is the most frequent value - three honest averages that can tell three different stories about one class. Reading a published statistic means asking who collected it, how, compared to what, on what base, and what it leaves out - and the Sindh literacy figure shows how much a single number can hide.

I can compute the mean, median and mode of a small data set and say what each hides. I can choose the honest average for data with an outlier, with a reason. I can interrogate a published statistic with the five interpretation questions.

Take one class's latest test (anonymised, with permission). Compute the mean, median and mode, and write two sentences for a parents' meeting: which average you would quote and what the gap between mean and median reveals about the class.

documents.t: The 2023 census reports Sindh's literacy (10 years and above) as 57.54 percent overall, 64.23 percent male and 50.21 percent female, against 54.57 percent in 2017; the out-of-school rate (ages 5 to 16) is 46.29 percent (PBS, 2023). In a short written answer: (a) compute the male-female literacy gap in percentage points, (b) state the rise since 2017 in percentage points and say whether it is large or small compared with the gap, and (c) write the two interpretation questions a teacher should ask before quoting the 57.54 percent figure to a parents' meeting, and what each guards against. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Gap: 64.23 - 50.21 = 14.02 percentage points. Rise compared: 57.54 - 54.57 = 2.97 percentage points; the gap (14.02) is more than four times the rise, so the gap dwarfs the improvement. (Analyze) Questions: two of the five interpretation questions chosen with a correct guard (for example, "what is the base?" guards against counting under-10s as non-literate; "what is missing?" surfaces the female gap or the out-of-school rate).

Data are raw facts collected for a question, by observation, survey or records; tallies and frequency tables organize them so summary is simple counting, and a table whose total does not close names a collection problem. Each display answers one kind of question - bar charts compare categories, pie charts show shares of one whole, line graphs track change over time - and reading a display means reading its construction. The mean is the fair share outliers drag, the median the middle that ignores them, the mode the most frequent value; the honest average depends on the data. A published statistic is read with five questions: who collected it, how, compared to what, on what base, and what is missing - and Sindh's 57.54 percent literacy against a 46.29 percent out-of-school rate shows how much one number can hide.

The five stages of the data cycle, in order, are: (Remember) a) collect, question, summarize, organize, interpret b) question, collect, organize, summarize, interpret c) question, organize, collect, interpret, summarize d) collect, organize, question, summarize, interpret To learn how many pupils arrive after the bell each day this week, the best method is: (Apply) a) a survey of pupils b) observation at the gate c) the census report d) a pie chart A survey of 40 returns frequencies 12, 14 and 9. The table tells you: (Apply) a) the survey is complete b) 5 responses are unrecorded c) the mode is 14 d) the mean is 35 The display that best shows each travel mode's share of the class is: (Apply) a) a bar chart b) a line graph c) a pie chart d) a tally The display that best tracks attendance across a week is: (Apply) a) a pie chart b) a line graph c) a pictograph d) a frequency table A category that is 30 percent of the whole takes a pie-slice angle of: (Apply) a) 30 degrees b) 90 degrees c) 108 degrees d) 144 degrees A bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 10 instead of 0: (Understand) a) is correct if labelled b) exaggerates small differences between bars c) makes bars harder to read d) shows shares of a whole For the takings 4,000, 4,200, 4,100, 4,300, 39,000 rupees, the honest "typical day" is the: (Apply) a) mean, 11,120 rupees b) median, 4,200 rupees c) mode, 4,000 rupees d) total, 55,600 rupees The only average that works for categories (like travel modes) is the: (Remember) a) mean b) median c) mode d) range Sindh's 2023 literacy rate of 57.54 percent is measured on the base: (Understand) a) all ages b) 10 years and above c) 15 years and above d) enrolled pupils only

b - question, collect, organize, summarize, interpret. b - watching arrivals records what actually happens; a survey asks what pupils remember. b - 12 + 14 + 9 = 35, so 5 of 40 are unrecorded. c - shares of one whole are the pie chart's job. b - change over time is the line graph's job. c - 30% x 360 = 108 degrees. b - the truncated axis stretches small differences into large-looking ones. b - one wedding-order outlier drags the mean to 11,120, which no ordinary day resembled. c - the mode is the most frequent value and works for categories too. b - the census literacy rate counts persons 10 years and above.

Model: observation (arrivals at the gate), survey (which snack to stock), records (last month's absences) - or equivalent pairings with reasons. Marks (3): 1 per method with a fitting question. Model: the total 35 against the sample 40 shows 5 responses unrecorded; the next move is to find them (or rerun), not to summarize. Marks (2): 1 - the gap identified; 1 - the correct next move. Model: total 660, mean 60; median 62 (sixth of 11 sorted); mode 70 (three times). Marks (3): 1 each. Model: Class A 30, Class B 50; without the key the icons suggest a 3-to-5 count (a 20-pupil error). Marks (2): 1 - both counts; 1 - the missing-key danger. Model: sorted 35, 38, 40, 42, 45: median 40; no repeated value, so no mode. Marks (2): 1 - median 40; 1 - no mode stated. Model: differences between bars look larger than the values justify, because the bars' visible heights start from 10. Marks (2): 1 - exaggeration named; 1 - mechanism. Model: 22.5% x 360 = 81 degrees. Marks (2): 1 - method; 1 - value. Model: a few very high prices drag the mean above what almost any house costs; the median reports the middle of the market, unaffected by the extremes. Marks (2): 1 - outlier effect on mean; 1 - median's resistance. Model: gap = 64.23 - 50.21 = 14.02 percentage points; the headline 57.54 hides the 14-point divide between male and female literacy (and the 46.29 percent out-of-school rate). Marks (2): 1 - gap computed; 1 - what is hidden named. Model: who collected it, how was it collected, compared to what, what is the base, what is missing. Marks (5): 1 per question.

The three topics are the data cycle's three turns: collect and organize (5.1), display (5.2), summarize and interpret (5.3). Do not let trainees skip to displays before they have collected something real; a chart of invented numbers teaches nothing about the cycle's honesty lessons. The unit's three weeks close with the census figures, which deserve a full session.

Use the guide's real-life case-study mode: the attendance-dip investigation and the marksheet clinic are real contexts; ask trainees for their school's equivalents. Run the travel-to-school survey (Topic 5.1) as genuine group work with real classmates as respondents - the bias discussion only lands when the bias was possible. Use question-answer on the display-choice diagram (Topic 5.2): give a question, take the display choice from the class before revealing the rule.

"Data means numbers." Hold up the attendance register: mostly ticks and words. Numbers arrive at the summarize step, when the facts are counted. "A graph's impression is the data." Redraw one bar chart with a truncated axis on the board and ask the class what changed. Nothing in the data changed; the construction did. "The mean is the average." The wedding-order takings example exists for this moment: let the class compute both averages and argue which one a newspaper should print. "The published number settles it." The 57.54 percent literacy figure is the probe: ask what it hides before telling them. The female-male gap and the out-of-school rate are in the same report.

The travel-to-school survey (Topic 5.1): enforce the swap so no group surveys its own question; the master-table combination shows sampling effects for free. Display the same data three ways (Topic 5.2): the swap question ("which single question does this display answer best?") is the assessment; drawing neatly is not. Marksheet clinic (Topic 5.3): keep one marksheet outlier-free so the class sees that the three averages can also coincide - and that the gap between them, not any one of them, is the diagnostic.

Group work in the three activities; a group assignment running the full data cycle on a school question of the group's choosing; the individual assignment is the Topic 5.3 practicum marksheet; presentations come from ERQ-5's own-cycle reports.

The bank's traps are deliberate: MCQ-03 tests the total check, MCQ-07 the truncated axis, RRQ-9 and ERQ-3 the census reading. When marking ERQ-3, reward trainees who notice that the 2.97-point rise is dwarfed by the 14.02-point gap: comparing a number to its right comparator is the unit's highest skill. ERQ-5 must use real data; a cycle run on invented numbers caps at half marks.

Trainees collect three artefacts: a register tally (Topic 5.1), a displayed chart or table with a construction note (Topic 5.2), and a marksheet with the honest-average sentences (Topic 5.3). All three feed Unit 6's decision-making work, so date them.

The course closes where its students live: money, media and decisions. The tools are all from earlier units - percentages from Unit 2, expressions from Unit 3, the check-habit from Units 1 and 4, the data questions from Unit 5 - now pointed at a fair stall's ledger, a toothpaste advertisement, and a father choosing a school. The final lesson is the quietest one: numbers inform decisions; they never replace the decider.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Compute profit, loss and their percentages from a ledger, simple interest for saving and borrowing, and build a five-part monthly budget with savings before spending. Audit a numeric claim in an advertisement or news item with the five questions, and rebuild a hidden interest rate from an instalment. Run the decision loop (question, evidence, options, trade-offs) on a school or policy choice, reading the standard education indicators with their bases and blind spots.
Units 1-5: the four-step strategy, percentages, expressions and inequalities, the reasonableness check, and the data questions. This unit adds no new mathematics.

Topic 6.1 - Financial literacy: profit, loss, interest and budgeting - the fair stall, the savings account, the household plan. Topic 6.2 - Quantitative reasoning in media and advertisements - the truncated axis, the convenient base, the hidden rate. Topic 6.3 - Decision-making with data in education and society - the decision loop and the indicators, with Sindh's census figures.

Work the topics in order; each builds directly on the last (the instalment example opens Topic 6.2; the census figures return in 6.3). The practicum tasks collect a canteen ledger, an advertisement and a school decision - ERQ work will use all three. This is the closing unit: when you finish it, read your Unit 1 self-assessment again and mark what changed. Glossary terms are underlined; hover or tap them for the Urdu definition.

textbook.com.pk The Class 8 stall at the school fair sells 120 plates of biryani at 60 rupees each. The ingredients cost 4,800 rupees, the stall fee was 500, and a borrowed canopy cost 300 to hire. The stall's takings were 7,200 rupees, and the pupils are thrilled - "we made 7,200!" Their teacher, who has this topic, writes four lines on the board: takings 7,200; costs 4,800 + 500 + 300 = 5,600; profit = 7,200 - 5,600 = 1,600 rupees; and profit as a share of costs, 1,600 / 5,600 = about 28.6 percent. Same event, two different numbers - and only the second pair is a financial statement. Financial literacy is not a new branch of mathematics; it is the arithmetic of Units 2 and 3 pointed at money, where the difference between takings and profit is the difference between a feeling and a fact.

Loss is profit's negative twin: costs above takings. Both are always computed against costs when a percentage is wanted: profit percent = (profit / total costs) x 100 loss percent = (loss / total costs) x 100 Worked example. If a rainstorm halves the fair's customers, takings fall to 3,600 rupees against the same 5,600 of costs: loss = 2,000 rupees, and loss percent = 2,000 / 5,600 = about 35.7 percent. The percentage is what lets one stall compare itself with another of a different size - a 2,000-rupee loss on a small stall is a disaster, on a large one a shrug. Steen (2001) built the case for quantitative literacy on ground like this: a person who cannot check the arithmetic of their own livelihood must simply take the quoted number on trust.

textbook.com.pk Interest is the price of money over time: the saver's reward or the borrower's cost. Simple interest pays a fixed percentage of the original amount each year: simple interest = principal x rate x time Worked example. A teacher saves 10,000 rupees at 5 percent simple interest per year. After 3 years: interest = 10,000 x 0.05 x 3 = 1,500 rupees; the account holds 11,500. After 6 years: 3,000 rupees of interest. The interest grows in a straight line - which is exactly what "simple" means, and the pattern-and-sequence eye from Unit 3 sees it at once. Borrowing flips the sign. A 20,000-rupee loan at the same 5 percent simple interest costs 1,000 rupees a year; the interest the saver earns and the interest the borrower pays are the same formula wearing opposite signs. Shops and banks rarely advertise the formula; they advertise the monthly instalment, and the instalment hides the rate. The asymmetry is the point: one side has done the arithmetic, the other has not - and Steen's (2001) case for quantitative literacy is written for citizens on exactly that side of the bargain. A trainee who can rebuild the rate from the instalment is a trainee an advertisement cannot easily fool - which is Topic 6.2's bridge.

A budget is a plan for money before it arrives, not a record after it leaves. The flowchart above shows its five parts. The order matters: savings come out before variable spending, not after, because what is left after spending is usually nothing. Worked example. A trainee's monthly stipend is 25,000 rupees. Fixed costs (room rent, transport pass, a loan instalment): 12,000. Savings target: 3,000. Variable costs (food, phone, extras): the remaining 10,000. The budget is not the arithmetic alone - it is the discipline of checking at month end: did variable spending really stay at 10,000? A budget without the review step is a wish. The same discipline scales beyond the stipend: a school council planning an enrolment drive budgets against counted need, not felt need - Sindh's out-of-school rate for ages 5 to 16 stands at 46.29 percent (PBS, 2023), and a budget line aimed at that number is arithmetic in the service of a plan. A common misconception to correct. Trainees often believe "profit is whatever money comes in". The fair stall exists for this: takings of 7,200 felt like profit until the 5,600 of costs appeared. The second misconception follows the first: that a budget restricts. A budget is a decision made once, calmly, instead of thirty small decisions made under hunger and hurry - it is freedom with a plan, not a cage.

Work in groups of four. Your tutor gives each group a mock fair-stall ledger (takings, ingredient costs, stall fee, one hire cost, and two days of records). Each group computes profit or loss for each day and for the fair overall, then the percentage, then writes a two-sentence recommendation for next year's stall: keep, change the price, or change the quantity - with the computation that supports it. About 25 minutes.

Compute the profit and profit percent: takings 9,000 rupees, costs 7,500 rupees. (Apply) Compute the loss and loss percent: takings 4,000 rupees, costs 5,600 rupees. (Apply) Compute the simple interest on 15,000 rupees at 4 percent for 5 years, and the total in the account. (Apply) A stipend of 25,000 rupees has fixed costs of 12,000 and a savings target of 3,000. State the variable-costs allowance, and why savings are subtracted before variable costs. (Understand) A friend says the fair stall "made 7,200 rupees". Correct the statement in two sentences using the cost and percentage ideas. (Analyze)

Profit is takings minus total costs, and its percentage is always against costs; loss is the same subtraction with the sign flipped. Simple interest is a fixed percent of the original amount per year - principal x rate x time - growing in a straight line for savers and borrowers alike. A budget plans income, fixed costs, variable costs and savings (in that order, savings before spending), and its review step turns a wish into a plan.

I can compute profit, loss and their percentages from a ledger. I can compute simple interest for saving and borrowing, and rebuild a rate from an instalment. I can build a five-part monthly budget with savings before variable spending, and say why the review step matters.

Ask the clerk (or canteen manager) for one week's canteen takings and costs (anonymised if needed). Compute the week's profit or loss and its percentage, and write one sentence on what the number means for next week's stock order.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: A school cooperative wants to lend 50,000 rupees to buy a photocopy machine that earns 3,000 rupees a month for the school. A bank offers the same 50,000 at 6 percent simple interest per year. In a short written answer: (a) compute the school's yearly earnings from the machine and the yearly interest the bank would charge, (b) state whether the machine pays for its loan, and by how much per year, and (c) identify one cost the comparison ignores (paper, repairs, the machine's life) and show how a rough estimate of it could change the conclusion. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Yearly figures: machine 3,000 x 12 = 36,000 rupees; interest 50,000 x 0.06 x 1 = 3,000 rupees. Comparison: the machine earns 33,000 rupees more than the loan costs. Ignored cost analysed: a real cost named with a rough estimate (for example, paper at even 5,000 a year still leaves the machine ahead; a machine lasting only two years changes the picture) and its effect on the conclusion shown. (Analyze)

Steen, L. A. (Ed.). (2001). Mathematics and Democracy: The Case for Quantitative Literacy. National Council on Education and the Disciplines. https://archive.org/details/mathematicsdemoc0000unse (cited at bibliographic level) Pakistan Bureau of Statistics. (2023). Provincial Census Report 2023 - Sindh. Government of Pakistan. https://www.pbs.gov.pk/ (report verified 2026-09-23)

textbook.com.pk A toothpaste advertisement declares: "88 percent of dentists recommend it." The claim sounds scientific, and it may even be true. But a trainee who has Unit 5 asks the questions: 88 percent of how many dentists? Recommended over what - over other brands, or over not brushing at all? Was the survey run by the company? And what happened to the other 12 percent? None of these questions needs new mathematics; they need the habit of asking where a number came from before repeating it. This topic collects the standard moves that make numbers persuade, and the questions that restore the arithmetic. Steen (2001) built the case for quantitative literacy on exactly this ground: a democracy whose citizens cannot question numbers must simply believe them.

textbook.com.pk The table above is the working toolkit; the moves it polices are the same ones Unit 5 met inside the classroom, now pointed outward. The truncated axis. The diagram above shows the classic: a bar chart whose vertical axis starts near the data instead of at zero, turning a 6-point difference into a towering victory. The honest chart beside it carries the same numbers. Advertisers truncate axes; so do news graphics; so, sometimes, do school results boards. The convenient base. "Now with 50 percent more fruit!" - more than what? Fifty percent more than a rival, or than the same product's previous tiny amount? A percentage without its base is a sentence without its subject. Unit 5's census reading practised the same guard: 57.54 percent meant nothing until "10 years and above" was read with it (PBS, 2023). The missing comparison. "The fastest-growing brand in Sindh" may be fastest-growing because it started smallest. Growth rates, exam passes, attendance figures - all persuade most when the comparison is chosen by the persuader. The cure is always the same question: compared to what, over what period? The instalment that hides the rate. From Topic 6.1: a shop advertises "only 2,000 rupees a month" on a 20,000-rupee item. Twelve instalments collect 24,000 rupees; the hidden interest is 4,000 rupees on 20,000 for one year - a 20 percent rate, four times a bank's. The monthly number feels small; the rate is the fact. A common misconception to correct. Trainees often believe "numbers in the media must be true, because numbers are facts". A number is a fact about a question someone asked, in a way someone chose. The advertisement's arithmetic is usually correct; what is engineered is the question, the base and the comparison. Tout (2020) draws the same lesson from international assessments: what a number says depends on the task that produced it, and cross-comparing figures without reading their construction misleads. The reader's job is not cynicism - it is the five questions, which a truthful claim survives easily.
documents.s: Quantitative reasoning in media and advertisements

documents.t: Work in pairs. Your tutor displays five real-style advertisements and headlines (a toothpaste survey, a "50 percent more" food claim, a growth-rate boast, a monthly instalment offer, a news chart). Each pair picks two and writes, for each: the claim in one sentence, the two questions that most need answering, and what the honest version of the claim would say. Pairs present one audit to the class. About 25 minutes.

Name the move at work: a bar chart's vertical axis starts at 80, not 0. (Remember) "Now with 50 percent more fruit." State the question the claim hides, and two possible bases that would change its meaning. (Apply) A 20,000-rupee item at "2,000 a month for 12 months": compute the total paid and the hidden first-year interest as a percentage. (Apply) "The fastest-growing school in the district." Write the two questions you would ask before believing the headline. (Analyze) Explain in two sentences why correct arithmetic can still mislead. (Understand)

Numbers persuade through construction, not lies: the truncated axis exaggerates, the convenient base hides the denominator, the missing comparison chooses the rival, and the instalment hides the rate. The five questions - source, base, comparison, unit, what is missing - restore the arithmetic, and a truthful claim survives them easily.
I can name the four standard moves and spot each in a real advertisement. I can rebuild a hidden interest rate from an instalment offer. I can write the honest version of a persuasive claim.

Collect one advertisement or news number from the school's notice board, a newspaper at the staff room, or a shop near the school. Write the claim, the two questions it raises, and what the honest version would say. Bring it to class for the unit assessment.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: A canteen supplier's poster reads: "9 out of 10 pupils prefer our samosas - and now 30 percent bigger!" In a short written answer: (a) state the two questions each claim needs answered before a school orders, (b) compute what "30 percent bigger" means if the old samosa was 80 grams, and (c) write the honest one-sentence version of the combined claim that a headteacher could act on. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Questions: for the survey, who counted and how the 10 were chosen; for the size, the base of the 30 percent - both named. Computation: 80 x 1.30 = 104 grams. Honest version: a sentence carrying both numbers with their bases, for example "in the supplier's own survey of 10 pupils, 9 preferred its samosas, which now weigh 104 grams against the previous 80". (Analyze)

Evolution of adult numeracy from quantitative literacy to numeracy: Lessons learned from international assessments. International Review of Education, 66, 183-209. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1266633

textbook.com.pk A father in Naushahro Feroze must choose between two schools for his daughter: Government High School A, with 900 pupils and a 75 percent pass rate, and a private school B, with 300 pupils and a 90 percent pass rate. The private school's brochure quotes only the 90. The father, helped by his daughter's cousin - a B.Ed trainee with this course - asks one more question of each school: "How many pupils sat the exam?" School A entered 300 and passed 225; school B entered 60 and passed 54. The pass rates hold - but the trainee notices two more things: A's rate is built on five times the candidates, and B charges 1,500 rupees a month while A is free. The decision is the father's; the data's job is to make sure he decides on the whole picture, not on the one number someone chose to print.

A data-informed decision runs the loop in the concept map above: name the question, gather the evidence, list the options with their costs, and weigh the trade-offs before deciding. It is Unit 1's four-step strategy grown up: the "plan" step has become "options and trade-offs", because real decisions are choices between incomparable goods - money against class size, one year's result against five years' trend. Worked example: the school choice. Listing the evidence for the father's decision: pass rates (75 vs 90 percent), candidates (300 vs 60 - the small base makes B's rate wobblier), fees (0 vs 1,500/month = 18,000/year), distance, and the female teachers question his daughter cares about. The trade-off step names what each choice gives up: A gives up 15 points of pass rate but keeps 18,000 rupees a year in the family; B buys the rate and spends the money. There is no formula that settles this - and that is the point: the numbers inform the decision; they do not replace the decider.

textbook.com.pk The indicators in the table above are the ones a teacher will meet in staff meetings, news reports and policy documents. Three of them carry the unit's verified Sindh figures (PBS, 2023): literacy (10 years and above) at 57.54 percent, with its 14-point male-female gap; the out-of-school rate (ages 5 to 16) at 46.29 percent; and behind every school, the pupil-teacher ratio. Each indicator answers one question and hides another - the literacy rate hides its base, the out-of-school rate hides where the children are, and the ratio hides how pupils are distributed among classes. McClure (2020) built a quantitative-literacy unit for high-school STEM teachers around exactly this skill: reading an indicator's construction before using it to argue. A common misconception to correct. Trainees often believe "the data decides". Data never decides; people decide, using data. The belief is dangerous in both directions - it lets a bad number overrule good judgement, and it lets a decision hide behind a number that was never questioned. The honest statement is quieter: a good decision names its question, shows its evidence, owns its trade-offs, and can say what would change its mind.
documents.s: Interpreting quantitative information in education and society

documents.t: Work in groups of four. Each group receives the two-school dossier (pass rates, candidates, fees, distances, teacher numbers) plus one extra fact that differs by group (a new bus route, a sibling already at B, A's five-year rising trend). Groups run the decision loop and present a recommendation in exactly four sentences: question, evidence, options and costs, trade-off and choice. The class votes on which recommendation is best argued, not which school it picks. About 25 minutes.

Name the four stages of the decision loop in order. (Remember) School A passes 225 of 300; school B passes 54 of 60. Compute both rates, and state which rate rests on the firmer base and why. (Apply) State what a pupil-teacher ratio of 30 can hide, with a concrete example. (Analyze) Name the indicator behind each figure: (a) 57.54 percent of persons 10 and above; (b) 46.29 percent of ages 5 to 16. (Understand) A committee says "the data decided". Correct the statement in two sentences. (Analyze)

A data-informed decision runs question, evidence, options, trade-offs - the four-step strategy grown up, where the plan step becomes a choice between incomparable goods. The standard indicators (literacy, out-of-school, enrolment, attendance, pupil-teacher ratio) each answer one question and hide another, and the verified Sindh figures give them real weight. Data informs the decision; it never replaces the decider.

I can run the decision loop on a real choice and present it in four sentences. I can read the standard education indicators with their bases and their blind spots. I can state, for a given decision, what evidence it used and what would change its mind.

Take one decision your cooperating school made this term (a purchase, a timetable change, an event). Reconstruct it as the decision loop: the question, the evidence actually used, the options considered, and the trade-off that settled it. Ask the decision-maker whether your reconstruction is fair, and note their correction.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: A district committee must spend one grant of 500,000 rupees either on hiring two new teachers for a school with a pupil-teacher ratio of 50, or on a bus for 40 pupils who walk 5 kilometres, in a district whose out-of-school rate (ages 5 to 16) is 46.29 percent (PBS, 2023). In a short written answer: (a) run the decision loop - state the question, the evidence, the two options with their costs, and the trade-off each choice makes, (b) recommend one option with the computation that supports it, and (c) state one piece of evidence that would change your recommendation. Mini-rubric (each criterion 0-2 marks): Loop run: question, evidence, options and trade-offs all present and separated. Recommendation with computation: for example, two teachers cut the ratio for 100 pupils from 50 to 25 (100/4: two teachers become four), while the bus moves 40 pupils - the support names which population each option serves. (Analyze) Changing evidence: a concrete item (a survey showing the 40 walkers would drop out without the bus; a second grant arriving) that would genuinely flip the choice.

The fair stall took 7,200 rupees against costs of 5,600. Its profit is: (Apply) a) 7,200 rupees b) 1,600 rupees c) 2,800 rupees d) 5,600 rupees Profit percent is always computed against: (Remember) a) takings b) total costs c) the price per plate d) last year's profit 10,000 rupees at 5 percent simple interest for 3 years earns: (Apply) a) 500 rupees b) 1,000 rupees c) 1,500 rupees d) 15,000 rupees In the five-part budget, savings are subtracted: (Understand) a) after variable costs, from what is left b) before variable costs, right after fixed costs c) only at year end d) never, if income is tight A bar chart whose axis starts at 80 instead of 0: (Remember) a) is the truncated-axis move b) is the convenient-base move c) is the hidden-rate move d) is honest if the bars are equal width "Now with 50 percent more fruit" hides: (Understand) a) the survey size b) the base of the percentage c) the axis start d) the instalment count A 20,000-rupee item at 2,000 rupees a month for 12 months carries a hidden first-year interest of: (Apply) a) 0 rupees b) 2,000 rupees (10 percent) c) 4,000 rupees (20 percent) d) 24,000 rupees School A passes 225 of 300; school B passes 54 of 60. Compute the profit and profit percent: takings 9,000 rupees, costs 7,500 rupees. (Apply) Compute the simple interest on 15,000 rupees at 4 percent for 5 years, and the total in the account. (Apply) A stipend of 25,000 rupees has fixed costs of 12,000 and a savings target of 3,000. State the variable-costs allowance and why savings come out before variable costs. (Understand) A friend says the fair stall "made 7,200 rupees". Correct the statement in two sentences using cost and percentage. (Analyze) Name the two questions the claim "9 out of 10 dentists recommend it" needs answered before you repeat it. (Analyze) A 20,000-rupee item at 2,000 a month for 12 months: compute the total paid and the hidden rate as a percentage. (Apply) Explain in two sentences why correct arithmetic can still mislead. (Understand) School A passes 225 of 300; school B passes 54 of 60. Compute both rates and state which rests on the firmer base, with a reason. (Apply) State what a pupil-teacher ratio of 30 can hide, with a concrete example. (Analyze) Name the four stages of the decision loop, and say which stage Unit 1's four-step strategy grew into. (Understand)

A school cooperative wants to lend 50,000 rupees for a photocopy machine earning 3,000 rupees a month, while a bank charges 6 percent simple interest per year. Compute the yearly earnings and the yearly interest; state whether the machine pays for its loan and by how much; and identify one cost the comparison ignores, with a rough estimate showing how it could change the conclusion. (Analyze) A canteen supplier's poster reads: "9 out of 10 pupils prefer our samosas - and now 30 percent bigger!" State the two questions each claim needs answered; compute what "30 percent bigger" means if the old samosa was 80 grams; and write the honest one-sentence version a headteacher could act on. (Analyze) A district committee must spend 500,000 rupees either on two new teachers for a school with a pupil-teacher ratio of 50, or on a bus for 40 pupils who walk 5 kilometres, in a district whose out-of-school rate (ages 5 to 16) is 46.29 percent (PBS, 2023). Run the decision loop - question, evidence, options with costs, trade-offs; recommend one option with the computation that supports it; and state one piece of evidence that would change your recommendation. (Analyze) Using the canteen ledger from your Topic 6.1 practicum task (or the mock ledger from the fair stall audit), present the week's profit or loss with its percentage; then write the two-sentence recommendation for next week's stock order, and evaluate what the percentage adds that the rupee figure alone does not. (Evaluate) Return to your Unit 1 self-assessment checklist. Using one decision from your practicum reconstruction (Topic 6.3) and one advertisement audit (Topic 6.2), evaluate how your quantitative reasoning has changed across the course: name two habits you now have that you lacked in Unit 1, one situation where the numbers changed your first instinct, and one thing you still want to strengthen. (Evaluate)

b - 7,200 - 5,600 = 1,600 rupees. b - the percentage base is total costs. c - 10,000 x 0.05 x 3 = 1,500 rupees. b - savings come out before variable spending, or they do not happen. a - starting the axis near the data is the truncated-axis move. b - "50 percent more" hides more than what. c - 24,000 paid on 20,000 for a year is 4,000 interest, a 20 percent rate. b - 300 candidates give A's rate a steadier base than B's 60. b - the out-of-school rate counts children ages 5 to 16. b - question, evidence, options, trade-offs.

Model: profit = 1,500 rupees; 1,500 / 7,500 = 20 percent. Marks (2): 1 - value; 1 - percentage. Model: 15,000 x 0.04 x 5 = 3,000 rupees; total 18,000. Marks (2): 1 - interest; 1 - total. Model: 25,000 - 12,000 - 3,000 = 10,000 rupees; savings come out first because what is left after spending is usually nothing. Marks (2): 1 - allowance; 1 - the reason. Model: the 7,200 is takings, not profit; costs of 5,600 leave a profit of 1,600 rupees, about 28.6 percent of costs. Marks (2): 1 - takings vs profit; 1 - the corrected figure with percentage. Model: how many dentists, chosen how (the base); and who ran and paid for the survey (the source). Marks (2): 1 each. Model: total paid 24,000; interest 4,000 on 20,000 for one year = 20 percent. Marks (2): 1 - total; 1 - rate. Model: the arithmetic can be correct while the question, base or comparison was engineered to persuade; the construction, not the calculation, carries the misleading. Marks (2): 1 - construction vs calculation; 1 - an example or restatement. Model: A = 75 percent, B = 90 percent; A's base of 300 candidates makes its rate steadier (B's 60 means each pupil moves B's rate by more than a point). Marks (2): 1 - both rates; 1 - the base judgement with reason. Model: a ratio of 30 can hide one class of 80 and three of 20 - the same average, opposite realities. Marks (2): 1 - the hiding named; 1 - a concrete example. Model: question, evidence, options, trade-offs; the plan step grew into options and trade-offs. documents.t: Photocopy loan. Analytic rubric: Yearly figures (0-2: 36,000 earned; 3,000 interest); Comparison (0-2: the machine earns 33,000 more than the loan costs); Ignored cost (0-2, Analyze: a real cost with a rough estimate and its effect on the conclusion). Total 6. Samosa poster. Analytic rubric: Questions (0-2: the survey's who-and-how-many; the size claim's base); Computation (0-2: 104 grams); Honest version (0-2, Analyze: one sentence carrying both numbers with their bases). Total 6. Committee grant. Analytic rubric: Loop run (0-2: all four stages present and separated); Recommendation with computation (0-2, Analyze: e.g. two teachers cut a 100-pupil school's ratio from 50 to 25 (100/4), while the bus moves 40 pupils; the support names which population each option serves); Changing evidence (0-2: a concrete item that would flip the choice). Total 6. Canteen ledger. Analytic rubric: Profit with percentage (0-2: correct computation against costs); Recommendation (0-2: two sentences tied to the numbers); Percentage's added value evaluated (0-3, Analyze: what the percentage enables that the rupee figure cannot - comparison across weeks or stalls, size independence). Total 7. Course reflection. Analytic rubric: Two habits named (0-2: real, specific habits like the total check or the five questions); Numbers vs instinct (0-3, Analyze: a concrete case where data changed the first instinct); Strength to build (0-2: honest and specific); Clarity (0-1). Total 8.

Topic 6.1 gives the financial arithmetic; 6.2 points it outward at persuasion; 6.3 points it at decisions. The instalment example is the bridge from 6.1 to 6.2, and the census figures return from Unit 5 in 6.3 - teach the three topics in order and name the bridges. The unit closes the course; reserve the last session's final twenty minutes for ERQ-5's reflection on the Unit 1 checklist.

Use the guide's real-life case-study mode throughout: the fair stall, the toothpaste advertisement and the school choice are all real situations - invite the class's own before revealing each worked example. Run the fair stall audit (Topic 6.1) as guided practice with the ledger on every table; the recommendation step is where arithmetic becomes judgement. Use brainstorming for the advertisement audit (Topic 6.2): collect the class's questions before showing the five-question table, and let them discover they already asked most of them.

"Profit is whatever money comes in." The 7,200-rupee takings exist for this; ask the class what the stall made before showing the cost lines. "A budget is a restriction." Ask who has ended a month with money left over without planning one. The budget is thirty decisions made once, calmly. "Numbers in the media must be true." Show the two-panel toothpaste chart from Topic 6.2; both panels are arithmetically correct. "The data decided." The committee phrase, met in Topic 6.3; ask the class who signed the order. Data informs; a person decides and owns the trade-off.

The fair stall audit (Topic 6.1): each group's ledger differs slightly so the recommendations cannot be copied; the vote at the end is on the best-argued recommendation, not the highest profit. The advertisement audit (Topic 6.2): insist on real-style claims (bring clippings if possible); invented advertisements are too honest. The school choice panel (Topic 6.3): the group-varying extra fact is the point - it shows how one new piece of evidence re-runs the whole loop.

Group work in the three activities; the group assignment is the full decision-loop dossier on a real school question; the individual assignments are the canteen ledger, the advertisement audit and the practicum decision reconstruction; presentations come from the school choice panels.

The bank's traps are deliberate: MCQ-02 and RRQ-4 punish the takings-is-profit error, MCQ-07 and RRQ-6 the hidden rate, MCQ-08 and RRQ-8 the small-base rate. ERQ-3 has no single fixed answer - only correct reasoning - and the rubric grades the loop, the computation and the named changing-evidence. Say this aloud before the class attempts it; the unit's last lesson is that a defensible decision, not a single right one, is the goal.

The three artefacts (ledger, advertisement, decision reconstruction) feed ERQs 2-5. The course closes with the Unit 1 self-assessment re-read; collect the trainees' "what changed" notes - they are the course's own evidence, and the next cohort's first reading.

This course equips prospective teachers with a grounded understanding of critical thinking and reflective practice as professional capabilities - the nature of thinking, the barriers to it, and the habits of mind that make reflection a disciplined professional act rather than an occasional one.
documents.s: Critical Thinking and Reflective Practices - Course Overview

documents.t: Assessment follows the GECE default: 60% summative / 40% formative (Constitution Art. III.7). This course's guide does not specify a course-wide breakdown of teaching strategies or practical work beyond what each unit's own topics cover - see each unit's Teacher Notes for the strategies used to teach it.
Recommended sources from the course guide are listed for scope and further reading only; they are never reproduced as content.

Before you can teach pupils to think critically, it helps to be clear about what critical thinking actually is - and, just as importantly, what it is not. In everyday staffroom talk the phrase is sometimes used to mean "being sceptical about everything" or "finding fault with what other people say". This unit uses a different meaning, the one the course guide follows: critical thinking is the habit of judging a piece of reasoning against a set of clear standards. It is a skill you can train, not a personality you either have or lack.

By the end of this unit you will be able to: Explain what critical thinking is and distinguish it from merely criticising or from general scepticism. Name and apply the recognised standards used to judge a piece of reasoning. Identify the common barriers that stop people - including teachers - from thinking critically. Distinguish a statement, a claim, an issue and an argument, and recognise when a piece of text is making an argument. Analyse a described teacher's reasoning against the standards and name the barrier it shows.

None beyond HSC-level general study skills. This is the opening unit of the course. No prior logic or philosophy is assumed, and none is needed. If you have ever had to decide whether a colleague's argument was convincing and why, you already have the experience this unit builds on.

What thinking is, and what makes it critical - the functions of thought and the idea of critical thinking. The standards, and what they are for - the standards applied to reasoning and why they matter. What gets in the way - the barriers that stop critical thinking. Statements, claims, issues and arguments - the basic units reasoning is built from. The critical thinker, and the teacher as one - the characteristics of a critical thinker, applied to teachers.

Each topic is one learning cycle. Start with the classroom situation, work through the explanation, and try the activity before you move on. The "Check your understanding" items are there to help you retrieve what you have learned - have a go at them without looking back, then check your answer. The unit ends with a summative assessment that draws the five topics together.

documents.s: Topic 1.1 - How humans learn: three theories

documents.t: A teacher in a government primary school in interior Sindh is told at a staff meeting that her results would improve if she "made the pupils think more". She is not sure what that means. She already asks questions, she sets written work, and she walks around the room while the class works. When she pictures "thinking", she imagines a quiet child staring at a sums page. She wonders what she is supposed to do differently - and whether the problem is her teaching or her pupils' ability. textbook.com.pk textbook.com.pk Her uncertainty is common, and it matters. Without a clear picture of what thinking is and what makes it critical, the instruction to "make them think" is too vague to act on. This topic gives you that picture.

Thinking is not a single thing the mind does. Thinking covers a range of functions: remembering a fact, imagining a possibility, believing a claim, deciding between options, and reasoning from evidence to a conclusion (Bassham, Irwin, Nardone & Wallace, 2010). These functions are not fixed abilities you are born with. Like any skill, they improve with practice and with being shown how. A pupil who is asked only to copy from the board is exercising memory; a pupil who is asked to compare two answers and decide which is better is exercising reasoning. The difference is in the demand the task makes, not in the pupil.
documents.s: Thinking as a skill that can be trained

documents.t: Bassham et al. (2010) group the functions of thought into two broad kinds: taking in (perceiving, remembering, believing) and working on (reasoning, deciding, judging). Critical thinking belongs to the second kind. It is the function that steps back from what you have taken in and asks, "Is this belief well supported? Does this conclusion follow from the reasons given?" You use it when you evaluate a newspaper claim, decide whether a new teaching method is worth trying, or judge whether a pupil's wrong answer reveals a careless mistake or a genuine misconception.

Here is the distinction many introductory treatments blur, and it is the heart of this unit: critical thinking is a set of standards applied to a piece of reasoning, not a personality trait and not a habit of doubting everything. It is not the same as "criticising" in the everyday sense of finding fault. A person who dismisses every new idea is not thinking critically; they are being dismissive. Critical thinking judges reasoning on its merits, whether the conclusion turns out to be right or wrong. It is not general scepticism. Refusing to accept anything without proof is a stance, not a skill. Critical thinking accepts well-supported claims and challenges weak ones. It is the habit of asking of any piece of reasoning: Is it clear? Is it accurate? Is it relevant? Is it deep enough for the question at stake? Those questions are the standards, and the next topic examines them in detail. A useful way to hold the distinction is as a contrast pair: two teachers hear a workshop claim that a new method "raises results by 30 per cent". The first teacher accepts it because the speaker sounded confident. The second asks, "Thirty per cent of what, measured how, compared with what?" The second teacher is not being difficult; they are applying a standard. That is critical thinking in action. Common misconception. Many trainees arrive with the idea that "being intelligent and thinking critically are the same thing". They are not. A person of high intelligence can hold a poorly supported belief and defend it cleverly. Critical thinking is a practice - a set of moves you make when you judge reasoning - and it can be learned and improved regardless of how "naturally clever" you are.
documents.s: What critical thinking is, and what it is not

documents.t: Work in pairs. About 20 minutes. Take the staffroom claim: "This class cannot do word problems." For each of the four questions below, write one sentence saying what would have to be true for the claim to stand up. Is it clear - do we know what "cannot do" means and what kind of word problems are meant? Is it accurate - what evidence shows the whole class fails at this? Is it relevant - is the problem the pupils' ability, the way the problems are written, or the teaching they have had? Is it deep - does the claim explain why they struggle, or only report that they do? Compare your sentences with another pair. Where you disagree, explain your reasoning.
documents.s: Activity: What would have to be true?

documents.t: (Remember) In your own words, name two functions of thought that are not critical thinking and one that is. (Understand) Explain the difference between critical thinking and general scepticism in one or two sentences. (Apply) A colleague says, "Critical people just complain all the time." Using the is/is-not distinction from this topic, give two reasons that statement confuses critical thinking with something else.

Thinking is a set of functions, not a single ability. Critical thinking is the function that judges reasoning against standards. It is a skill that can be trained, not a personality you have or lack, and it is not the same as criticising or doubting everything. The standards it applies are the subject of the next topic.

I can explain what critical thinking is in a way that distinguishes it from merely criticising. I can give an example of a classroom moment that shows critical thinking and one that does not. I can name at least two functions of thought that are not critical thinking.

At your next staff meeting or team conversation, listen for one claim about pupils or teaching (for example, "these children cannot read" or "that method never works here"). Write it down. Then write one sentence for each of these: what would have to be true for the claim to be clear, accurate, relevant, and deep? Bring your notes to the next session.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Take the claim "Homework does not improve learning in primary school." Write a short paragraph (80-120 words) evaluating it against two of the four standards introduced in this activity (clarity, accuracy, relevance, depth). For each standard, state whether the claim meets it and give one piece of reasoning for your judgement. Mini-rubric Criterion Levels Standards identified 0-2: names two standards and uses them correctly / names one / none. Evidence used 0-3: gives specific reasoning for each judgement / vague or generic reasoning / none. (Analyze: cites a concrete reason the claim does or does not meet the standard.) Clarity 0-2: paragraph is coherent and within the word band / unclear or over length.

documents.s: Topic 1.2 - The standards, and what they are for

documents.t: At a school in Hyderabad, the head teacher announces that the school will adopt "activity-based learning" the following term because, he says, "children learn better when they are doing, not just listening". Several teachers nod. One teacher, Ayesha, wants to agree but is unsure whether the claim is sound or merely fashionable. She has seen activity-based lessons that were busy but taught little, and she has seen quiet direct instruction that worked well. She wishes she had a way to judge the claim rather than just trusting the head's confidence. textbook.com.pk textbook.com.pk Ayesha's wish is exactly what the standards give you: a checklist to apply to any piece of reasoning so that your judgement rests on something firmer than a speaker's confidence.

Bassham et al. (2010) set out a small set of standards that good reasoning is expected to meet. Think of them as questions you put to any claim or argument. Research with teacher candidates confirms that these standards are a measurable construct: trainees' attitudes toward critical thinking predict how well they apply the standards, accounting for a large share of the variance in standard scores (Zeybek, 2025). Clear - Is it understandable? A claim you cannot paraphrase in your own words is too vague to judge. Accurate - Is it true, or at least supported by evidence? A claim that sounds plausible but has no backing fails here. Precise - Is it specific enough? "Results will improve" is less precise than "punctuation errors in weekly drafts will fall by a quarter over one term". Relevant - Does it bear on the question at hand? A true but off-point fact is a distraction, not a reason. Deep - Does it get to the real cause, or only the surface? Saying "the pupils failed because the test was hard" may be accurate without being deep. Broad - Does it consider other angles, or only the one the speaker prefers? Logical - Does the conclusion follow from the reasons given? Fair - Has the reasoning considered the strongest version of the opposing view, or only a weakened one? You do not need to memorise the list as a chant. You need to use it as a habit: when you meet a claim, run it past the two or three standards that matter most for the question at stake.

When a teacher applies the standards to her own planning, the benefit is better decisions. Instead of adopting a method because a workshop recommended it, she asks: What is the evidence? Is it relevant to my pupils' age and context? Does it address the actual learning problem I face? That habit protects against fads and against the assumption that what worked elsewhere will work unchanged in her room.
documents.s: Benefits of critical thinking in the classroom

documents.t: The same habit matters among colleagues. Staffroom decisions - grouping pupils, choosing a textbook, setting homework policy - are often made on habit or on the strongest voice in the room. A teacher who asks "How do we know that is true?" or "What would count as evidence that this is not working?" makes the discussion more honest and usually more useful. Critical thinking is, in this sense, a professional responsibility, not a private talent.
documents.s: Benefits of critical thinking in the workplace

documents.t: Outside school, the standards help you judge the claims you meet daily: a health remedy advertised on social media, a political promise, a news report about exam results. In each case the same questions apply - Clear? Accurate? Relevant? Logical? - and a person who asks them is less easily misled. For a teacher, this everyday habit also models for pupils what it looks like to take ideas seriously without taking them on trust. Common misconception. Many trainees arrive believing that "a claim and an argument are the same thing". They are not. A claim is a statement that something is true ("activity-based learning is better"). An argument is a claim plus at least one reason offered to support it ("activity-based learning is better because it raises test scores, as a 2019 study showed"). The standards apply to both, but an argument gives you more to judge: you can ask whether the reason actually supports the claim. The next two topics look at these units of reasoning in detail.
documents.s: Benefits of critical thinking in everyday life

documents.t: Work in small groups. About 20 minutes. Take the head teacher's claim: "Children learn better when they are doing, not just listening." As a group, choose three standards from the list above. For each chosen standard, write one sentence judging whether the claim meets it and one sentence saying what would need to be added or changed for it to pass. Compare your judgements with another group. Where you disagree, explain which standard you applied and why.
documents.s: Activity: Run a claim through the standards

documents.t: (Remember) Name four of the eight critical-thinking standards. (Understand) Explain the difference between a claim being accurate and a claim being deep, using a classroom example. (Apply) A colleague says, "We should ban mobile phones because they distract pupils." Apply the relevance and precision standards to that claim in one or two sentences each.

The standards - clear, accurate, precise, relevant, deep, broad, logical, fair - are a checklist for judging any piece of reasoning. Applying them in the classroom, the staffroom and everyday life is what turns "critical thinking" from a vague compliment into a usable professional skill.
I can name and explain at least four of the eight standards. I can apply a standard to judge whether a described claim meets it. I can explain why a claim can be accurate without being deep.

Find a written claim in your school - a notice, a policy line, or a sentence from a textbook. Choose two standards and write one sentence each judging the claim against them. Note what evidence you would want to see for the claim to pass.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Take the claim "Our pupils' Urdu results dropped because the new textbook is harder." Write a short paragraph (80-120 words) evaluating it against three of the eight standards. For each standard, state whether the claim meets it and give one piece of reasoning. Mini-rubric Criterion Levels Standards applied 0-2: three standards named and used correctly / fewer than three or misapplied. Reasoning quality 0-3: specific reasoning for each judgement / vague or generic / none. (Analyze: cites a concrete reason the claim does or does not meet the standard.) Clarity 0-2: paragraph coherent and within word band / unclear or over length.

documents.s: Topic 1.3 - What gets in the way

documents.t: A head teacher in a Karachi primary school decides to keep the same timetable he has used for twelve years because, he says, "we have always done it this way and our results have been fine." When a younger teacher suggests trialling a different afternoon order so that the hardest subject is not last, the head dismisses the idea without examining it. He is not being stubborn on purpose. He is caught in one of the most common barriers to critical thinking, and he cannot see it from the inside. textbook.com.pk textbook.com.pk This topic names the barriers that stop people - including experienced teachers - from reasoning well, so that you can spot them in your own thinking and in staffroom discussion.

Critical thinking is not stopped by a lack of intelligence. It is stopped by habits of mind that feel reasonable from the inside but distort judgement. Bassham et al. (2010) group them by where they come from. From the self. Egocentrism is the habit of seeing everything from your own position and assuming your view is the natural one. In a staffroom it sounds like, "I was taught this way and I turned out fine, so there is nothing wrong with it." A related barrier is self-confirming search: noticing every fact that supports what you already believe and ignoring the rest. A teacher who is sure a pupil is "lazy" will notice every missed assignment and overlook the weeks the pupil tried hard. From the group. Group conformity is the pressure to think along with those around you. In a school it is often stronger than people admit: a teacher who privately doubts a new policy will stay silent when everyone else nods, because disagreeing feels disloyal or risky. The barrier is not that the group is always wrong; it is that the group's view is accepted without being examined. From the wish. Wishful thinking is believing a claim because you want it to be true. "If I set less homework, my pupils will learn just as well" may be right, but if the reason for believing it is that marking is tiring, the wish is doing the work, not the evidence. From the assumption. Every piece of reasoning rests on assumptions the speaker does not state. Often they are harmless. But sometimes an unexamined assumption carries the whole argument: "These practise-school pupils cannot manage group work" rests on an assumption about what they have been prepared for, and if that assumption is wrong, the conclusion falls with it.

None of these barriers is a character flaw. Egocentrism and group conformity are ordinary cognitive defaults - the mind's way of saving effort. That is precisely why they are dangerous: they feel normal. Empirical work with university students confirms the picture: making learners aware of confirmation bias, social pressure to conform, framing and poor risk assessment - the same family of barriers this topic names - measurably grows their critical dispositions (Aston, 2024). A teacher who treats them as personal faults in others ("he is stubborn", "she just follows the crowd") will stop listening. A teacher who treats them as habits to watch for - in herself as much as in others - is thinking more critically already. Common misconception. "Critical thinking means criticising" and "a claim and an argument are the same thing" are not the only barriers trainees bring. Two others sit inside this topic: the idea that "being intelligent and thinking critically are the same" (intelligence can defend a bad belief cleverly) and the idea that critical thinking is a personality you have or lack. Naming the barriers as ordinary habits, not character flaws, is what makes them something you can work on.
documents.s: Why the barriers matter for teachers

documents.t: Work in pairs. About 15 minutes. Read each short classroom reasoning below and decide which barrier it most shows: egocentrism, group conformity, wishful thinking, or an unexampled assumption. Write one sentence explaining your choice and one question that would interrupt the reasoning. "We should not change the exam format; the parents expect the old one." "My pupils will do fine in the board exam because I have covered every topic." "Streaming by ability cannot be unfair - every school does it." "This pupil failed because she did not revise." Compare your answers with another pair. Where you chose different barriers, explain your reasoning.

(Remember) Name the four sources from which barriers to critical thinking come. (Understand) Explain why group conformity is a cognitive default rather than a character flaw, in one or two sentences. (Apply) A teacher says, "I know my method works because my results are always good." Which barrier does that reasoning most show, and why?

The barriers to critical thinking come from the self, the group, the wish and unexamined assumptions. They are ordinary habits of mind, not character flaws, which is what makes them hard to spot and worth watching for - especially in your own reasoning.

I can name the four sources of barriers and give an example of each. I can recognise which barrier a described piece of teacher reasoning shows. I can explain why treating barriers as habits rather than flaws matters in a staffroom.

Recall one recent staffroom or classroom decision you were part of. Write down the reasoning that was offered and then write one sentence naming the barrier it most showed. Be honest with yourself the point is to practise spotting the habit, not to judge the people involved.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Take this reasoning: "We cannot try peer assessment in grade 4; the parents will think we are not doing our job." Write a short paragraph (80-120 words) naming the barrier it most shows, explaining why, and offering one question that would interrupt the reasoning. Mini-rubric Criterion Levels Barrier identified 0-2: names the barrier correctly and from the right source / names a barrier but misreads the source / none. Explanation 0-3: specific reasoning linking the text to the barrier / vague or generic / none. (Analyze: cites a specific piece of the reasoning as evidence.) Clarity 0-2: paragraph coherent and within word band / unclear or over length.

documents.s: Topic 1.4 - Statements, claims, issues and arguments

documents.t: A teacher training college in Punjab sets this assignment: "Standardised testing improves the quality of education." Trainees must write a short response. One pupil writes, "I disagree." Another writes, "Standardised testing improves education because it lets the government compare schools and direct resources where they are most needed." A third writes, "Standardised testing is one form of assessment." The tutor wants to mark not just whether the trainees agree, but whether they can reason - and that means knowing which of the three is an argument. textbook.com.pk textbook.com.pk This topic gives you the vocabulary to tell those three apart, because you cannot evaluate reasoning until you can see what kind of reasoning you are looking at.

A Statement is a sentence that claims something is (or is not) the case - something that can, at least in principle, be true or false. "The school has 400 pupils." "Monday is the first day of the week." Not every sentence is a statement: a question ("May I come in?") or an exclamation ("Well done!") makes no claim about what is true, so it is not a statement in the logical sense.

A Claim is a statement that someone puts forward as true, often in the face of possible disagreement. In practice the words "statement" and "claim" overlap a great deal. The useful difference is emphasis: calling something a claim signals that it needs support. When a colleague says "homework always improves learning", treating that as a claim means asking "what is the evidence?" rather than just accepting it.

An Issue is a question that invites more than one reasonable answer - something people can disagree about. "Should homework be set in grade 1?" is an issue. "How many pupils are in this class?" is not, because it has a single factual answer. Critical thinking spends its time on issues, because they are the questions that need reasoning rather than just looking something up.

An Argument is the unit this whole topic has been building towards. An argument is a claim plus at least one reason offered to support it. The claim is the conclusion; the reasons are the premises. This is the meaning of "argument" in critical thinking, and it is not the everyday meaning of "quarrel". A calm, well-supported case is an argument in the logical sense. How do you tell an argument from a mere claim? Use a short decision path: Does the text assert something is true? If not, it is not an argument. Is a reason given for the assertion? If there is only a claim, it is a mere claim. Is the reason meant to support the claim, or only to explain it? If the text says "X because Y" and Y is offered as evidence for X, that is an argument. If Y only explains how X came to be, that is an explanation, not an argument. Common misconception. Many trainees arrive believing "a claim and an argument are the same thing". The difference matters because an argument gives you more to judge. A claim alone ("streaming is unfair") asks only whether you agree. An argument ("streaming is unfair because it fixes labels too early and the evidence shows pupils move between levels") lets you ask whether the reasons actually support the conclusion - and that is where critical thinking gets to work.

Work in pairs. About 20 minutes. For each of the three short reasoning below, decide whether it is an argument, a mere claim, or an explanation. Write one sentence each, naming the conclusion and the reason where they exist. "Attendance is poor on Mondays because many pupils travel back from their villages on Monday morning." "The school should start the week on Tuesday." "Practical work helps pupils understand science, because it lets them see the idea rather than only hearing it." For the two that are arguments, state the conclusion and the reason in your own words.

(Remember) Name the four basic units of reasoning and state which one a critical thinker spends most time on. (Understand) Explain the difference between a mere claim and an argument in one or two sentences. (Apply) A colleague says, "These pupils cannot read Urdu because the textbook is in English." Is that reasoning an argument, a mere claim, or an explanation? Give one reason for your answer.

The basic units of reasoning are statements, claims, issues and arguments. An argument - a claim plus at least one supporting reason - is the unit critical thinking evaluates. Telling an argument from a mere claim or an explanation lets you ask the question that matters: do the reasons actually support the conclusion?

I can distinguish a statement, a claim, an issue and an argument. I can use a decision path to decide whether a piece of text is an argument. I can explain why an argument gives a critical thinker more to evaluate than a claim.

Take one paragraph from a textbook you are using or from a notice in the staffroom. Identify whether it contains an argument, a mere claim, or an explanation. If it is an argument, write down the conclusion and the reason in your own words.

documents.t: Here is a short piece of reasoning: "Morning assembly should be shortened. The first period after assembly always loses ten minutes, and the term timetable is already too full to spare them." Write a short paragraph (80-120 words) that (a) states whether this is an argument, a claim or an explanation, (b) gives one reason for your classification, and (c) names the conclusion and the reason if it is an argument. Mini-rubric Criterion Levels Classification 0-2: correctly classifies and gives a valid reason / correct classification but weak reason / wrong. Use of scenario evidence 0-3: cites specific words from the text to justify the classification / vague / none. (Analyze: ties the classification to the actual reasoning in the scenario.) Clarity 0:2: paragraph coherent and within word band / unclear or over length.

documents.s: Topic 1.5 - The critical thinker, and the teacher as one

documents.t: A workshop trainer tells a group of teachers in Sukkur that a new reading method "raises results by 30 per cent". Three teachers hear the claim. The first accepts it and plans to adopt the method. The second dismisses it because "these workshops never understand our classrooms". The third asks, "Thirty per cent of what, measured how, compared with which schools, over how long?" None of the three is being rude. But only one of them is treating the claim as something to examine rather than simply to accept or reject. textbook.com.pk textbook.com.pk This topic describes the habits that make someone a critical thinker and shows what those habits look like in a teacher's working day.

A critical thinker is not a different kind of person. They are someone who has made certain habits routine. Bassham et al. (2010) describe them as a set of paired opposites: a critical thinker leans toward the first in each pair and away from the second. Open to evidence rather than wedded to their first view. When new facts arrive, they adjust. Fair to opposing views rather than dismissive. They consider the strongest version of the other side, not a weakened one. Precise rather than vague in the claims they make and accept. "Results improved" is less useful than "punctuation errors fell by a quarter over one term". Willing to say "I don't know" rather than guessing or bluffing. In a staffroom this sounds like, "I have no evidence either way - let us look before we decide." These are habits, not talents. A trainee who is unsure of herself can still ask, "What is the evidence for that?" - and that question is the move that matters.

For a teacher, critical thinking is not an abstract skill. It shows up in three ordinary situations. Evaluating a workshop or training claim. Trainers and resource sellers make strong claims. A critical-thinking teacher treats each claim as something to examine: What is the evidence? Is it relevant to my pupils' age and context? Has it been tested in a setting like mine? This is not cynicism; it is the professional habit of adopting only what is well supported. Reading a textbook or guide critically. A textbook is not wrong by definition, but it is also not above question. A teacher who asks, "Does this example fit my pupils? Is this the only way to teach this idea?" is thinking critically about the material rather than following it mechanically. Handling claims from colleagues. A head teacher's announcement, a senior colleague's advice, a parent's expectation - each may be right, but none is right only because of who said it. A critical-thinking teacher respects the person and still asks whether the reasoning holds. Common misconception. Many trainees arrive believing that "critical thinking is a personality you have or lack rather than a set of standards you apply". The opposite is true. The characteristics of a critical thinker are habits you can practise, and this unit has given you the standards to practise them with. You do not need to become a different person; you need to make a few questions routine.

Work in small groups. About 20 minutes. The claim: "Mind-mapping improves pupils' writing." It reaches a teacher from three sources at the same time: a workshop handout, a page in the textbook, and a senior colleague who says it worked in her class. For each source, write one question a critical-thinking teacher would ask before adopting the idea. As a group, decide which source you would trust most and give one reason drawn from the characteristics of a critical thinker (not "because the person is senior"). Share your decision with another group and compare reasons.
documents.s: Activity: Evaluate three sources of a claim

documents.t: (Remember) Name three characteristics of a critical thinker. (Understand) Explain why "willing to say I don't know" is a characteristic of a critical thinker rather than a weakness. (Apply) A senior teacher says, "Set less homework; my pupils always do well." Which characteristic of a critical thinker would lead you to ask for evidence, and what question would you ask?

The characteristics of a critical thinker - open to evidence, fair to opposing views, precise in claims, willing to say "I don't know" - are habits, not talents. For a teacher they show up in the ordinary work of evaluating workshop claims, reading textbooks critically and handling colleagues' advice on its merits.

I can name and explain at least three characteristics of a critical thinker. I can recognise when I am accepting or rejecting a claim for the wrong reason (the source rather than the evidence). I can ask an evidence-based question of a claim I meet in a workshop, a textbook or a staffroom.
At your next training or staff meeting, write down one claim you hear. Then write the one question a critical-thinking teacher would ask before adopting it. If you feel able, ask the question.
